cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define biodiversity.
cards.back: Biodiversity refers to the sum total of diversity that exists at all levels of biological organisation.
cards.quote: Biodiversity refers to the sum total of diversity that exists at all levels of biological organisation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Biodiversity is the term popularised by the sociobiologist ____
cards.back:
Edward Wilson
Biodiversity is the term popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson
cards.quote: Biodiversity is the term popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three most important levels of biodiversity.
cards.back:
Genetic diversity : A single species might show high diversity at the genetic level over its distributional range.
Species diversity : The diversity at the species level
Ecological diversity : At the ecosystem level
cards.quote: (i) Genetic diversity : A single species might show high diversity at the genetic level over its distributional range. The genetic variation shown by the medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different Himalayan ranges might be in terms of the potency and concentration of the active chemical (reserpine) that the plant produces. India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice, and 1,000 varieties of mango. (ii) Species diversity : The diversity at the species level, for example, the Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats. (iii) Ecological diversity : At the ecosystem level, India, for instance, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, and alpine meadows has a greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which active chemical of Rauwolfia vomitoria varies in potency across Himalayan ranges (genetic diversity)?
cards.back: The genetic variation shown by the medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different Himalayan ranges might be in terms of the potency and concentration of the active chemical (reserpine) that the plant produces.
cards.quote: The genetic variation shown by the medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different Himalayan ranges might be in terms of the potency and concentration of the active chemical (reserpine) that the plant produces.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many genetically different strains of rice and varieties of mango does India have?
cards.back: India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice, and 1,000 varieties of mango.
cards.quote: India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice, and 1,000 varieties of mango.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which has greater amphibian species diversity, the Western Ghats or the Eastern Ghats?
cards.back: the Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats
cards.quote: the Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which has greater ecosystem diversity, India or a Scandinavian country like Norway?
cards.back: India, for instance, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, and alpine meadows has a greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.
cards.quote: India, for instance, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, and alpine meadows has a greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: According to IUCN (2004), how many plant and animal species have been described so far?
cards.back: the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than 1.5 million
cards.quote: the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than 1.5 million

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which ecologist's conservative estimate puts global species diversity at about 7 million?
cards.back: a more conservative and scientifically sound estimate made by Robert May places the global species diversity at about 7 million
cards.quote: a more conservative and scientifically sound estimate made by Robert May places the global species diversity at about 7 million

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What share of recorded species are animals, and what share are plants?
cards.back: More than 70 per cent of all the species recorded are animals, while plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) comprise no more than 22 per cent of the total.
cards.quote: More than 70 per cent of all the species recorded are animals, while plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) comprise no more than 22 per cent of the total.

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which animal group is the most species-rich, and what share of animal species does it make up?
cards.back: Among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total.
cards.quote: Among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total.

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does the number of fungi species compare with fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals combined?
cards.back: The number of fungi species in the world is more than the combined total of the species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.
cards.quote: The number of fungi species in the world is more than the combined total of the species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are there no species estimates for prokaryotes?
cards.back: The problem is that conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species and many species are simply not culturable under laboratory conditions.
cards.quote: The problem is that conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species and many species are simply not culturable under laboratory conditions.

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is India's share of the world's land area and of global species diversity?
cards.back: Although India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, its share of the global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent.
cards.quote: Although India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, its share of the global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent.

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: India is one of how many mega diversity countries of the world?
cards.back: That is what makes our country one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world.
cards.quote: That is what makes our country one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world.

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many plant and animal species have been recorded from India?
cards.back: Nearly 45,000 species of plants and twice as many of animals have been recorded from India.
cards.quote: Nearly 45,000 species of plants and twice as many of animals have been recorded from India.

source.section: How Many Species are there on Earth and How Many in India?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does species diversity change as we move from the equator towards the poles?
cards.back: In general, species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles.
cards.quote: In general, species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the latitudinal range of the tropics, and do they have more or fewer species than temperate areas?
cards.back: With very few exceptions, tropics (latitudinal range of 23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas.
cards.quote: With very few exceptions, tropics (latitudinal range of 23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which rain forest has the greatest biodiversity on earth?
cards.back: The largely tropical Amazonian rain forest in South America has the greatest biodiversity on earth
cards.quote: The largely tropical Amazonian rain forest in South America has the greatest biodiversity on earth

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Give three explanations for the greater species richness of the tropics.
cards.back:
Tropics had more evolutionary time
they provide a relatively constant environment
they receive more solar energy which contributes to greater productivity
cards.quote: Important explanations for the species richness of the tropics are: Tropics had more evolutionary time; they provide a relatively constant environment and, they receive more solar energy which contributes to greater productivity.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who observed that species richness increases with explored area, but only up to a limit?
cards.back: the great German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region species richness increased with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit.
cards.quote: the great German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region species richness increased with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What shape is the relation between species richness and area for a wide variety of taxa?
cards.back: the relation between species richness and area for a wide variety of taxa (angiosperm plants, birds, bats, freshwater fishes) turns out to be a rectangular hyperbola
cards.quote: the relation between species richness and area for a wide variety of taxa (angiosperm plants, birds, bats, freshwater fishes) turns out to be a rectangular hyperbola

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: species-area relationship on a logarithmic scale.
cards.back: log S = log C + Z log A where S= Species richness A= Area Z = slope of the line (regression coefficient) C = Y-intercept
cards.quote: log S = log C + Z log A where S= Species richness A= Area Z = slope of the line (regression coefficient) C = Y-intercept

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the range of Z values for species-area relationships among entire continents?
cards.back: if you analyse the species-area relationships among very large areas like the entire continents, you will find that the slope of the line to be much steeper (Z values in the range of 0.6 to 1.2)
cards.quote: if you analyse the species-area relationships among very large areas like the entire continents, you will find that the slope of the line to be much steeper (Z values in the range of 0.6 to 1.2)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a stable biological community?
cards.back: A stable community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year; it must be either resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances (natural or man-made), and it must also be resistant to invasions by alien species.
cards.quote: A stable community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year; it must be either resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances (natural or man-made), and it must also be resistant to invasions by alien species.

source.section: The importance of Species Diversity to the Ecosystem

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did David Tilman's long-term plot experiments show about species-rich plots?
cards.back: Tilman found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass. He also showed that in his experiments, increased diversity contributed to higher productivity.
cards.quote: Tilman found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass. He also showed that in his experiments, increased diversity contributed to higher productivity.

source.section: The importance of Species Diversity to the Ecosystem

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who proposed the rivet popper hypothesis?
cards.back: used by Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich
cards.quote: used by Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich

source.section: The importance of Species Diversity to the Ecosystem

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the rivet popper hypothesis, what do the airplane and its rivets stand for?
cards.back: In an airplane (ecosystem) all parts are joined together using thousands of rivets (species).
cards.quote: In an airplane (ecosystem) all parts are joined together using thousands of rivets (species).

source.section: The importance of Species Diversity to the Ecosystem

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the rivet popper analogy, what do rivets on the wings stand for?
cards.back: Loss of rivets on the wings (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is obviously a more serious threat to flight safety than loss of a few rivets on the seats or windows inside the plane.
cards.quote: Loss of rivets on the wings (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) is obviously a more serious threat to flight safety than loss of a few rivets on the seats or windows inside the plane.

source.section: The importance of Species Diversity to the Ecosystem

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Some examples of recent extinctions include the ____ (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller’s Sea Cow (Russia)
cards.back: Some examples of recent extinctions include the dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller’s Sea Cow (Russia)
cards.quote: Some examples of recent extinctions include the dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller’s Sea Cow (Russia)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which group appears more vulnerable to extinction, as extinctions across taxa are not random?
cards.back: extinctions across taxa are not random; some groups like amphibians appear to be more vulnerable to extinction
cards.quote: extinctions across taxa are not random; some groups like amphibians appear to be more vulnerable to extinction

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many episodes of mass extinction occurred in the history of life on earth before the present one?
cards.back: there were five episodes of mass extinction of species
cards.quote: there were five episodes of mass extinction of species

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How is the Sixth Extinction different from the previous episodes of mass extinction?
cards.back: The difference is in the rates; the current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in the pre-human times and our activities are responsible for the faster rates.
cards.quote: The difference is in the rates; the current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in the pre-human times and our activities are responsible for the faster rates.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three effects of loss of biodiversity in a region.
cards.back:
decline in plant production
lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought
increased variability in certain ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use, and pest and disease cycles
cards.quote: In general, loss of biodiversity in a region may lead to (a) decline in plant production, (b) lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought and (c) increased variability in certain ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use, and pest and disease cycles.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the sobriquet for the four major causes of biodiversity loss?
cards.back: The Evil Quartet
cards.quote: The Evil Quartet

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the four major causes of biodiversity loss (The Evil Quartet).
cards.back:
habitat (particularly forests) loss and fragmentation
over-exploitation
biological invasions
co-extinctions
cards.quote: The causes of high extinction rates at present include habitat (particularly forests) loss and fragmentation, over-exploitation, biological invasions and co-extinctions.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: ____: This is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction.
cards.back:
Habitat loss and fragmentation
Habitat loss and fragmentation: This is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction.
cards.quote: Habitat loss and fragmentation: This is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What share of the earth’s land surface did tropical rain forests once cover, and what share do they cover now?
cards.back: Once covering more than 14 per cent of the earth's land surface, these rain forests now cover no more than 6 per cent.
cards.quote: Once covering more than 14 per cent of the earth's land surface, these rain forests now cover no more than 6 per cent.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which animals are badly affected when large habitats are broken into small fragments?
cards.back: When large habitats are broken up into small fragments due to various human activities, mammals and birds requiring large territories and certain animals with migratory habits are badly affected, leading to population declines.
cards.quote: When large habitats are broken up into small fragments due to various human activities, mammals and birds requiring large territories and certain animals with migratory habits are badly affected, leading to population declines.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens in alien species invasions?
cards.back: When alien species are introduced unintentionally or deliberately for whatever purpose, some of them turn invasive, and cause decline or extinction of indigenous species.
cards.quote: When alien species are introduced unintentionally or deliberately for whatever purpose, some of them turn invasive, and cause decline or extinction of indigenous species.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which introduced fish caused the extinction of over 200 cichlid species in Lake Victoria?
cards.back: The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria in east Africa led eventually to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in the lake.
cards.quote: The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria in east Africa led eventually to the extinction of an ecologically unique assemblage of more than 200 species of cichlid fish in the lake.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three invasive weed species that NCERT says threaten India's native species.
cards.back:
carrot grass (Parthenium)
Lantana
water hyacinth (Eicchornia)
cards.quote: invasive weed species like carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eicchornia)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which illegally introduced fish threatens India's indigenous catfishes?
cards.back: The recent illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture purposes is posing a threat to the indigenous catfishes in our rivers.
cards.quote: The recent illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture purposes is posing a threat to the indigenous catfishes in our rivers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is co-extinction?
cards.back: When a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct.
cards.quote: When a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Give NCERT's examples of co-extinction.
cards.back: When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also meets the same fate. Another example is the case of a coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism where extinction of one invariably leads to the extinction of the other.
cards.quote: When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites also meets the same fate. Another example is the case of a coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism where extinction of one invariably leads to the extinction of the other.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Into which three categories are the reasons for conserving biodiversity grouped?
cards.back:
narrowly utilitarian
broadly utilitarian
ethical
cards.quote: They can be grouped into three categories: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian, and ethical.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the narrowly utilitarian argument for conserving biodiversity?
cards.back: The narrowly utilitarian arguments for conserving biodiversity are obvious; humans derive countless direct economic benefits from nature
cards.quote: The narrowly utilitarian arguments for conserving biodiversity are obvious; humans derive countless direct economic benefits from nature

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What share of drugs sold worldwide is derived from plants?
cards.back: More than 25 per cent of the drugs currently sold in the market worldwide are derived from plants and 25,000 species of plants contribute to the traditional medicines used by native peoples around the world.
cards.quote: More than 25 per cent of the drugs currently sold in the market worldwide are derived from plants and 25,000 species of plants contribute to the traditional medicines used by native peoples around the world.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is bioprospecting?
cards.back: exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance
cards.quote: exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the broadly utilitarian argument for conserving biodiversity?
cards.back: The broadly utilitarian argument says that biodiversity plays a major role in many ecosystem services that nature provides.
cards.quote: The broadly utilitarian argument says that biodiversity plays a major role in many ecosystem services that nature provides.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What share of the earth's atmospheric oxygen is the Amazon forest estimated to produce?
cards.back: Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere.
cards.quote: Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the ecosystem services through which biodiversity gives indirect benefits.
cards.back:
pollination
pest control
climate moderation
flood control
cards.quote: there are many indirect benefits we receive through ecosystem services such as pollination, pest control, climate moderation and flood control.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the ethical argument for conserving biodiversity?
cards.back: The ethical argument for conserving biodiversity relates to what we owe to millions of plant, animal and microbe species with whom we share this planet.
cards.quote: The ethical argument for conserving biodiversity relates to what we owe to millions of plant, animal and microbe species with whom we share this planet.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the ethical argument say about the value of every species?
cards.back: Philosophically or spiritually, we need to realise that every species has an intrinsic value, even if it may not be of current or any economic value to us.
cards.quote: Philosophically or spiritually, we need to realise that every species has an intrinsic value, even if it may not be of current or any economic value to us.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is in situ (on site) conservation?
cards.back: When we conserve and protect the whole ecosystem, its biodiversity at all levels is protected - we save the entire forest to save the tiger. This approach is called in situ (on site) conservation.
cards.quote: When we conserve and protect the whole ecosystem, its biodiversity at all levels is protected - we save the entire forest to save the tiger. This approach is called in situ (on site) conservation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is ex situ (off site) conservation?
cards.back: In this approach, threatened animals and plants are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in special setting where they can be protected and given special care.
cards.quote: In this approach, threatened animals and plants are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in special setting where they can be protected and given special care.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When is ex situ conservation the desirable approach?
cards.back: when there are situations where an animal or plant is endangered or threatened (organisms facing a very high risk of extinction in the wild in the near future) and needs urgent measures to save it from extinction, ex situ (off site) conservation is the desirable approach
cards.quote: when there are situations where an animal or plant is endangered or threatened (organisms facing a very high risk of extinction in the wild in the near future) and needs urgent measures to save it from extinction, ex situ (off site) conservation is the desirable approach

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are biodiversity hotspots?
cards.back: regions with very high levels of species richness and high degree of endemism (that is, species confined to that region and not found anywhere else)
cards.quote: regions with very high levels of species richness and high degree of endemism (that is, species confined to that region and not found anywhere else)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is endemism?
cards.back: species confined to that region and not found anywhere else
cards.quote: species confined to that region and not found anywhere else

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many biodiversity hotspots are there in the world?
cards.back: Initially 25 biodiversity hotspots were identified but subsequently nine more have been added to the list, bringing the total number of biodiversity hotspots in the world to 34.
cards.quote: Initially 25 biodiversity hotspots were identified but subsequently nine more have been added to the list, bringing the total number of biodiversity hotspots in the world to 34.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three biodiversity hotspots that cover India's rich biodiversity regions.
cards.back:
Western Ghats-Sri Lanka
Himalaya
Indo-Burma
cards.quote: Of these, three (Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Himalaya and Indo-Burma) cover India's rich biodiversity regions.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: By how much could strict protection of the hotspots reduce the ongoing mass extinctions?
cards.back: strict protection of these hotspots could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent
cards.quote: strict protection of these hotspots could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are ecologically unique, biodiversity-rich regions legally protected in India?
cards.back: In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries.
cards.quote: In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are sacred groves?
cards.back: In many cultures, tracts of forest were set aside, and all the trees and wildlife within were venerated and given total protection.
cards.quote: In many cultures, tracts of forest were set aside, and all the trees and wildlife within were venerated and given total protection.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where are sacred groves found in India?
cards.back: Such sacred groves are found in Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh.
cards.quote: Such sacred groves are found in Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What role do the sacred groves of Meghalaya play?
cards.back: In Meghalaya, the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.
cards.quote: In Meghalaya, the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which facilities serve ex situ conservation?
cards.back: Zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks serve this purpose.
cards.quote: Zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks serve this purpose.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the advanced techniques of ex situ conservation.
cards.back:
gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods using cryopreservation techniques
eggs can be fertilised in vitro
plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods
cards.quote: Now gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods using cryopreservation techniques, eggs can be fertilised in vitro, and plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where can seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants be kept for long periods?
cards.back: Seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks.
cards.quote: Seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did the 1992 Rio de Janeiro Convention on Biological Diversity (Earth Summit) call upon all nations to do?
cards.back: held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilisation of its benefits.
cards.quote: held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilisation of its benefits.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did 190 countries pledge at the 2002 World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg?
cards.back: In a follow-up, the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in 2002 in Johannesburg, South Africa, 190 countries pledged their commitment to achieve by 2010, a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss at global, regional and local levels.
cards.quote: In a follow-up, the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in 2002 in Johannesburg, South Africa, 190 countries pledged their commitment to achieve by 2010, a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss at global, regional and local levels.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is totipotency?
cards.back: This capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell/explant is called totipotency.
cards.quote: This capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell/explant is called totipotency.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is an explant?
cards.back: any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube, under sterile conditions in special nutrient media
cards.quote: whole plants could be regenerated from explants, i.e., any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube, under sterile conditions in special nutrient media.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the components the nutrient medium must provide in tissue culture.
cards.back:
a carbon source such as sucrose
inorganic salts
vitamins
amino acids
growth regulators like auxins, cytokinins etc.
cards.quote: the nutrient medium must provide a carbon source such as sucrose and also inorganic salts, vitamins, amino acids and growth regulators like auxins, cytokinins etc.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is micro-propagation?
cards.back: This method of producing thousands of plants through tissue culture is called micro-propagation.
cards.quote: This method of producing thousands of plants through tissue culture is called micro-propagation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are somaclones?
cards.back: genetically identical to the original plant from which they were grown, i.e., they are somaclones
cards.quote: Each of these plants will be genetically identical to the original plant from which they were grown, i.e., they are somaclones.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the ____ (apical and axillary) is free of virus.
cards.back: Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus.
cards.quote: Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are naked protoplasts isolated from plant cells?
cards.back: Scientists have even isolated single cells from plants and after digesting their cell walls have been able to isolate naked protoplasts (surrounded by plasma membranes).
cards.quote: Scientists have even isolated single cells from plants and after digesting their cell walls have been able to isolate naked protoplasts (surrounded by plasma membranes).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How is a somatic hybrid plant obtained from protoplasts?
cards.back: Isolated protoplasts from two different varieties of plants – each having a desirable character – can be fused to get hybrid protoplasts, which can be further grown to form a new plant.
cards.quote: Isolated protoplasts from two different varieties of plants – each having a desirable character – can be fused to get hybrid protoplasts, which can be further grown to form a new plant.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are hybrids formed by fusing protoplasts of two varieties called?
cards.back: somatic hybrids
cards.quote: These hybrids are called somatic hybrids

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which plant resulted from fusing tomato and potato protoplasts?
cards.back: resulting in formation of pomato; unfortunately this plant did not have all the desired combination of characteristics for its commercial utilisation.
cards.quote: resulting in formation of pomato; unfortunately this plant did not have all the desired combination of characteristics for its commercial utilisation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are Genetically Modified Organisms (GMO)?
cards.back: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called Genetically Modified Organisms (GMO).
cards.quote: Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called Genetically Modified Organisms (GMO).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the ways in which genetic modification has been useful in crops.
cards.back:
made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat)
reduced reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops)
helped to reduce post harvest losses
increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants (this prevents early exhaustion of fertility of soil)
enhanced nutritional value of food, e.g., golden rice, i.e., Vitamin 'A' enriched rice
cards.quote: Genetic modification has: (i) made crops more tolerant to abiotic stresses (cold, drought, salt, heat). (ii) reduced reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops). (iii) helped to reduce post harvest losses. (iv) increased efficiency of mineral usage by plants (this prevents early exhaustion of fertility of soil). (v) enhanced nutritional value of food, e.g., golden rice, i.e., Vitamin 'A' enriched rice.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which GM rice is enriched with Vitamin A?
cards.back: golden rice, i.e., Vitamin 'A' enriched rice
cards.quote: enhanced nutritional value of food, e.g., golden rice, i.e., Vitamin 'A' enriched rice

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Bt toxin is produced by a bacterium called ____ (Bt for short).
cards.back:
Bacillus thuringiensis
Bt toxin is produced by a bacterium called Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt for short).
cards.quote: Bt toxin is produced by a bacterium called Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt for short).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does the cloned Bt toxin gene give crops insect resistance?
cards.back: Bt toxin gene has been cloned from the bacteria and been expressed in plants to provide resistance to insects without the need for insecticides; in effect created a bio-pesticide.
cards.quote: Bt toxin gene has been cloned from the bacteria and been expressed in plants to provide resistance to insects without the need for insecticides; in effect created a bio-pesticide.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which insect groups are killed by Bt proteins (with examples)?
cards.back:
lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm)
coleopterans (beetles)
dipterans (flies, mosquitoes)
cards.quote: Some strains of Bacillus thuringiensis produce proteins that kill certain insects such as lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles) and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does Bt toxin kill an insect? (steps in order)
cards.back:
once an insect ingest the inactive toxin
it is converted into an active form of toxin due to the alkaline pH of the gut which solubilise the crystals
The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and create pores
that cause cell swelling and lysis and eventually cause death of the insect
cards.quote: once an insect ingest the inactive toxin, it is converted into an active form of toxin due to the alkaline pH of the gut which solubilise the crystals. The activated toxin binds to the surface of midgut epithelial cells and create pores that cause cell swelling and lysis and eventually cause death of the insect.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why does Bt toxin not kill Bacillus thuringiensis itself?
cards.back: the Bt toxin protein exist as inactive protoxins
cards.quote: the Bt toxin protein exist as inactive protoxins but once an insect ingest the inactive toxin, it is converted into an active form of toxin due to the alkaline pH of the gut which solubilise the crystals.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the Bt toxin gene named?
cards.back: The toxin is coded by a gene cryIAc named cry.
cards.quote: The toxin is coded by a gene cryIAc named cry.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which cry genes control cotton bollworms, and which controls corn borer?
cards.back: There are a number of them, for example, the proteins encoded by the genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworms, that of cryIAb controls corn borer.
cards.quote: There are a number of them, for example, the proteins encoded by the genes cryIAc and cryIIAb control the cotton bollworms, that of cryIAb controls corn borer.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: RNAi takes place in all ____ organisms as a method of cellular defense.
cards.back:
eukaryotic
RNAi takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defense.
cards.quote: RNAi takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defense.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does RNA interference (RNAi) involve?
cards.back: This method involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA (silencing).
cards.quote: This method involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA (silencing).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What can be the source of complementary RNA in RNAi?
cards.back: The source of this complementary RNA could be from an infection by viruses having RNA genomes or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.
cards.quote: The source of this complementary RNA could be from an infection by viruses having RNA genomes or mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which nematode infects tobacco roots, and was controlled using RNAi?
cards.back: A nematode Meloidegyne incognitia infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield.
cards.quote: A nematode Meloidegyne incognitia infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which vector was used to introduce nematode-specific genes into tobacco?
cards.back: Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant
cards.quote: Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes were introduced into the host plant

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How did the introduced DNA silence the nematode mRNA?
cards.back: The introduction of DNA was such that it produced both sense and anti-sense RNA in the host cells. These two RNA's being complementary to each other formed a double stranded (dsRNA) that initiated RNAi and thus, silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode.
cards.quote: The introduction of DNA was such that it produced both sense and anti-sense RNA in the host cells. These two RNA's being complementary to each other formed a double stranded (dsRNA) that initiated RNAi and thus, silenced the specific mRNA of the nematode.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why do recombinant therapeutics not induce unwanted immune responses?
cards.back: the recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses as is common in case of similar products isolated from non-human sources
cards.quote: Further, the recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses as is common in case of similar products isolated from non-human sources.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the structure of insulin?
cards.back: Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains: chain A and chain B, that are linked together by disulphide bridges
cards.quote: Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains: chain A and chain B, that are linked together by disulphide bridges

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: From where was insulin used for diabetes earlier extracted?
cards.back: Insulin used for diabetes was earlier extracted from pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs.
cards.quote: Insulin used for diabetes was earlier extracted from pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What problem did insulin from an animal source cause?
cards.back: Insulin from an animal source, though caused some patients to develop allergy or other types of reactions to the foreign protein.
cards.quote: Insulin from an animal source, though caused some patients to develop allergy or other types of reactions to the foreign protein.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How is insulin synthesised in mammals, and what is the C peptide?
cards.back: In mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone (like a pro-enzyme, the pro-hormone also needs to be processed before it becomes a fully mature and functional hormone) which contains an extra stretch called the C peptide.
cards.quote: In mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone (like a pro-enzyme, the pro-hormone also needs to be processed before it becomes a fully mature and functional hormone) which contains an extra stretch called the C peptide.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens to the C peptide during maturation of insulin?
cards.back: This C peptide is not present in the mature insulin and is removed during maturation into insulin.
cards.quote: This C peptide is not present in the mature insulin and is removed during maturation into insulin.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What was the main challenge in producing insulin using rDNA techniques?
cards.back: The main challenge for production of insulin using rDNA techniques was getting insulin assembled into a mature form.
cards.quote: The main challenge for production of insulin using rDNA techniques was getting insulin assembled into a mature form.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which company produced human insulin chains in E. coli in 1983, and how?
cards.back: In 1983, Eli Lilly an American company prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to A and B, chains of human insulin and introduced them in plasmids of E. coli to produce insulin chains.
cards.quote: In 1983, Eli Lilly an American company prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to A and B, chains of human insulin and introduced them in plasmids of E. coli to produce insulin chains.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How were chains A and B combined to form human insulin?
cards.back: Chains A and B were produced separately, extracted and combined by creating disulfide bonds to form human insulin.
cards.quote: Chains A and B were produced separately, extracted and combined by creating disulfide bonds to form human insulin.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define gene therapy.
cards.back: Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child/embryo.
cards.quote: Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child/embryo.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does correction of a genetic defect in gene therapy involve?
cards.back: Correction of a genetic defect involves delivery of a normal gene into the individual or embryo to take over the function of and compensate for the non-functional gene.
cards.quote: Correction of a genetic defect involves delivery of a normal gene into the individual or embryo to take over the function of and compensate for the non-functional gene.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The first clinical gene therapy was given in ____ to a 4-year old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
cards.back: The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.
cards.quote: The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What causes ADA deficiency?
cards.back: The disorder is caused due to the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase.
cards.quote: The disorder is caused due to the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How can ADA deficiency be treated other than by gene therapy?
cards.back: In some children ADA deficiency can be cured by bone marrow transplantation; in others it can be treated by enzyme replacement therapy, in which functional ADA is given to the patient by injection.
cards.quote: In some children ADA deficiency can be cured by bone marrow transplantation; in others it can be treated by enzyme replacement therapy, in which functional ADA is given to the patient by injection.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Steps of gene therapy for ADA deficiency, in order.
cards.back:
lymphocytes from the blood of the patient are grown in a culture outside the body
A functional ADA cDNA (using a retroviral vector) is then introduced into these lymphocytes
which are subsequently returned to the patient
cards.quote: As a first step towards gene therapy, lymphocytes from the blood of the patient are grown in a culture outside the body. A functional ADA cDNA (using a retroviral vector) is then introduced into these lymphocytes, which are subsequently returned to the patient.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why does a patient of ADA gene therapy need periodic infusions of lymphocytes?
cards.back: However, as these cells are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusion of such genetically engineered lymphocytes.
cards.quote: However, as these cells are not immortal, the patient requires periodic infusion of such genetically engineered lymphocytes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How could ADA deficiency be cured permanently?
cards.back: if the gene isolate from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could be a permanent cure.
cards.quote: if the gene isolate from marrow cells producing ADA is introduced into cells at early embryonic stages, it could be a permanent cure.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the techniques that serve the purpose of early diagnosis.
cards.back:
Recombinant DNA technology
Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR)
Enzyme Linked Immuno-sorbent Assay (ELISA)
cards.quote: Recombinant DNA technology, Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) and Enzyme Linked Immuno-sorbent Assay (ELISA) are some of the techniques that serve the purpose of early diagnosis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How can a very low concentration of a pathogen be detected before symptoms appear?
cards.back: very low concentration of a bacteria or virus (at a time when the symptoms of the disease are not yet visible) can be detected by amplification of their nucleic acid by PCR.
cards.quote: very low concentration of a bacteria or virus (at a time when the symptoms of the disease are not yet visible) can be detected by amplification of their nucleic acid by PCR.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: PCR is now routinely used to detect ____ in suspected AIDS patients.
cards.back:
HIV
PCR is now routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients.
cards.quote: PCR is now routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: PCR is being used to detect what in suspected cancer patients?
cards.back: It is being used to detect mutations in genes in suspected cancer patients too.
cards.quote: It is being used to detect mutations in genes in suspected cancer patients too.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a probe, and how is it used to detect a mutated gene?
cards.back: A single stranded DNA or RNA, tagged with a radioactive molecule (probe) is allowed to hybridise to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells followed by detection using autoradiography.
cards.quote: A single stranded DNA or RNA, tagged with a radioactive molecule (probe) is allowed to hybridise to its complementary DNA in a clone of cells followed by detection using autoradiography.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why does a clone with the mutated gene not appear on the photographic film?
cards.back: The clone having the mutated gene will hence not appear on the photographic film, because the probe will not have complementarity with the mutated gene.
cards.quote: The clone having the mutated gene will hence not appear on the photographic film, because the probe will not have complementarity with the mutated gene.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: ELISA is based on the principle of ____.
cards.back:
antigen-antibody interaction
ELISA is based on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction.
cards.quote: ELISA is based on the principle of antigen-antibody interaction.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How can ELISA detect infection by a pathogen?
cards.back: Infection by pathogen can be detected by the presence of antigens (proteins, glycoproteins, etc.) or by detecting the antibodies synthesised against the pathogen.
cards.quote: Infection by pathogen can be detected by the presence of antigens (proteins, glycoproteins, etc.) or by detecting the antibodies synthesised against the pathogen.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are transgenic animals?
cards.back: Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are known as transgenic animals.
cards.quote: Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are known as transgenic animals.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which animal makes up over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals?
cards.back: Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, although over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.
cards.quote: Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows and fish have been produced, although over 95 per cent of all existing transgenic animals are mice.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Transgenic animals: how are they used to study normal physiology and development?
cards.back: Transgenic animals can be specifically designed to allow the study of how genes are regulated, and how they affect the normal functions of the body and its development
cards.quote: Transgenic animals can be specifically designed to allow the study of how genes are regulated, and how they affect the normal functions of the body and its development

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Transgenic animals: how do they help in the study of disease?
cards.back: These are specially made to serve as models for human diseases so that investigation of new treatments for diseases is made possible.
cards.quote: These are specially made to serve as models for human diseases so that investigation of new treatments for diseases is made possible.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How can transgenic animals be made to produce useful biological products?
cards.back: Transgenic animals that produce useful biological products can be created by the introduction of the portion of DNA (or genes) which codes for a particular product such as human protein
cards.quote: Transgenic animals that produce useful biological products can be created by the introduction of the portion of DNA (or genes) which codes for a particular product such as human protein

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In 1997, the first transgenic cow, ____, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre).
cards.back:
Rosie
In 1997, the first transgenic cow, Rosie, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre).
cards.quote: In 1997, the first transgenic cow, Rosie, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4 grams per litre).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which human protein did the milk of the transgenic cow Rosie contain?
cards.back: The milk contained the human alpha-lactalbumin and was nutritionally a more balanced product for human babies than natural cow-milk.
cards.quote: The milk contained the human alpha-lactalbumin and was nutritionally a more balanced product for human babies than natural cow-milk.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of the ____.
cards.back:
polio vaccine
Transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of the polio vaccine.
cards.quote: Transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of the polio vaccine.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are transgenic animals used for chemical (toxicity) safety testing?
cards.back: Transgenic animals are made that carry genes which make them more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals.
cards.quote: Transgenic animals are made that carry genes which make them more sensitive to toxic substances than non-transgenic animals.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is GEAC, and what does it decide?
cards.back: the Indian Government has set up organisations such as GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee), which will make decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM-organisms for public services.
cards.quote: the Indian Government has set up organisations such as GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee), which will make decisions regarding the validity of GM research and the safety of introducing GM-organisms for public services.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What problem has the use of living organisms for public services created?
cards.back: The modification/usage of living organisms for public services (as food and medicine sources, for example) has also created problems with patents granted for the same.
cards.quote: The modification/usage of living organisms for public services (as food and medicine sources, for example) has also created problems with patents granted for the same.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is there growing public anger about patents on biological resources?
cards.back: There is growing public anger that certain companies are being granted patents for products and technologies that make use of the genetic materials, plants and other biological resources that have long been identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people of a specific region/country.
cards.quote: There is growing public anger that certain companies are being granted patents for products and technologies that make use of the genetic materials, plants and other biological resources that have long been identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people of a specific region/country.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In 1997, an American company got patent rights on ____ through the US Patent and Trademark Office.
cards.back:
Basmati rice
In 1997, an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office.
cards.quote: In 1997, an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through the US Patent and Trademark Office.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How was the patented 'new' Basmati variety actually derived?
cards.back: Indian Basmati was crossed with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed as an invention or a novelty.
cards.quote: Indian Basmati was crossed with semi-dwarf varieties and claimed as an invention or a novelty.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define biopiracy.
cards.back: Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned without compensatory payment.
cards.quote: Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned without compensatory payment.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Industrialised vs developing nations: what is each rich or poor in?
cards.back: Most of the industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. In contrast the developing and the underdeveloped world is rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge related to bio-resources.
cards.quote: Most of the industrialised nations are rich financially but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge. In contrast the developing and the underdeveloped world is rich in biodiversity and traditional knowledge related to bio-resources.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are some nations doing to prevent unauthorised exploitation of bio-resources?
cards.back: Therefore, some nations are developing laws to prevent such unauthorised exploitation of their bio-resources and traditional knowledge.
cards.quote: Therefore, some nations are developing laws to prevent such unauthorised exploitation of their bio-resources and traditional knowledge.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does human insulin made in bacteria compare with natural insulin?
cards.back: Human insulin is made in bacteria yet its structure is absolutely identical to that of the natural molecule.
cards.quote: Human insulin is made in bacteria yet its structure is absolutely identical to that of the natural molecule.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are used as vectors to transfer healthy genes in gene therapy?
cards.back: Viruses that attack their hosts and introduce their genetic material into the host cell as part of their replication cycle are used as vectors to transfer healthy genes or more recently portions of genes.
cards.quote: Viruses that attack their hosts and introduce their genetic material into the host cell as part of their replication cycle are used as vectors to transfer healthy genes or more recently portions of genes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define biotechnology.
cards.back: Biotechnology deals with techniques of using live organisms or enzymes from organisms to produce products and processes useful to humans.
cards.quote: Biotechnology deals with techniques of using live organisms or enzymes from organisms to produce products and processes useful to humans.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define biotechnology (European Federation of Biotechnology, EFB).
cards.back: The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services
cards.quote: The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In what restricted sense is the word biotechnology used today?
cards.back: it is used in a restricted sense today, to refer to such of those processes which use genetically modified organisms to achieve the same on a larger scale.
cards.quote: it is used in a restricted sense today, to refer to such of those processes which use genetically modified organisms to achieve the same on a larger scale.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define genetic engineering.
cards.back: Techniques to alter the chemistry of genetic material (DNA and RNA)
cards.quote: Techniques to alter the chemistry of genetic material (DNA and RNA)
cards.note: Genetic engineering also introduces the altered DNA or RNA into host organisms and so changes the phenotype of the host organism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define bioprocess engineering.
cards.back: Maintenance of sterile (microbial contamination-free) ambience in chemical engineering processes to enable growth of only the desired microbe/eukaryotic cell in large quantities for the manufacture of biotechnological products like antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes, etc.
cards.quote: Maintenance of sterile (microbial contamination-free) ambience in chemical engineering processes to enable growth of only the desired microbe/eukaryotic cell in large quantities for the manufacture of biotechnological products like antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes, etc.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Contrast asexual and sexual reproduction in terms of genetic information.
cards.back: Asexual reproduction preserves the genetic information, while sexual reproduction permits variation.
cards.quote: Asexual reproduction preserves the genetic information, while sexual reproduction permits variation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does genetic engineering overcome the limitation of traditional hybridisation?
cards.back: The techniques of genetic engineering which include creation of recombinant DNA, use of gene cloning and gene transfer, overcome this limitation and allows us to isolate and introduce only one or a set of desirable genes without introducing undesirable genes into the target organism.
cards.quote: The techniques of genetic engineering which include creation of recombinant DNA, use of gene cloning and gene transfer, overcome this limitation and allows us to isolate and introduce only one or a set of desirable genes without introducing undesirable genes into the target organism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In a chromosome there is a specific DNA sequence called the ____, which is responsible for initiating replication.
cards.back: In a chromosome there is a specific DNA sequence called the origin of replication, which is responsible for initiating replication.
cards.quote: In a chromosome there is a specific DNA sequence called the origin of replication, which is responsible for initiating replication.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define cloning.
cards.back: cloning or making multiple identical copies of any template DNA
cards.quote: cloning or making multiple identical copies of any template DNA

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who constructed the first artificial recombinant DNA molecule, and in which year?
cards.back: Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer accomplished this in 1972 by isolating the antibiotic resistance gene by cutting out a piece of DNA from a plasmid which was responsible for conferring antibiotic resistance.
cards.quote: Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer accomplished this in 1972 by isolating the antibiotic resistance gene by cutting out a piece of DNA from a plasmid which was responsible for conferring antibiotic resistance.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The first recombinant DNA linked an antibiotic resistance gene with a plasmid of which bacterium?
cards.back: The construction of the first recombinant DNA emerged from the possibility of linking a gene encoding antibiotic resistance with a native plasmid (autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA) of Salmonella typhimurium.
cards.quote: The construction of the first recombinant DNA emerged from the possibility of linking a gene encoding antibiotic resistance with a native plasmid (autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA) of Salmonella typhimurium.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define a plasmid.
cards.back: plasmid (autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA)
cards.quote: plasmid (autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the function of the enzyme DNA ligase?
cards.back: The linking of antibiotic resistance gene with the plasmid vector became possible with the enzyme DNA ligase, which acts on cut DNA molecules and joins their ends.
cards.quote: The linking of antibiotic resistance gene with the plasmid vector became possible with the enzyme DNA ligase, which acts on cut DNA molecules and joins their ends.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define recombinant DNA.
cards.back: This makes a new combination of circular autonomously replicating DNA created in vitro and is known as recombinant DNA.
cards.quote: This makes a new combination of circular autonomously replicating DNA created in vitro and is known as recombinant DNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism, in order.
cards.back:
(i) identification of DNA with desirable genes
(ii) introduction of the identified DNA into the host
(iii) maintenance of introduced DNA in the host and transfer of the DNA to its progeny
cards.quote: there are three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism -- (i) identification of DNA with desirable genes; (ii) introduction of the identified DNA into the host; (iii) maintenance of introduced DNA in the host and transfer of the DNA to its progeny.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the key tools of recombinant DNA technology.
cards.back:
restriction enzymes
polymerase enzymes
ligases
vectors
the host organism
cards.quote: genetic engineering or recombinant DNA technology can be accomplished only if we have the key tools, i.e., restriction enzymes, polymerase enzymes, ligases, vectors and the host organism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In 1963 two enzymes restricting phage growth in E. coli were isolated. What did each do?
cards.back: One of these added methyl groups to DNA, while the other cut DNA. The later was called restriction endonuclease.
cards.quote: One of these added methyl groups to DNA, while the other cut DNA. The later was called restriction endonuclease.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which was the first restriction endonuclease isolated and characterised?
cards.back: The first restriction endonuclease Hind II, whose functioning depended on a specific DNA nucleotide sequence was isolated and characterised five years later.
cards.quote: The first restriction endonuclease Hind II, whose functioning depended on a specific DNA nucleotide sequence was isolated and characterised five years later.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Hind II always cut DNA molecules at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of ____.
cards.back: Hind II always cut DNA molecules at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of six base pairs.
cards.quote: Hind II always cut DNA molecules at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of six base pairs.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are restriction enzymes named? Explain with EcoRI.
cards.back: the first letter of the name comes from the genus and the second two letters come from the species of the prokaryotic cell from which they were isolated, e.g., EcoRI comes from Escherichia coli RY 13.
cards.quote: the first letter of the name comes from the genus and the second two letters come from the species of the prokaryotic cell from which they were isolated, e.g., EcoRI comes from Escherichia coli RY 13.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In a restriction enzyme name, what do the Roman numbers following the name indicate?
cards.back: Roman numbers following the names indicate the order in which the enzymes were isolated from that strain of bacteria.
cards.quote: Roman numbers following the names indicate the order in which the enzymes were isolated from that strain of bacteria.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of nucleases.
cards.back:
Exonucleases
Endonucleases
cards.quote: Restriction enzymes belong to a larger class of enzymes called nucleases. These are of two kinds; exonucleases and endonucleases.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Exonucleases vs endonucleases: the difference in action.
cards.back: Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA whereas, endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA.
cards.quote: Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA whereas, endonucleases make cuts at specific positions within the DNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where does a restriction endonuclease cut once it finds its recognition sequence?
cards.back: Once it finds its specific recognition sequence, it will bind to the DNA and cut each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar-phosphate backbones
cards.quote: Once it finds its specific recognition sequence, it will bind to the DNA and cut each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar-phosphate backbones

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a palindrome in DNA?
cards.back: the palindrome in DNA is a sequence of base pairs that reads same on the two strands
cards.quote: the palindrome in DNA is a sequence of base pairs that reads same on the two strands
cards.note: It reads the same on both strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where do restriction enzymes cut a palindrome site, and what does this leave?
cards.back: Restriction enzymes cut the strand of DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but between the same two bases on the opposite strands. This leaves single stranded portions at the ends.
cards.quote: Restriction enzymes cut the strand of DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but between the same two bases on the opposite strands. This leaves single stranded portions at the ends.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are sticky ends, and why are they so named?
cards.back: There are overhanging stretches called sticky ends on each strand (Figure 9.1). These are named so because they form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts.
cards.quote: There are overhanging stretches called sticky ends on each strand (Figure 9.1). These are named so because they form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why does the stickiness of the ends matter in genetic engineering?
cards.back: This stickiness of the ends facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase.
cards.quote: This stickiness of the ends facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens to DNA fragments cut by the same restriction enzyme?
cards.back: When cut by the same restriction enzyme, the resultant DNA fragments have the same kind of sticky-ends and, these can be joined together (end-to-end) using DNA ligases
cards.quote: When cut by the same restriction enzyme, the resultant DNA fragments have the same kind of sticky-ends and, these can be joined together (end-to-end) using DNA ligases

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why must the vector and the source DNA be cut with the same restriction enzyme?
cards.back: normally, unless one cuts the vector and the source DNA with the same restriction enzyme, the recombinant vector molecule cannot be created.
cards.quote: normally, unless one cuts the vector and the source DNA with the same restriction enzyme, the recombinant vector molecule cannot be created.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which technique separates the DNA fragments produced by restriction endonucleases?
cards.back: These fragments can be separated by a technique known as gel electrophoresis.
cards.quote: These fragments can be separated by a technique known as gel electrophoresis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Towards which electrode do DNA fragments move in gel electrophoresis, and why?
cards.back: Since DNA fragments are negatively charged molecules they can be separated by forcing them to move towards the anode under an electric field through a medium/matrix.
cards.quote: Since DNA fragments are negatively charged molecules they can be separated by forcing them to move towards the anode under an electric field through a medium/matrix.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which matrix is most commonly used in gel electrophoresis, and what is it?
cards.back: Nowadays the most commonly used matrix is agarose which is a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds.
cards.quote: Nowadays the most commonly used matrix is agarose which is a natural polymer extracted from sea weeds.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How do DNA fragments separate in an agarose gel, and which move farthest?
cards.back: The DNA fragments separate (resolve) according to their size through sieving effect provided by the agarose gel. Hence, the smaller the fragment size, the farther it moves.
cards.quote: The DNA fragments separate (resolve) according to their size through sieving effect provided by the agarose gel. Hence, the smaller the fragment size, the farther it moves.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are separated DNA fragments visualised in a gel?
cards.back: The separated DNA fragments can be visualised only after staining the DNA with a compound known as ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation
cards.quote: The separated DNA fragments can be visualised only after staining the DNA with a compound known as ethidium bromide followed by exposure to UV radiation

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the step of extracting separated DNA bands from the cut-out gel piece called?
cards.back: extracted from the gel piece. This step is known as elution.
cards.quote: extracted from the gel piece. This step is known as elution.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which two kinds of DNA replicate in bacterial cells independent of chromosomal DNA control?
cards.back: plasmids and bacteriophages have the ability to replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of chromosomal DNA.
cards.quote: plasmids and bacteriophages have the ability to replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of chromosomal DNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are the vectors used at present engineered?
cards.back: Vectors used at present, are engineered in such a way that they help easy linking of foreign DNA and selection of recombinants from non-recombinants.
cards.quote: Vectors used at present, are engineered in such a way that they help easy linking of foreign DNA and selection of recombinants from non-recombinants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the origin of replication (ori) in a vector?
cards.back: This is a sequence from where replication starts and any piece of DNA when linked to this sequence can be made to replicate within the host cells.
cards.quote: This is a sequence from where replication starts and any piece of DNA when linked to this sequence can be made to replicate within the host cells.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the ori sequence of a vector control?
cards.back: This sequence is also responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA.
cards.quote: This sequence is also responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the role of a selectable marker in a vector?
cards.back: the vector requires a selectable marker, which helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants.
cards.quote: the vector requires a selectable marker, which helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define transformation.
cards.back: Transformation is a procedure through which a piece of DNA is introduced in a host bacterium
cards.quote: Transformation is a procedure through which a piece of DNA is introduced in a host bacterium

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the antibiotic resistance genes used as selectable markers for E. coli.
cards.back:
ampicillin
chloramphenicol
tetracycline
kanamycin
cards.quote: Normally, the genes encoding resistance to antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin, etc., are considered useful selectable markers for E. coli.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What recognition-site feature must a vector have for cloning?
cards.back: the vector needs to have very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes.
cards.quote: the vector needs to have very few, preferably single, recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are several recognition sites for one enzyme in a vector a problem?
cards.back: Presence of more than one recognition sites within the vector will generate several fragments, which will complicate the gene cloning
cards.quote: Presence of more than one recognition sites within the vector will generate several fragments, which will complicate the gene cloning

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In pBR322, what happens to tetracycline resistance when foreign DNA is ligated at the BamH I site?
cards.back: The recombinant plasmids will lose tetracycline resistance due to insertion of foreign DNA but can still be selected out from non-recombinant ones by plating the transformants on ampicillin
cards.quote: The recombinant plasmids will lose tetracycline resistance due to insertion of foreign DNA but can still be selected out from non-recombinant ones by plating the transformants on ampicillin

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the pBR322 selection, where do recombinants and non-recombinants grow?
cards.back: The recombinants will grow in ampicillin containing medium but not on that containing tetracycline. But, non-recombinants will grow on the medium containing both the antibiotics.
cards.quote: The recombinants will grow in ampicillin containing medium but not on that containing tetracycline. But, non-recombinants will grow on the medium containing both the antibiotics.

cards.subject: biology
