cards.front: What is insertional inactivation (in the β-galactosidase marker)?
cards.back: a recombinant DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of an enzyme, β-galactosidase. This results into inactivation of the gene for synthesis of this enzyme, which is referred to as insertional inactivation.
cards.quote: a recombinant DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of an enzyme, β-galactosidase. This results into inactivation of the gene for synthesis of this enzyme, which is referred to as insertional inactivation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: With a chromogenic substrate, which colonies are blue and which are recombinant?
cards.back: The presence of a chromogenic substrate gives blue coloured colonies if the plasmid in the bacteria does not have an insert. Presence of insert results into insertional inactivation of the β-galactosidase gene and the colonies do not produce any colour, these are identified as recombinant colonies.
cards.quote: The presence of a chromogenic substrate gives blue coloured colonies if the plasmid in the bacteria does not have an insert. Presence of insert results into insertional inactivation of the β-galactosidase gene and the colonies do not produce any colour, these are identified as recombinant colonies.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Agrobacterium tumifaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as ____
cards.back: Agrobacterium tumifaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as T-DNA
cards.quote: Agrobacterium tumifaciens, a pathogen of several dicot plants is able to deliver a piece of DNA known as T-DNA

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which plasmid of Agrobacterium tumifaciens has been modified into a cloning vector for plants?
cards.back: The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumifaciens has now been modified into a cloning vector which is no more pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants.
cards.quote: The tumor inducing (Ti) plasmid of Agrobacterium tumifaciens has now been modified into a cloning vector which is no more pathogenic to the plants but is still able to use the mechanisms to deliver genes of our interest into a variety of plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which disarmed viruses are used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells?
cards.back: Similarly, retroviruses have also been disarmed and are now used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells.
cards.quote: Similarly, retroviruses have also been disarmed and are now used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why can DNA not pass through cell membranes?
cards.back: Since DNA is a hydrophilic molecule, it cannot pass through cell membranes.
cards.quote: Since DNA is a hydrophilic molecule, it cannot pass through cell membranes.

source.section: Competent Host (For Transformation with Recombinant DNA)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are bacterial cells made competent to take up DNA?
cards.back: This is done by treating them with a specific concentration of a divalent cation, such as calcium
cards.quote: This is done by treating them with a specific concentration of a divalent cation, such as calcium

source.section: Competent Host (For Transformation with Recombinant DNA)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Besides the heat-shock treatment, name the three methods of introducing alien DNA into host cells.
cards.back:
In a method known as micro-injection, recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell.
In another method, suitable for plants, cells are bombarded with high velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA in a method known as biolistics or gene gun.
And the last method uses ‘disarmed pathogen’ vectors, which when allowed to infect the cell, transfer the recombinant DNA into the host.
cards.quote: In a method known as micro-injection, recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell. In another method, suitable for plants, cells are bombarded with high velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA in a method known as biolistics or gene gun. And the last method uses ‘disarmed pathogen’ vectors, which when allowed to infect the cell, transfer the recombinant DNA into the host.

source.section: Competent Host (For Transformation with Recombinant DNA)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Steps in recombinant DNA technology, in order.
cards.back:
isolation of DNA
fragmentation of DNA by restriction endonucleases
isolation of a desired DNA fragment
ligation of the DNA fragment into a vector
transferring the recombinant DNA into the host
culturing the host cells in a medium at large scale
extraction of the desired product
cards.quote: Recombinant DNA technology involves several steps in specific sequence such as isolation of DNA, fragmentation of DNA by restriction endonucleases, isolation of a desired DNA fragment, ligation of the DNA fragment into a vector, transferring the recombinant DNA into the host, culturing the host cells in a medium at large scale and extraction of the desired product.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why must DNA be in pure form before cutting with restriction enzymes?
cards.back: In order to cut the DNA with restriction enzymes, it needs to be in pure form, free from other macro-molecules.
cards.quote: In order to cut the DNA with restriction enzymes, it needs to be in pure form, free from other macro-molecules.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the enzymes used to break open cells to release DNA, and the cells each acts on.
cards.back:
lysozyme (bacteria)
cellulase (plant cells)
chitinase (fungus)
cards.quote: lysozyme (bacteria), cellulase (plant cells), chitinase (fungus)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which enzymes remove RNA and proteins during DNA isolation?
cards.back: treatment with ribonuclease whereas proteins can be removed by treatment with protease
cards.quote: treatment with ribonuclease whereas proteins can be removed by treatment with protease

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What precipitates purified DNA out of the suspension?
cards.back: purified DNA ultimately precipitates out after the addition of chilled ethanol.
cards.quote: purified DNA ultimately precipitates out after the addition of chilled ethanol.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is used to check the progression of a restriction enzyme digestion?
cards.back: Agarose gel electrophoresis is employed to check the progression of a restriction enzyme digestion.
cards.quote: Agarose gel electrophoresis is employed to check the progression of a restriction enzyme digestion.

source.section: Cutting of DNA at Specific Locations

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How is recombinant DNA prepared after cutting the source DNA and the vector?
cards.back: the cut out gene of interest from the source DNA and the cut vector with space are mixed and ligase is added. This results in the preparation of recombinant DNA.
cards.quote: the cut out gene of interest from the source DNA and the cut vector with space are mixed and ligase is added. This results in the preparation of recombinant DNA.

source.section: Cutting of DNA at Specific Locations

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: PCR stands for ____.
cards.back: PCR stands for Polymerase Chain Reaction.
cards.quote: PCR stands for Polymerase Chain Reaction.

source.section: Amplification of Gene of Interest using PCR

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does PCR do?
cards.back: multiple copies of the gene (or DNA) of interest is synthesised in vitro
cards.quote: multiple copies of the gene (or DNA) of interest is synthesised in vitro

source.section: Amplification of Gene of Interest using PCR

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are primers in PCR?
cards.back: primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides that are complementary to the regions of DNA)
cards.quote: primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides that are complementary to the regions of DNA)

source.section: Amplification of Gene of Interest using PCR

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In PCR, what does the enzyme DNA polymerase do with the primers?
cards.back:
It extends the primers.
The enzyme extends the primers using the nucleotides provided in the reaction and the genomic DNA as template.
cards.quote: The enzyme extends the primers using the nucleotides provided in the reaction and the genomic DNA as template.

source.section: Amplification of Gene of Interest using PCR

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Steps in each PCR cycle, in order.
cards.back:
(i) Denaturation
(ii) Primer annealing
(iii) Extension of primers
cards.quote: Each cycle has three steps: (i) Denaturation; (ii) Primer annealing; and (iii) Extension of primers

source.section: Amplification of Gene of Interest using PCR

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which DNA polymerase is used in PCR, and from which bacterium is it isolated?
cards.back: Such repeated amplification is achieved by the use of a thermostable DNA polymerase (isolated from a bacterium, Thermus aquaticus), which remain active during the high temperature induced denaturation of double stranded DNA.
cards.quote: Such repeated amplification is achieved by the use of a thermostable DNA polymerase (isolated from a bacterium, Thermus aquaticus), which remain active during the high temperature induced denaturation of double stranded DNA.

source.section: Amplification of Gene of Interest using PCR

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens when transformed E. coli cells are spread on agar plates containing ampicillin?
cards.back: If we spread the transformed cells on agar plates containing ampicillin, only transformants will grow, untransformed recipient cells will die.
cards.quote: If we spread the transformed cells on agar plates containing ampicillin, only transformants will grow, untransformed recipient cells will die.

source.section: Insertion of Recombinant DNA into the Host Cell/Organism

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: If any protein encoding gene is expressed in a heterologous host, it is called a ____.
cards.back: If any protein encoding gene is expressed in a heterologous host, it is called a recombinant protein.
cards.quote: If any protein encoding gene is expressed in a heterologous host, it is called a recombinant protein.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In a continuous culture system, how is the medium handled?
cards.back: wherein the used medium is drained out from one side while fresh medium is added from the other
cards.quote: wherein the used medium is drained out from one side while fresh medium is added from the other

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is continuous culture used for producing a desired protein?
cards.back: This type of culturing method produces a larger biomass leading to higher yields of desired protein.
cards.quote: This type of culturing method produces a larger biomass leading to higher yields of desired protein.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a bioreactor?
cards.back: bioreactors can be thought of as vessels in which raw materials are biologically converted into specific products, individual enzymes, etc., using microbial plant, animal or human cells.
cards.quote: bioreactors can be thought of as vessels in which raw materials are biologically converted into specific products, individual enzymes, etc., using microbial plant, animal or human cells.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the optimum growth conditions a bioreactor provides.
cards.back:
temperature
pH
substrate
salts
vitamins
oxygen
cards.quote: A bioreactor provides the optimal conditions for achieving the desired product by providing optimum growth conditions (temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins, oxygen).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which type of bioreactor is the most commonly used?
cards.back: The most commonly used bioreactors are of stirring type
cards.quote: The most commonly used bioreactors are of stirring type

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the shape of a stirred-tank reactor, and why?
cards.back: A stirred-tank reactor is usually cylindrical or with a curved base to facilitate the mixing of the reactor contents.
cards.quote: A stirred-tank reactor is usually cylindrical or with a curved base to facilitate the mixing of the reactor contents.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the function of the stirrer in a stirred-tank bioreactor?
cards.back: The stirrer facilitates even mixing and oxygen availability throughout the bioreactor.
cards.quote: The stirrer facilitates even mixing and oxygen availability throughout the bioreactor.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the systems a stirred-tank bioreactor has.
cards.back:
agitator system
oxygen delivery system
foam control system
temperature control system
pH control system
sampling ports
cards.quote: the bioreactor has an agitator system, an oxygen delivery system and a foam control system, a temperature control system, pH control system and sampling ports so that small volumes of the culture can be withdrawn periodically.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define downstream processing.
cards.back: The processes include separation and purification, which are collectively referred to as downstream processing.
cards.quote: The processes include separation and purification, which are collectively referred to as downstream processing.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What must a product undergo after downstream processing before marketing?
cards.back: The product has to be formulated with suitable preservatives. Such formulation has to undergo thorough clinical trials as in case of drugs. Strict quality control testing for each product is also required.
cards.quote: The product has to be formulated with suitable preservatives. Such formulation has to undergo thorough clinical trials as in case of drugs. Strict quality control testing for each product is also required.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the key process of altering the chemistry of DNA and constructing recombinant DNA called?
cards.back: This key process is called recombinant DNA technology or genetic engineering.
cards.quote: This key process is called recombinant DNA technology or genetic engineering.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of ecosystem (the two basic categories).
cards.back:
Terrestrial
Aquatic
cards.quote: it is convenient to divide it into two basic categories, namely terrestrial and aquatic.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which are mentioned as man-made ecosystems?
cards.back: Crop fields and an aquarium may also be considered as man-made ecosystems.
cards.quote: Crop fields and an aquarium may also be considered as man-made ecosystems.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the species composition of an ecosystem?
cards.back: Identification and enumeration of plant and animal species of an ecosystem gives its species composition.
cards.quote: Identification and enumeration of plant and animal species of an ecosystem gives its species composition.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define stratification.
cards.back: Vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels is called stratification.
cards.quote: Vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels is called stratification.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In stratification of a forest, which plants occupy the top, second and bottom layers?
cards.back: For example, trees occupy top vertical strata or layer of a forest, shrubs the second and herbs and grasses occupy the bottom layers.
cards.quote: For example, trees occupy top vertical strata or layer of a forest, shrubs the second and herbs and grasses occupy the bottom layers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the four aspects in which the components of the ecosystem function as a unit.
cards.back:
Productivity
Decomposition
Energy flow
Nutrient cycling
cards.quote: (i) Productivity; (ii) Decomposition; (iii) Energy flow; and (iv) Nutrient cycling.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which are the autotrophic components of a pond ecosystem?
cards.back: The autotrophic components include the phytoplankton, some algae and the floating, submerged and marginal plants found at the edges.
cards.quote: The autotrophic components include the phytoplankton, some algae and the floating, submerged and marginal plants found at the edges.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which organisms represent the consumers in a pond ecosystem?
cards.back: The consumers are represented by the zooplankton, the free swimming and bottom dwelling forms.
cards.quote: The consumers are represented by the zooplankton, the free swimming and bottom dwelling forms.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which organisms are the decomposers of a pond ecosystem?
cards.back: The decomposers are the fungi, bacteria and flagellates especially abundant in the bottom of the pond.
cards.quote: The decomposers are the fungi, bacteria and flagellates especially abundant in the bottom of the pond.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define primary production.
cards.back: Primary production is defined as the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis.
cards.quote: Primary production is defined as the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is productivity?
cards.back: The rate of biomass production is called productivity.
cards.quote: The rate of biomass production is called productivity.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Primary productivity can be divided into which two types?
cards.back:
Gross primary productivity (GPP)
Net primary productivity (NPP)
cards.quote: It can be divided into gross primary productivity (GPP) and net primary productivity (NPP).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define gross primary productivity (GPP).
cards.back: Gross primary productivity of an ecosystem is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis.
cards.quote: Gross primary productivity of an ecosystem is the rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: A considerable amount of GPP is utilised by plants in ____.
cards.back: A considerable amount of GPP is utilised by plants in respiration.
cards.quote: A considerable amount of GPP is utilised by plants in respiration.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: net primary productivity (NPP).
cards.back:
Gross primary productivity minus respiration losses (R), is the net primary productivity (NPP).
GPP – R = NPP
cards.quote: Gross primary productivity minus respiration losses (R), is the net primary productivity (NPP). GPP – R = NPP

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: For whom is net primary productivity the available biomass?
cards.back: Net primary productivity is the available biomass for the consumption to heterotrophs (herbiviores and decomposers).
cards.quote: Net primary productivity is the available biomass for the consumption to heterotrophs (herbiviores and decomposers).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define secondary productivity.
cards.back: Secondary productivity is defined as the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.
cards.quote: Secondary productivity is defined as the rate of formation of new organic matter by consumers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Besides plant species, what does primary productivity depend on?
cards.back: It also depends on a variety of environmental factors, availability of nutrients and photosynthetic capacity of plants.
cards.quote: It also depends on a variety of environmental factors, availability of nutrients and photosynthetic capacity of plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is decomposition?
cards.back: decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients and the process is called decomposition.
cards.quote: decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients and the process is called decomposition.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is detritus?
cards.back: Dead plant remains such as leaves, bark, flowers and dead remains of animals, including fecal matter, constitute detritus, which is the raw material for decomposition.
cards.quote: Dead plant remains such as leaves, bark, flowers and dead remains of animals, including fecal matter, constitute detritus, which is the raw material for decomposition.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the important steps in the process of decomposition.
cards.back:
Fragmentation
Leaching
Catabolism
Humification
Mineralisation
cards.quote: The important steps in the process of decomposition are fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is fragmentation in decomposition?
cards.back: Detritivores (e.g., earthworm) break down detritus into smaller particles. This process is called fragmentation.
cards.quote: Detritivores (e.g., earthworm) break down detritus into smaller particles. This process is called fragmentation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens in leaching?
cards.back: By the process of leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.
cards.quote: By the process of leaching, water-soluble inorganic nutrients go down into the soil horizon and get precipitated as unavailable salts.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is catabolism in decomposition?
cards.back: Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. This process is called as catabolism.
cards.quote: Bacterial and fungal enzymes degrade detritus into simpler inorganic substances. This process is called as catabolism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Do the steps of decomposition operate one after another or together?
cards.back: It is important to note that all the above steps in decomposition operate simultaneously on the detritus
cards.quote: It is important to note that all the above steps in decomposition operate simultaneously on the detritus

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is humus?
cards.back: a dark coloured amorphous substance called humus that is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition at an extremely slow rate.
cards.quote: a dark coloured amorphous substance called humus that is highly resistant to microbial action and undergoes decomposition at an extremely slow rate.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What property of humus lets it serve as a reservoir of nutrients?
cards.back: Being colloidal in nature it serves as a reservoir of nutrients.
cards.quote: Being colloidal in nature it serves as a reservoir of nutrients.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The humus is further degraded by some microbes and release of inorganic nutrients occur by the process known as ____.
cards.back: The humus is further degraded by some microbes and release of inorganic nutrients occur by the process known as mineralisation.
cards.quote: The humus is further degraded by some microbes and release of inorganic nutrients occur by the process known as mineralisation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Decomposition is largely an ____-requiring process.
cards.back: Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process.
cards.quote: Decomposition is largely an oxygen-requiring process.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What controls the rate of decomposition?
cards.back: The rate of decomposition is controlled by chemical composition of detritus and climatic factors.
cards.quote: The rate of decomposition is controlled by chemical composition of detritus and climatic factors.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Decomposition rate: detritus rich in lignin and chitin vs rich in nitrogen and sugars.
cards.back: In a particular climatic condition, decomposition rate is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quicker, if detritus is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars.
cards.quote: In a particular climatic condition, decomposition rate is slower if detritus is rich in lignin and chitin, and quicker, if detritus is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble substances like sugars.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which are the most important climatic factors regulating decomposition?
cards.back: Temperature and soil moisture are the most important climatic factors that regulate decomposition through their effects on the activities of soil microbes.
cards.quote: Temperature and soil moisture are the most important climatic factors that regulate decomposition through their effects on the activities of soil microbes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which conditions favour decomposition and which inhibit it?
cards.back: Warm and moist environment favour decomposition whereas low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition resulting in build up of organic materials.
cards.quote: Warm and moist environment favour decomposition whereas low temperature and anaerobiosis inhibit decomposition resulting in build up of organic materials.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which ecosystem is the exception to the sun being the source of energy?
cards.back: Except for the deep sea hydro-thermal ecosystem, sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth.
cards.quote: Except for the deep sea hydro-thermal ecosystem, sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Of the incident solar radiation less than ____ per cent of it is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).
cards.back: Of the incident solar radiation less than 50 per cent of it is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).
cards.quote: Of the incident solar radiation less than 50 per cent of it is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Plants capture only ____ per cent of the PAR and this small amount of energy sustains the entire living world.
cards.back: Plants capture only 2-10 per cent of the PAR and this small amount of energy sustains the entire living world.
cards.quote: Plants capture only 2-10 per cent of the PAR and this small amount of energy sustains the entire living world.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: There is ____ movement of energy towards the higher trophic levels and its dissipation and loss as heat to the environment.
cards.back: There is unidirectional movement of energy towards the higher trophic levels and its dissipation and loss as heat to the environment.
cards.quote: There is unidirectional movement of energy towards the higher trophic levels and its dissipation and loss as heat to the environment.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The green plant in the ecosystem are called ____.
cards.back: The green plant in the ecosystem are called producers.
cards.quote: The green plant in the ecosystem are called producers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who are the major producers in a terrestrial ecosystem?
cards.back: In a terrestrial ecosystem, major producers are herbaceous and woody plants.
cards.quote: In a terrestrial ecosystem, major producers are herbaceous and woody plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who are the producers in an aquatic ecosystem?
cards.back: Likewise, producers in an aquatic ecosystem are various species like phytoplankton, algae and higher plants.
cards.quote: Likewise, producers in an aquatic ecosystem are various species like phytoplankton, algae and higher plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Death of organism is the beginning of the ____ food chain/web.
cards.back: Death of organism is the beginning of the detritus food chain/web.
cards.quote: Death of organism is the beginning of the detritus food chain/web.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who are consumers?
cards.back: All animals depend on plants (directly or indirectly) for their food needs. They are hence called consumers and also heterotrophs.
cards.quote: All animals depend on plants (directly or indirectly) for their food needs. They are hence called consumers and also heterotrophs.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who are primary and secondary consumers?
cards.back: If they feed on the producers, the plants, they are called primary consumers, and if the animals eat other animals which in turn eat the plants (or their produce) they are called secondary consumers.
cards.quote: If they feed on the producers, the plants, they are called primary consumers, and if the animals eat other animals which in turn eat the plants (or their produce) they are called secondary consumers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Obviously the primary consumers will be ____.
cards.back: Obviously the primary consumers will be herbivores.
cards.quote: Obviously the primary consumers will be herbivores.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the consumers that feed on herbivores called?
cards.back: The consumers that feed on these herbivores are carnivores, or more correctly primary carnivores (though secondary consumers).
cards.quote: The consumers that feed on these herbivores are carnivores, or more correctly primary carnivores (though secondary consumers).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the animals that depend on the primary carnivores for food labelled?
cards.back:
Secondary carnivores.
Those animals that depend on the primary carnivores for food are labelled secondary carnivores.
cards.quote: Those animals that depend on the primary carnivores for food are labelled secondary carnivores.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where does the detritus food chain (DFC) begin?
cards.back: The detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter.
cards.quote: The detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the detritus food chain made up of?
cards.back: It is made up of decomposers which are heterotrophic organisms, mainly fungi and bacteria.
cards.quote: It is made up of decomposers which are heterotrophic organisms, mainly fungi and bacteria.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are decomposers also known as?
cards.back: These are also known as saprotrophs
cards.quote: These are also known as saprotrophs

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How do decomposers obtain their nutrients from dead matter?
cards.back: Decomposers secrete digestive enzymes that breakdown dead and waste materials into simple, inorganic materials, which are subsequently absorbed by them.
cards.quote: Decomposers secrete digestive enzymes that breakdown dead and waste materials into simple, inorganic materials, which are subsequently absorbed by them.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: GFC vs DFC: the major energy conduit in aquatic and in terrestrial ecosystems.
cards.back: In an aquatic ecosystem, GFC is the major conduit for energy flow. As against this, in a terrestrial ecosystem, a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain than through the GFC.
cards.quote: In an aquatic ecosystem, GFC is the major conduit for energy flow. As against this, in a terrestrial ecosystem, a much larger fraction of energy flows through the detritus food chain than through the GFC.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a food web?
cards.back: Detritus food chain may be connected with the grazing food chain at some levels: some of the organisms of DFC are prey to the GFC animals, and in a natural ecosystem, some animals like cockroaches, crows, etc., are omnivores. These natural interconnection of food chains make it a food web.
cards.quote: Detritus food chain may be connected with the grazing food chain at some levels: some of the organisms of DFC are prey to the GFC animals, and in a natural ecosystem, some animals like cockroaches, crows, etc., are omnivores. These natural interconnection of food chains make it a food web.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a trophic level?
cards.back: Based on the source of their nutrition or food, organisms occupy a specific place in the food chain that is known as their trophic level.
cards.quote: Based on the source of their nutrition or food, organisms occupy a specific place in the food chain that is known as their trophic level.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which organisms belong to the first, second and third trophic levels?
cards.back: Producers belong to the first trophic level, herbivores (primary consumer) to the second and carnivores (secondary consumer) to the third
cards.quote: Producers belong to the first trophic level, herbivores (primary consumer) to the second and carnivores (secondary consumer) to the third

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does the amount of energy change at successive trophic levels?
cards.back: The important point to note is that the amount of energy decreases at successive trophic levels.
cards.quote: The important point to note is that the amount of energy decreases at successive trophic levels.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the standing crop?
cards.back: Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time called as the standing crop.
cards.quote: Each trophic level has a certain mass of living material at a particular time called as the standing crop.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How is the standing crop measured?
cards.back: The standing crop is measured as the mass of living organisms (biomass) or the number in a unit area.
cards.quote: The standing crop is measured as the mass of living organisms (biomass) or the number in a unit area.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is the number of trophic levels in the grazing food chain restricted?
cards.back: The number of trophic levels in the grazing food chain is restricted as the transfer of energy follows 10 per cent law
cards.quote: The number of trophic levels in the grazing food chain is restricted as the transfer of energy follows 10 per cent law

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: State the 10 per cent law of energy transfer.
cards.back: only 10 per cent of the energy is transferred to each trophic level from the lower trophic level.
cards.quote: only 10 per cent of the energy is transferred to each trophic level from the lower trophic level.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of ecological pyramids usually studied.
cards.back:
Pyramid of number
Pyramid of biomass
Pyramid of energy
cards.quote: The three types of ecological pyramids that are usually studied are (a) pyramid of number; (b) pyramid of biomass and (c) pyramid of energy.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do the base and the apex of an ecological pyramid represent?
cards.back: The base of each pyramid represents the producers or the first trophic level while the apex represents tertiary or top level consumer.
cards.quote: The base of each pyramid represents the producers or the first trophic level while the apex represents tertiary or top level consumer.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What percent of sunlight energy do producers convert into NPP in the ideal pyramid of energy?
cards.back: primary producers convert only 1% of the energy in the sunlight available to them into NPP
cards.quote: primary producers convert only 1% of the energy in the sunlight available to them into NPP

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: One must remember that the trophic level represents a ____, not a species as such.
cards.back: One must remember that the trophic level represents a functional level, not a species as such.
cards.quote: One must remember that the trophic level represents a functional level, not a species as such.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: At which trophic levels does a sparrow function?
cards.back: A given species may occupy more than one trophic level in the same ecosystem at the same time; for example, a sparrow is a primary consumer when it eats seeds, fruits, peas, and a secondary consumer when it eats insects and worms.
cards.quote: A given species may occupy more than one trophic level in the same ecosystem at the same time; for example, a sparrow is a primary consumer when it eats seeds, fruits, peas, and a secondary consumer when it eats insects and worms.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What shape are the pyramids in most ecosystems?
cards.back: In most ecosystems, all the pyramids, of number, of energy and biomass are upright, i.e., producers are more in number and biomass than the herbivores, and herbivores are more in number and biomass than the carnivores.
cards.quote: In most ecosystems, all the pyramids, of number, of energy and biomass are upright, i.e., producers are more in number and biomass than the herbivores, and herbivores are more in number and biomass than the carnivores.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which pyramid is generally inverted in the sea, and why?
cards.back: The pyramid of biomass in sea is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton.
cards.quote: The pyramid of biomass in sea is generally inverted because the biomass of fishes far exceeds that of phytoplankton.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why can the pyramid of energy never be inverted?
cards.back: Pyramid of energy is always upright, can never be inverted, because when energy flows from a particular trophic level to the next trophic level, some energy is always lost as heat at each step.
cards.quote: Pyramid of energy is always upright, can never be inverted, because when energy flows from a particular trophic level to the next trophic level, some energy is always lost as heat at each step.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does each bar in the energy pyramid indicate?
cards.back: Each bar in the energy pyramid indicates the amount of energy present at each trophic level in a given time or annually per unit area.
cards.quote: Each bar in the energy pyramid indicates the amount of energy present at each trophic level in a given time or annually per unit area.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the limitations of ecological pyramids.
cards.back:
it does not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels
It assumes a simple food chain, something that almost never exists in nature
it does not accommodate a food web
saprophytes are not given any place in ecological pyramids even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem
cards.quote: it does not take into account the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels. It assumes a simple food chain, something that almost never exists in nature; it does not accommodate a food web. Moreover, saprophytes are not given any place in ecological pyramids even though they play a vital role in the ecosystem.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is an ecosystem?
cards.back: An ecosystem is a structural and functional unit of nature and it comprises abiotic and biotic components.
cards.quote: An ecosystem is a structural and functional unit of nature and it comprises abiotic and biotic components.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Components of an ecosystem: abiotic and biotic.
cards.back:
Abiotic components are inorganic materials- air, water and soil
biotic components are producers, consumers and decomposers
cards.quote: Abiotic components are inorganic materials- air, water and soil, whereas biotic components are producers, consumers and decomposers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the two main structural features of an ecosystem.
cards.back:
Species composition
Stratification
cards.quote: Species composition and stratification are the two main structural features of an ecosystem.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which theory attempts to explain the origin of the universe?
cards.back: The Big Bang theory attempts to explain to us the origin of universe.
cards.quote: The Big Bang theory attempts to explain to us the origin of universe.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How old is the universe?
cards.back: The universe is very old – almost 13.8 billion years old.
cards.quote: The universe is very old – almost 13.8 billion years old.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: About how long ago was the earth formed?
cards.back: In the solar system of the milky way galaxy, earth was supposed to have been formed about 4.5 billion years back.
cards.quote: In the solar system of the milky way galaxy, earth was supposed to have been formed about 4.5 billion years back.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the idea of Panspermia?
cards.back: Early Greek thinkers thought units of life called spores were transferred to different planets including earth. “Panspermia” is still a favourite idea for some astronomers.
cards.quote: Early Greek thinkers thought units of life called spores were transferred to different planets including earth. “Panspermia” is still a favourite idea for some astronomers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What was the theory of spontaneous generation?
cards.back: For a long time it was also believed that life came out of decaying and rotting matter like straw, mud, etc. This was the theory of spontaneous generation.
cards.quote: For a long time it was also believed that life came out of decaying and rotting matter like straw, mud, etc. This was the theory of spontaneous generation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who dismissed spontaneous generation by careful experimentation, and what did he show?
cards.back: Louis Pasteur by careful experimentation demonstrated that life comes only from pre-existing life.
cards.quote: Louis Pasteur by careful experimentation demonstrated that life comes only from pre-existing life.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who proposed that the first life came from pre-existing non-living organic molecules?
cards.back: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules
cards.quote: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is chemical evolution, which Oparin and Haldane said preceded life?
cards.back: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g. RNA, protein, etc.) and that formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution, i.e., formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents.
cards.quote: Oparin of Russia and Haldane of England proposed that the first form of life could have come from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (e.g. RNA, protein, etc.) and that formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution, i.e., formation of diverse organic molecules from inorganic constituents.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What were the conditions on early earth, as proposed by Oparin and Haldane?
cards.back: The conditions on earth were – high temperature, volcanic storms, reducing atmosphere containing CH4 , NH3 , etc.
cards.quote: The conditions on earth were – high temperature, volcanic storms, reducing atmosphere containing CH4 , NH3 , etc.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who recreated early earth conditions in a laboratory in 1953?
cards.back: In 1953, S.L. Miller, an American scientist created similar conditions in a laboratory scale
cards.quote: In 1953, S.L. Miller, an American scientist created similar conditions in a laboratory scale

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Miller's experiment: what did the closed flask contain under electric discharge?
cards.back: He created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour
cards.quote: He created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did Miller observe in his experiment?
cards.back: He observed formation of amino acids.
cards.quote: He observed formation of amino acids.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did similar experiments by others show formed?
cards.back: In similar experiments others observed, formation of sugars, nitrogen bases, pigment and fats.
cards.quote: In similar experiments others observed, formation of sugars, nitrogen bases, pigment and fats.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When could the first non-cellular forms of life have originated?
cards.back: The first non-cellular forms of life could have originated 3 billion years back.
cards.quote: The first non-cellular forms of life could have originated 3 billion years back.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When did the first cellular form of life possibly originate?
cards.back: The first cellular form of life did not possibly originate till about 2000 million years ago.
cards.quote: The first cellular form of life did not possibly originate till about 2000 million years ago.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three connotations of the theory of special creation.
cards.back:
One, that all living organisms (species or types) that we see today were created as such.
Two, that the diversity was always the same since creation and will be the same in future also.
Three, that earth is about 4000 years old.
cards.quote: One, that all living organisms (species or types) that we see today were created as such. Two, that the diversity was always the same since creation and will be the same in future also. Three, that earth is about 4000 years old.

source.section: 6.2 Evolution of Life Forms - A Theory

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: On which voyage did Charles Darwin make the observations behind his theory?
cards.back: Based on observations made during a sea voyage in a sail ship called H.M.S. Beagle round the world, Charles Darwin concluded that existing living forms share similarities to varying degrees
cards.quote: Based on observations made during a sea voyage in a sail ship called H.M.S. Beagle round the world, Charles Darwin concluded that existing living forms share similarities to varying degrees

source.section: 6.2 Evolution of Life Forms - A Theory

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The fitness, according to Darwin, refers ultimately and only to ____ fitness.
cards.back: The fitness, according to Darwin, refers ultimately and only to reproductive fitness.
cards.quote: The fitness, according to Darwin, refers ultimately and only to reproductive fitness.

source.section: 6.2 Evolution of Life Forms - A Theory

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which naturalist of the Malay Archipelago reached conclusions similar to Darwin's?
cards.back: Alfred Wallace, a naturalist who worked in Malay Archipelago had also come to similar conclusions around the same time.
cards.quote: Alfred Wallace, a naturalist who worked in Malay Archipelago had also come to similar conclusions around the same time.

source.section: 6.2 Evolution of Life Forms - A Theory

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does the geological history of earth relate to its biological history?
cards.back: The geological history of earth closely correlates with the biological history of earth.
cards.quote: The geological history of earth closely correlates with the biological history of earth.

source.section: 6.2 Evolution of Life Forms - A Theory

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are fossils?
cards.back: Fossils are remains of hard parts of life-forms found in rocks.
cards.quote: Fossils are remains of hard parts of life-forms found in rocks.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is evidence for evolution from fossils in different sediments called?
cards.back: Hence, new forms of life have arisen at different times in the history of earth. All this is called paleontological evidence.
cards.quote: Hence, new forms of life have arisen at different times in the history of earth. All this is called paleontological evidence.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does a study of fossils in different sedimentary layers indicate?
cards.back: A study of fossils in different sedimentary layers indicates the geological period in which they existed.
cards.quote: A study of fossils in different sedimentary layers indicates the geological period in which they existed.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who proposed embryological support for evolution?
cards.back: Embryological support for evolution was also proposed by Ernst Heckel based upon the observation of certain features during embryonic stage common to all vertebrates that are absent in adult.
cards.quote: Embryological support for evolution was also proposed by Ernst Heckel based upon the observation of certain features during embryonic stage common to all vertebrates that are absent in adult.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In which vertebrates is the embryonic gill slit a functional organ (Heckel)?
cards.back: Embryological support for evolution was also proposed by Ernst Heckel based upon the observation of certain features during embryonic stage common to all vertebrates that are absent in adult. For example, the embryos of all vertebrates including human develop a row of vestigial gill slit just behind the head but it is a functional organ only in fish and not found in any other adult vertebrates.
cards.quote: Embryological support for evolution was also proposed by Ernst Heckel based upon the observation of certain features during embryonic stage common to all vertebrates that are absent in adult. For example, the embryos of all vertebrates including human develop a row of vestigial gill slit just behind the head but it is a functional organ only in fish and not found in any other adult vertebrates.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who disproved Heckel's embryological proposal, and what did he note?
cards.back: For example, the embryos of all vertebrates including human develop a row of vestigial gill slit just behind the head but it is a functional organ only in fish and not found in any other adult vertebrates. However, this proposal was disapproved on careful study performed by Karl Ernst von Baer. He noted that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.
cards.quote: For example, the embryos of all vertebrates including human develop a row of vestigial gill slit just behind the head but it is a functional organ only in fish and not found in any other adult vertebrates. However, this proposal was disapproved on careful study performed by Karl Ernst von Baer. He noted that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the bones in the forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetah and human.
cards.back:
humerus
radius
ulna
carpals
metacarpals
phalanges
cards.quote: all of them have humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges in their forelimbs.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is divergent evolution (e.g. forelimbs of whales, bats, cheetah, human)?
cards.back: Hence, in these animals, the same structure developed along different directions due to adaptations to different needs. This is divergent evolution and these structures are homologous.
cards.quote: Hence, in these animals, the same structure developed along different directions due to adaptations to different needs. This is divergent evolution and these structures are homologous.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does homology indicate?
cards.back: Homology indicates common ancestry.
cards.quote: Homology indicates common ancestry.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which plant structures of Bougainvillea and Cucurbita represent homology?
cards.back: In plants also, the thorn and tendrils of Bougainvillea and Cucurbita represent homology (Figure 6.3a).
cards.quote: In plants also, the thorn and tendrils of Bougainvillea and Cucurbita represent homology (Figure 6.3a).

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Homology is based on ____
cards.back: Homology is based on divergent evolution
cards.quote: Homology is based on divergent evolution

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is convergent evolution (analogous structures)?
cards.back: Hence, analogous structures are a result of convergent evolution - different structures evolving for the same function and hence having similarity.
cards.quote: Hence, analogous structures are a result of convergent evolution - different structures evolving for the same function and hence having similarity.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are the wings of butterfly and of birds analogous structures?
cards.back: Wings of butterfly and of birds look alike. They are not anatomically similar structures though they perform similar functions.
cards.quote: Wings of butterfly and of birds look alike. They are not anatomically similar structures though they perform similar functions.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Give examples of analogy involving the eye and flippers.
cards.back: Other examples of analogy are the eye of the octopus and of mammals or the flippers of Penguins and Dolphins.
cards.quote: Other examples of analogy are the eye of the octopus and of mammals or the flippers of Penguins and Dolphins.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Sweet potato and potato are an example of which relationship?
cards.back: Sweet potato (root modification) and potato (stem modification) is another example for analogy.
cards.quote: Sweet potato (root modification) and potato (stem modification) is another example for analogy.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do similarities in proteins and genes among diverse organisms indicate?
cards.back: In the same line of argument, similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function among diverse organisms give clues to common ancestry.
cards.quote: In the same line of argument, similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function among diverse organisms give clues to common ancestry.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What argument for evolution comes from man's breeding of plants and animals?
cards.back: It is argued that if within hundreds of years, man could create new breeds, could not nature have done the same over millions of years?
cards.quote: It is argued that if within hundreds of years, man could create new breeds, could not nature have done the same over millions of years?

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Moths in England: which were more common on trees before industrialisation (1850s)?
cards.back: In a collection of moths made in 1850s, i.e., before industrialisation set in, it was observed that there were more white-winged moths on trees than dark-winged or melanised moths.
cards.quote: In a collection of moths made in 1850s, i.e., before industrialisation set in, it was observed that there were more white-winged moths on trees than dark-winged or melanised moths.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Moths in England: what was observed in the collection made in 1920?
cards.back: in the collection carried out from the same area, but after industrialisation, i.e., in 1920, there were more dark-winged moths in the same area, i.e., the proportion was reversed.
cards.quote: in the collection carried out from the same area, but after industrialisation, i.e., in 1920, there were more dark-winged moths in the same area, i.e., the proportion was reversed.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What explanation was put forth for the change in proportion of white- and dark-winged moths?
cards.back: The explanation put forth for this observation was that ‘predators will spot a moth against a contrasting background’.
cards.quote: The explanation put forth for this observation was that ‘predators will spot a moth against a contrasting background’.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What has excess use of herbicides and pesticides resulted in?
cards.back: Similarly, excess use of herbicides, pesticides, etc., has only resulted in selection of resistant varieties in a much lesser time scale.
cards.quote: Similarly, excess use of herbicides, pesticides, etc., has only resulted in selection of resistant varieties in a much lesser time scale.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Resistant organisms appearing in months or years are examples of what?
cards.back: Hence, resistant organisms/cells are appearing in a time scale of months or years and not centuries. These are examples of evolution by anthropogenic action.
cards.quote: Hence, resistant organisms/cells are appearing in a time scale of months or years and not centuries. These are examples of evolution by anthropogenic action.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Is evolution a directed process? What kind of process is it?
cards.back: This also tells us that evolution is not a directed process in the sense of determinism. It is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutation in the organisms.
cards.quote: This also tells us that evolution is not a directed process in the sense of determinism. It is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutation in the organisms.

source.section: 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution?

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is adaptive radiation (Darwin's finches)?
cards.back: From the original seed-eating features, many other forms with altered beaks arose, enabling them to become insectivorous and vegetarian finches (Figure 6.5). This process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and literally radiating to other areas of geography (habitats) is called adaptive radiation.
cards.quote: From the original seed-eating features, many other forms with altered beaks arose, enabling them to become insectivorous and vegetarian finches (Figure 6.5). This process of evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from a point and literally radiating to other areas of geography (habitats) is called adaptive radiation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which birds are one of the best examples of adaptive radiation?
cards.back: Darwin's finches represent one of the best examples of this phenomenon.
cards.quote: Darwin's finches represent one of the best examples of this phenomenon.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How did Darwin's finches diversify from seed-eating ancestors?
cards.back: From the original seed-eating features, many other forms with altered beaks arose, enabling them to become insectivorous and vegetarian finches
cards.quote: From the original seed-eating features, many other forms with altered beaks arose, enabling them to become insectivorous and vegetarian finches

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which Australian mammals are another example of adaptive radiation?
cards.back: A number of marsupials, each different from the other (Figure 6.6) evolved from an ancestral stock, but all within the Australian island continent.
cards.quote: A number of marsupials, each different from the other (Figure 6.6) evolved from an ancestral stock, but all within the Australian island continent.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which placental mammal corresponds to the Tasmanian wolf, a marsupial?
cards.back: Placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf-marsupial
cards.quote: Placental wolf and Tasmanian wolf-marsupial

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When would evolution by natural selection, in a true sense, have started?
cards.back: Evolution by natural selection, in a true sense would have started when cellular forms of life with differences in metabolic capability originated on earth.
cards.quote: Evolution by natural selection, in a true sense would have started when cellular forms of life with differences in metabolic capability originated on earth.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The essence of Darwinian theory about evolution is ____.
cards.back: The essence of Darwinian theory about evolution is natural selection.
cards.quote: The essence of Darwinian theory about evolution is natural selection.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the rate of appearance of new forms linked to?
cards.back: The rate of appearance of new forms is linked to the life cycle or the life span.
cards.quote: The rate of appearance of new forms is linked to the life cycle or the life span.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: On what is so-called fitness based?
cards.back: One must remember that the so-called fitness is based on characteristics which are inherited.
cards.quote: One must remember that the so-called fitness is based on characteristics which are inherited.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is fitness?
cards.back: Fitness is the end result of the ability to adapt and get selected by nature.
cards.quote: Fitness is the end result of the ability to adapt and get selected by nature.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the two key concepts of Darwinian Theory of Evolution.
cards.back:
Branching descent
Natural selection
cards.quote: Branching descent and natural selection are the two key concepts of Darwinian Theory of Evolution

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which French naturalist said, before Darwin, that evolution was driven by use and disuse of organs?
cards.back: Even before Darwin, a French naturalist Lamarck had said that evolution of life forms had occurred but driven by use and disuse of organs.
cards.quote: Even before Darwin, a French naturalist Lamarck had said that evolution of life forms had occurred but driven by use and disuse of organs.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which example did Lamarck give for use and disuse of organs?
cards.back: He gave the examples of Giraffes who in an attempt to forage leaves on tall trees had to adapt by elongation of their necks.
cards.quote: He gave the examples of Giraffes who in an attempt to forage leaves on tall trees had to adapt by elongation of their necks.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Whose work on populations may have influenced Darwin?
cards.back: It is possible that the work of Thomas Malthus on populations influenced Darwin.
cards.quote: It is possible that the work of Thomas Malthus on populations influenced Darwin.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the factual observations on which natural selection is based.
cards.back:
natural resources are limited
populations are stable in size except for seasonal fluctuation
members of a population vary in characteristics
most of variations are inherited
cards.quote: natural resources are limited, populations are stable in size except for seasonal fluctuation, members of a population vary in characteristics (infact no two individuals are alike) even though they look superficially similar, most of variations are inherited

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What was the novelty and brilliant insight of Darwin?
cards.back: The novelty and brilliant insight of Darwin was this: he asserted that variations, which are heritable and which make resource utilisation better for few (adapted to habitat better) will enable only those to reproduce and leave more progeny.
cards.quote: The novelty and brilliant insight of Darwin was this: he asserted that variations, which are heritable and which make resource utilisation better for few (adapted to habitat better) will enable only those to reproduce and leave more progeny.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who, working on evening primrose, brought forth the idea of mutations?
cards.back: Hugo deVries based on his work on evening primrose brought forth the idea of mutations
cards.quote: Hugo deVries based on his work on evening primrose brought forth the idea of mutations

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are mutations (Hugo deVries)?
cards.back: In the first decade of twentieth century, Hugo deVries based on his work on evening primrose brought forth the idea of mutations – large difference arising suddenly in a population.
cards.quote: In the first decade of twentieth century, Hugo deVries based on his work on evening primrose brought forth the idea of mutations – large difference arising suddenly in a population.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did deVries believe caused evolution, rather than the minor variations of Darwin?
cards.back: He believed that it is mutation which causes evolution and not the minor variations (heritable) that Darwin talked about.
cards.quote: He believed that it is mutation which causes evolution and not the minor variations (heritable) that Darwin talked about.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Mutations (deVries) vs Darwinian variations: the difference in nature
cards.back: Mutations are random and directionless while Darwinian variations are small and directional.
cards.quote: Mutations are random and directionless while Darwinian variations are small and directional.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Darwin vs deVries: the difference on how evolution proceeds
cards.back: Evolution for Darwin was gradual while deVries believed mutation caused speciation and hence called it saltation (single step large mutation).
cards.quote: Evolution for Darwin was gradual while deVries believed mutation caused speciation and hence called it saltation (single step large mutation).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: State the Hardy-Weinberg principle.
cards.back: This principle says that allele frequencies in a population are stable and is constant from generation to generation.
cards.quote: This principle says that allele frequencies in a population are stable and is constant from generation to generation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is genetic equilibrium?
cards.back: The gene pool (total genes and their alleles in a population) remains a constant. This is called genetic equilibrium.
cards.quote: The gene pool (total genes and their alleles in a population) remains a constant. This is called genetic equilibrium.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Sum total of all the allelic frequencies is ____.
cards.back: Sum total of all the allelic frequencies is 1.
cards.quote: Sum total of all the allelic frequencies is 1.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In a diploid, what do p and q represent?
cards.back: In a diploid, p and q represent the frequency of allele A and allele a .
cards.quote: In a diploid, p and q represent the frequency of allele A and allele a .

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the Hardy-Weinberg equation, what is the frequency of AA individuals?
cards.back: The frequency of AA individuals in a population is simply p^2.
cards.quote: The frequency of AA individuals in a population is simply p^2.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the Hardy-Weinberg equation, what are the frequencies of aa and Aa individuals?
cards.back: Similarly of aa is q^2, of Aa 2pq.
cards.quote: Similarly of aa is q^2, of Aa 2pq.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: the Hardy-Weinberg equation
cards.back: Hence, p^2+2pq+q^2=1. This is a binomial expansion of (p+q)^2.
cards.quote: Hence, p^2+2pq+q^2=1. This is a binomial expansion of (p+q)^2.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How is a disturbance of Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium interpreted?
cards.back: Disturbance in genetic equilibrium, or Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, i.e., change of frequency of alleles in a population would then be interpreted as resulting in evolution.
cards.quote: Disturbance in genetic equilibrium, or Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, i.e., change of frequency of alleles in a population would then be interpreted as resulting in evolution.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the five factors known to affect Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
cards.back:
gene migration or gene flow
genetic drift
mutation
genetic recombination
natural selection
cards.quote: Five factors are known to affect Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. These are gene migration or gene flow, genetic drift, mutation, genetic recombination and natural selection.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens to gene frequencies when a section of a population migrates to another place?
cards.back: When migration of a section of population to another place and population occurs, gene frequencies change in the original as well as in the new population.
cards.quote: When migration of a section of population to another place and population occurs, gene frequencies change in the original as well as in the new population.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is it called when a section of a population migrating to another place does so multiple times?
cards.back: When migration of a section of population to another place and population occurs, gene frequencies change in the original as well as in the new population. New genes/alleles are added to the new population and these are lost from the old population. There would be a gene flow if this gene migration, happens multiple times.
cards.quote: When migration of a section of population to another place and population occurs, gene frequencies change in the original as well as in the new population. New genes/alleles are added to the new population and these are lost from the old population. There would be a gene flow if this gene migration, happens multiple times.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is it called when a change in allele frequency occurs by chance?
cards.back: If the same change occurs by chance, it is called genetic drift.
cards.quote: If the same change occurs by chance, it is called genetic drift.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the founder effect?
cards.back: Sometimes the change in allele frequency is so different in the new sample of population that they become a different species. The original drifted population becomes founders and the effect is called founder effect.
cards.quote: Sometimes the change in allele frequency is so different in the new sample of population that they become a different species. The original drifted population becomes founders and the effect is called founder effect.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do pre-existing advantageous mutations produce when selected, as microbial experiments show?
cards.back: Microbial experiments show that pre-existing advantageous mutations when selected will result in observation of new phenotypes.
cards.quote: Microbial experiments show that pre-existing advantageous mutations when selected will result in observation of new phenotypes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define natural selection.
cards.back: Natural selection is a process in which heritable variations enabling better survival are enabled to reproduce and leave greater number of progeny.
cards.quote: Natural selection is a process in which heritable variations enabling better survival are enabled to reproduce and leave greater number of progeny.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which variations, per a critical analysis, change gene and allele frequencies in future generations?
cards.back: A critical analysis makes us believe that variation due to mutation or variation due to recombination during gametogenesis, or due to gene flow or genetic drift results in changed frequency of genes and alleles in future generation.
cards.quote: A critical analysis makes us believe that variation due to mutation or variation due to recombination during gametogenesis, or due to gene flow or genetic drift results in changed frequency of genes and alleles in future generation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of natural selection
cards.back:
stabilisation (in which more individuals acquire mean character value)
directional change (more individuals acquire value other than the mean character value)
disruption (more individuals acquire peripheral character value at both ends of the distribution curve)
cards.quote: Natural selection can lead to stabilisation (in which more individuals acquire mean character value), directional change (more individuals acquire value other than the mean character value) or disruption (more individuals acquire peripheral character value at both ends of the distribution curve)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What ability did some of the first cells have?
cards.back: Some of these cells had the ability to release O2.
cards.quote: Some of these cells had the ability to release O2.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: By when were invertebrates formed and active?
cards.back: By the time of 500 mya, invertebrates were formed and active.
cards.quote: By the time of 500 mya, invertebrates were formed and active.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When did jawless fish probably evolve?
cards.back: Jawless fish probably evolved around 350 mya.
cards.quote: Jawless fish probably evolved around 350 mya.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When did sea weeds and a few plants probably exist?
cards.back: Sea weeds and few plants existed probably around 320 mya.
cards.quote: Sea weeds and few plants existed probably around 320 mya.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which organisms were the first to invade land?
cards.back: We are told that the first organisms that invaded land were plants.
cards.quote: We are told that the first organisms that invaded land were plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When could fish with stout and strong fins move on land and go back to water?
cards.back: Fish with stout and strong fins could move on land and go back to water. This was about 350 mya.
cards.quote: Fish with stout and strong fins could move on land and go back to water. This was about 350 mya.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which fish caught in South Africa in 1938 was thought to be extinct?
cards.back: In 1938, a fish caught in South Africa happened to be a Coelacanth which was thought to be extinct.
cards.quote: In 1938, a fish caught in South Africa happened to be a Coelacanth which was thought to be extinct.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Lobefins (coelacanth) evolved into which first vertebrates living on both land and water?
cards.back: In 1938, a fish caught in South Africa happened to be a Coelacanth which was thought to be extinct. These animals called lobefins evolved into the first amphibians that lived on both land and water. There are no specimens of these left with us. However, these were ancestors of modern day frogs and salamanders.
cards.quote: In 1938, a fish caught in South Africa happened to be a Coelacanth which was thought to be extinct. These animals called lobefins evolved into the first amphibians that lived on both land and water. There are no specimens of these left with us. However, these were ancestors of modern day frogs and salamanders.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which animals evolved from amphibians?
cards.back: The amphibians evolved into reptiles.
cards.quote: The amphibians evolved into reptiles.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which are the modern day descendants of early reptiles?
cards.back: Again we only see their modern day descendents, the turtles, tortoises and crocodiles.
cards.quote: Again we only see their modern day descendents, the turtles, tortoises and crocodiles.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happened to the giant ferns (pteridophytes)?
cards.back: Giant ferns (pteridophytes) were present but they all fell to form coal deposits slowly.
cards.quote: Giant ferns (pteridophytes) were present but they all fell to form coal deposits slowly.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the fish-like reptiles that evolved when land reptiles went back into water.
cards.back: Some of these land reptiles went back into water to evolve into fish like reptiles probably 200 mya (e.g. Ichthyosaurs).
cards.quote: Some of these land reptiles went back into water to evolve into fish like reptiles probably 200 mya (e.g. Ichthyosaurs).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which were the land reptiles that dominated the earth?
cards.back: The land reptiles were, of course, the dinosaurs.
cards.quote: The land reptiles were, of course, the dinosaurs.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When did the dinosaurs suddenly disappear from the earth?
cards.back: About 65 mya, the dinosaurs suddenly disappeared from the earth.
cards.quote: About 65 mya, the dinosaurs suddenly disappeared from the earth.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What were the first mammals like?
cards.back: The first mammals were like shrews.
cards.quote: The first mammals were like shrews.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How did early mammals protect their unborn young?
cards.back: Mammals were viviparous and protected their unborn young inside the mother's body.
cards.quote: Mammals were viviparous and protected their unborn young inside the mother's body.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happened to South American mammals when South America joined North America?
cards.back: Due to continental drift, when South America joined North America, these animals were overridden by North American fauna.
cards.quote: Due to continental drift, when South America joined North America, these animals were overridden by North American fauna.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why did the pouched mammals of Australia survive?
cards.back: Due to the same continental drift pouched mammals of Australia survived because of lack of competition from any other mammal.
cards.quote: Due to the same continental drift pouched mammals of Australia survived because of lack of competition from any other mammal.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name some mammals that live wholly in water.
cards.back: some mammals live wholly in water. Whales, dolphins, seals and sea cows are some examples.
cards.quote: some mammals live wholly in water. Whales, dolphins, seals and sea cows are some examples.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is described as the most successful story of evolution?
cards.back: The most successful story is the evolution of man with language skills and self-consciousness.
cards.quote: The most successful story is the evolution of man with language skills and self-consciousness.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: About 15 mya, which primates were existing?
cards.back: About 15 mya, primates called Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus were existing.
cards.quote: About 15 mya, primates called Dryopithecus and Ramapithecus were existing.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Ramapithecus vs Dryopithecus: the difference in resemblance
