cards.back: The above discussion indicate that both RNA and DNA can function as genetic material, but DNA being more stable is preferred for storage of genetic information. For the transmission of genetic information, RNA is better.
cards.quote: The above discussion indicate that both RNA and DNA can function as genetic material, but DNA being more stable is preferred for storage of genetic information. For the transmission of genetic information, RNA is better.

source.section: 5.2.2 Properties of Genetic Material (DNA versus RNA)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which was the first genetic material?
cards.back: RNA was the first genetic material.
cards.quote: RNA was the first genetic material.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the RNA world, what two roles did RNA play?
cards.back: RNA used to act as a genetic material as well as a catalyst
cards.quote: RNA used to act as a genetic material as well as a catalyst

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How did DNA evolve, according to the RNA world idea?
cards.back: Therefore, DNA has evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable.
cards.quote: Therefore, DNA has evolved from RNA with chemical modifications that make it more stable.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In semiconservative DNA replication, what does each DNA molecule have after replication is complete?
cards.back: After the completion of replication, each DNA molecule would have one parental and one newly synthesised strand.
cards.quote: After the completion of replication, each DNA molecule would have one parental and one newly synthesised strand.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who wrote: 'It has not escaped our notice ... a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material'?
cards.back: It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material (Watson and Crick, 1953).
cards.quote: It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material (Watson and Crick, 1953).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who proved the semiconservative replication of DNA in E. coli, and when?
cards.back: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl performed the following experiment in 1958
cards.quote: Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl performed the following experiment in 1958

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Meselson and Stahl: how was heavy DNA obtained in E. coli?
cards.back: They grew E. coli in a medium containing 15NH4Cl (15N is the heavy isotope of nitrogen) as the only nitrogen source for many generations.
cards.quote: They grew E. coli in a medium containing 15NH4Cl (15N is the heavy isotope of nitrogen) as the only nitrogen source for many generations.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Meselson and Stahl: how was heavy DNA distinguished from normal DNA?
cards.back: This heavy DNA molecule could be distinguished from the normal DNA by centrifugation in a cesium chloride (CsCl) density gradient
cards.quote: This heavy DNA molecule could be distinguished from the normal DNA by centrifugation in a cesium chloride (CsCl) density gradient

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Meselson and Stahl: density of DNA one generation after transfer from 15N to 14N medium?
cards.back: the DNA that was extracted from the culture one generation after the transfer from 15N to 14N medium [that is after 20 minutes; E. coli divides in 20 minutes] had a hybrid or intermediate density.
cards.quote: the DNA that was extracted from the culture one generation after the transfer from 15N to 14N medium [that is after 20 minutes; E. coli divides in 20 minutes] had a hybrid or intermediate density.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Meselson and Stahl: what was the DNA composition of E. coli after 40 minutes (II generation)?
cards.back: DNA extracted from the culture after another generation [that is after 40 minutes, II generation] was composed of equal amounts of this hybrid DNA and of 'light' DNA.
cards.quote: DNA extracted from the culture after another generation [that is after 40 minutes, II generation] was composed of equal amounts of this hybrid DNA and of 'light' DNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who showed semiconservative replication in chromosomes of Vicia faba?
cards.back: Very similar experiments involving use of radioactive thymidine to detect distribution of newly synthesised DNA in the chromosomes was performed on Vicia faba (faba beans) by Taylor and colleagues in 1958. The experiments proved that the DNA in chromosomes also replicate semiconservatively.
cards.quote: Very similar experiments involving use of radioactive thymidine to detect distribution of newly synthesised DNA in the chromosomes was performed on Vicia faba (faba beans) by Taylor and colleagues in 1958. The experiments proved that the DNA in chromosomes also replicate semiconservatively.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The main enzyme is referred to as ____, since it uses a DNA template
cards.back: The main enzyme is referred to as DNA-dependent DNA polymerase, since it uses a DNA template
cards.quote: The main enzyme is referred to as DNA-dependent DNA polymerase, since it uses a DNA template

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What dual purpose do deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve in replication?
cards.back: Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve dual purposes. In addition to acting as substrates, they provide energy for polymerisation reaction
cards.quote: Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates serve dual purposes. In addition to acting as substrates, they provide energy for polymerisation reaction

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The replication occur within a small opening of the DNA helix, referred to as ____.
cards.back: The replication occur within a small opening of the DNA helix, referred to as replication fork.
cards.quote: The replication occur within a small opening of the DNA helix, referred to as replication fork.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyse polymerisation only in one direction, that is ____.
cards.back: The DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyse polymerisation only in one direction, that is 5'→3'.
cards.quote: The DNA-dependent DNA polymerases catalyse polymerisation only in one direction, that is 5'→3'.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In DNA replication, on which template strand is synthesis continuous and on which discontinuous?
cards.back: Consequently, on one strand (the template with polarity 3'→5'), the replication is continuous, while on the other (the template with polarity 5'→3'), it is discontinuous.
cards.quote: Consequently, on one strand (the template with polarity 3'→5'), the replication is continuous, while on the other (the template with polarity 5'→3'), it is discontinuous.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The discontinuously synthesised fragments are later joined by the enzyme ____
cards.back: The discontinuously synthesised fragments are later joined by the enzyme DNA ligase
cards.quote: The discontinuously synthesised fragments are later joined by the enzyme DNA ligase

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: There is a definite region in E. coli DNA where the replication originates. Such regions are termed as ____.
cards.back: There is a definite region in E. coli DNA where the replication originates. Such regions are termed as origin of replication.
cards.quote: There is a definite region in E. coli DNA where the replication originates. Such regions are termed as origin of replication.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do vectors provide for propagating a piece of DNA in recombinant DNA procedures?
cards.back: The vectors provide the origin of replication.
cards.quote: The vectors provide the origin of replication.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In eukaryotes, the replication of DNA takes place at ____ of the cell-cycle.
cards.back: In eukaryotes, the replication of DNA takes place at S-phase of the cell-cycle.
cards.quote: In eukaryotes, the replication of DNA takes place at S-phase of the cell-cycle.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: A failure in cell division after DNA replication results into ____ (a chromosomal anomaly).
cards.back: A failure in cell division after DNA replication results into polyploidy (a chromosomal anomaly).
cards.quote: A failure in cell division after DNA replication results into polyploidy (a chromosomal anomaly).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the process of copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA called?
cards.back: The process of copying genetic information from one strand of the DNA into RNA is termed as transcription.
cards.quote: The process of copying genetic information from one strand of the DNA into RNA is termed as transcription.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Unlike replication, how much of the DNA is copied in transcription?
cards.back: However, unlike in the process of replication, which once set in, the total DNA of an organism gets duplicated, in transcription only a segment of DNA and only one of the strands is copied into RNA.
cards.quote: However, unlike in the process of replication, which once set in, the total DNA of an organism gets duplicated, in transcription only a segment of DNA and only one of the strands is copied into RNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What would happen if both DNA strands were transcribed at once into two RNA molecules?
cards.back: Second, the two RNA molecules if produced simultaneously would be complementary to each other, hence would form a double stranded RNA. This would prevent RNA from being translated into protein and the exercise of transcription would become a futile one.
cards.quote: Second, the two RNA molecules if produced simultaneously would be complementary to each other, hence would form a double stranded RNA. This would prevent RNA from being translated into protein and the exercise of transcription would become a futile one.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three regions that define a transcription unit.
cards.back:
A Promoter
The Structural gene
A Terminator
cards.quote: A transcription unit in DNA is defined primarily by the three regions in the DNA : (i) A Promoter (ii) The Structural gene (iii) A Terminator

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The strand that has the polarity 3'→5' acts as a template, and is also referred to as ____.
cards.back: The strand that has the polarity 3'→5' acts as a template, and is also referred to as template strand.
cards.quote: The strand that has the polarity 3'→5' acts as a template, and is also referred to as template strand.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In a transcription unit, which strand (3'→5') acts as template, and what is the other strand called?
cards.back:
Since the two strands have opposite polarity and the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase also catalyse the polymerisation in only one direction, that is, 5'→3', the strand that has the polarity 3'→5' acts as a template, and is also referred to as template strand.
The other strand which has the polarity (5'→3') and the sequence same as RNA (except thymine at the place of uracil), is displaced during transcription. Strangely, this strand (which does not code for anything) is referred to as coding strand.
cards.quote: Since the two strands have opposite polarity and the DNA-dependent RNA polymerase also catalyse the polymerisation in only one direction, that is, 5'→3', the strand that has the polarity 3'→5' acts as a template, and is also referred to as template strand. The other strand which has the polarity (5'→3') and the sequence same as RNA (except thymine at the place of uracil), is displaced during transcription. Strangely, this strand (which does not code for anything) is referred to as coding strand.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where is the promoter located relative to the structural gene?
cards.back: The promoter is said to be located towards 5'-end (upstream) of the structural gene
cards.quote: The promoter is said to be located towards 5'-end (upstream) of the structural gene

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the function of the promoter in a transcription unit?
cards.back: It is a DNA sequence that provides binding site for RNA polymerase, and it is the presence of a promoter in a transcription unit that also defines the template and coding strands.
cards.quote: It is a DNA sequence that provides binding site for RNA polymerase, and it is the presence of a promoter in a transcription unit that also defines the template and coding strands.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where is the terminator located and what does it define?
cards.back: The terminator is located towards 3'-end (downstream) of the coding strand and it usually defines the end of the process of transcription
cards.quote: The terminator is located towards 3'-end (downstream) of the coding strand and it usually defines the end of the process of transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define a gene.
cards.back: A gene is defined as the functional unit of inheritance.
cards.quote: A gene is defined as the functional unit of inheritance.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Monocistronic vs polycistronic structural genes: where is each mostly found?
cards.back: However by defining a cistron as a segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide, the structural gene in a transcription unit could be said as monocistronic (mostly in eukaryotes) or polycistronic (mostly in bacteria or prokaryotes).
cards.quote: However by defining a cistron as a segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide, the structural gene in a transcription unit could be said as monocistronic (mostly in eukaryotes) or polycistronic (mostly in bacteria or prokaryotes).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The coding sequences or expressed sequences are defined as ____.
cards.back: The coding sequences or expressed sequences are defined as exons.
cards.quote: The coding sequences or expressed sequences are defined as exons.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: ____ or intervening sequences do not appear in mature or processed RNA.
cards.back: Introns or intervening sequences do not appear in mature or processed RNA.
cards.quote: Introns or intervening sequences do not appear in mature or processed RNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Exons vs introns.
cards.back: The coding sequences or expressed sequences are defined as exons. Exons are said to be those sequence that appear in mature or processed RNA. The exons are interrupted by introns. Introns or intervening sequences do not appear in mature or processed RNA.
cards.quote: The coding sequences or expressed sequences are defined as exons. Exons are said to be those sequence that appear in mature or processed RNA. The exons are interrupted by introns. Introns or intervening sequences do not appear in mature or processed RNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are the structural genes of eukaryotes arranged?
cards.back: In eukaryotes, the monocistronic structural genes have interrupted coding sequences – the genes in eukaryotes are split.
cards.quote: In eukaryotes, the monocistronic structural genes have interrupted coding sequences – the genes in eukaryotes are split.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of RNA in bacteria.
cards.back:
mRNA (messenger RNA)
tRNA (transfer RNA)
rRNA (ribosomal RNA)
cards.quote: In bacteria, there are three major types of RNAs: mRNA (messenger RNA), tRNA (transfer RNA), and rRNA (ribosomal RNA).

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Roles of mRNA, tRNA and rRNA in protein synthesis.
cards.back:
The mRNA provides the template
tRNA brings aminoacids and reads the genetic code
rRNAs play structural and catalytic role during translation
cards.quote: The mRNA provides the template, tRNA brings aminoacids and reads the genetic code, and rRNAs play structural and catalytic role during translation.

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many RNA polymerases transcribe all types of RNA in bacteria?
cards.back: There is single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that catalyses transcription of all types of RNA in bacteria.
cards.quote: There is single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that catalyses transcription of all types of RNA in bacteria.

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does transcription terminate in bacteria?
cards.back: Once the polymerases reaches the terminator region, the nascent RNA falls off, so also the RNA polymerase. This results in termination of transcription.
cards.quote: Once the polymerases reaches the terminator region, the nascent RNA falls off, so also the RNA polymerase. This results in termination of transcription.

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The RNA polymerase is only capable of catalysing the process of ____.
cards.back: The RNA polymerase is only capable of catalysing the process of elongation.
cards.quote: The RNA polymerase is only capable of catalysing the process of elongation.

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why can transcription and translation be coupled in bacteria?
cards.back: In bacteria, since the mRNA does not require any processing to become active, and also since transcription and translation take place in the same compartment (there is no separation of cytosol and nucleus in bacteria), many times the translation can begin much before the mRNA is fully transcribed. Consequently, the transcription and translation can be coupled in bacteria.
cards.quote: In bacteria, since the mRNA does not require any processing to become active, and also since transcription and translation take place in the same compartment (there is no separation of cytosol and nucleus in bacteria), many times the translation can begin much before the mRNA is fully transcribed. Consequently, the transcription and translation can be coupled in bacteria.

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many RNA polymerases are there in the eukaryotic nucleus?
cards.back: There are at least three RNA polymerases in the nucleus (in addition to the RNA polymerase found in the organelles). There is a clear cut division of labour.
cards.quote: There are at least three RNA polymerases in the nucleus (in addition to the RNA polymerase found in the organelles). There is a clear cut division of labour.

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S)?
cards.back: The RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs
cards.quote: The RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The ____ transcribes precursor of mRNA, the heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
cards.back: The RNA polymerase II transcribes precursor of mRNA, the heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).
cards.quote: The RNA polymerase II transcribes precursor of mRNA, the heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA).

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The ____ is responsible for transcription of tRNA, 5srRNA, and snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs).
cards.back: The RNA polymerase III is responsible for transcription of tRNA, 5srRNA, and snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs).
cards.quote: The RNA polymerase III is responsible for transcription of tRNA, 5srRNA, and snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs).

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is splicing?
cards.back: The second complexity is that the primary transcripts contain both the exons and the introns and are non-functional. Hence, it is subjected to a process called splicing where the introns are removed and exons are joined in a defined order.
cards.quote: The second complexity is that the primary transcripts contain both the exons and the introns and are non-functional. Hence, it is subjected to a process called splicing where the introns are removed and exons are joined in a defined order.

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are capping and tailing of hnRNA?
cards.back: hnRNA undergoes additional processing called as capping and tailing. In capping an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA. In tailing, adenylate residues (200-300) are added at 3'-end in a template independent manner.
cards.quote: hnRNA undergoes additional processing called as capping and tailing. In capping an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5'-end of hnRNA. In tailing, adenylate residues (200-300) are added at 3'-end in a template independent manner.

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is transported out of the nucleus for translation in eukaryotes?
cards.back: It is the fully processed hnRNA, now called mRNA, that is transported out of the nucleus for translation
cards.quote: It is the fully processed hnRNA, now called mRNA, that is transported out of the nucleus for translation

source.section: 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who argued that the code should be a combination of bases?
cards.back: It was George Gamow, a physicist, who argued that since there are only 4 bases and if they have to code for 20 amino acids, the code should constitute a combination of bases.
cards.quote: It was George Gamow, a physicist, who argued that since there are only 4 bases and if they have to code for 20 amino acids, the code should constitute a combination of bases.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Gamow: how many nucleotides should make up the code for all 20 amino acids?
cards.back: It was George Gamow, a physicist, who argued that since there are only 4 bases and if they have to code for 20 amino acids, the code should constitute a combination of bases. He suggested that in order to code for all the 20 amino acids, the code should be made up of three nucleotides.
cards.quote: It was George Gamow, a physicist, who argued that since there are only 4 bases and if they have to code for 20 amino acids, the code should constitute a combination of bases. He suggested that in order to code for all the 20 amino acids, the code should be made up of three nucleotides.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: A permutation combination of 4^3 (4 × 4 × 4) would generate ____ codons
cards.back: A permutation combination of 4^3 (4 × 4 × 4) would generate 64 codons
cards.quote: A permutation combination of 4^3 (4 × 4 × 4) would generate 64 codons

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Har Gobind Khorana's chemical method was instrumental in doing what?
cards.back: The chemical method developed by Har Gobind Khorana was instrumental in synthesising RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases (homopolymers and copolymers).
cards.quote: The chemical method developed by Har Gobind Khorana was instrumental in synthesising RNA molecules with defined combinations of bases (homopolymers and copolymers).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Whose cell-free system for protein synthesis helped decipher the genetic code?
cards.back: Marshall Nirenberg's cell-free system for protein synthesis finally helped the code to be deciphered.
cards.quote: Marshall Nirenberg's cell-free system for protein synthesis finally helped the code to be deciphered.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which enzyme of Severo Ochoa helped polymerise RNA with defined sequences?
cards.back: Severo Ochoa enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase) was also helpful in polymerising RNA with defined sequences in a template independent manner
cards.quote: Severo Ochoa enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase) was also helpful in polymerising RNA with defined sequences in a template independent manner

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The codon is ____. ____ codons code for amino acids and 3 codons do not code for any amino acids, hence they function as stop codons.
cards.back: The codon is triplet. 61 codons code for amino acids and 3 codons do not code for any amino acids, hence they function as stop codons.
cards.quote: The codon is triplet. 61 codons code for amino acids and 3 codons do not code for any amino acids, hence they function as stop codons.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is ____.
cards.back: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is degenerate.
cards.quote: Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is degenerate.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Genetic code: how is the codon read in mRNA?
cards.back: The codon is read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion. There are no punctuations.
cards.quote: The codon is read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion. There are no punctuations.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The code is nearly ____: for example, from bacteria to human UUU would code for Phenylalanine (phe).
cards.back: The code is nearly universal: for example, from bacteria to human UUU would code for Phenylalanine (phe).
cards.quote: The code is nearly universal: for example, from bacteria to human UUU would code for Phenylalanine (phe).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where have exceptions to the universality of the genetic code been found?
cards.back: Some exceptions to this rule have been found in mitochondrial codons, and in some protozoans.
cards.quote: Some exceptions to this rule have been found in mitochondrial codons, and in some protozoans.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which amino acid does AUG code for (it also acts as the initiator codon)?
cards.back: AUG has dual functions. It codes for Methionine (met)
cards.quote: AUG has dual functions. It codes for Methionine (met)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three stop codons.
cards.back:
UAA
UAG
UGA
cards.quote: UAA, UAG, UGA are stop terminator codons.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name a classical point mutation and its effect.
cards.back: A classical example of point mutation is a change of single base pair in the gene for beta globin chain that results in the change of amino acid residue glutamate to valine. It results into a diseased condition called as sickle cell anemia.
cards.quote: A classical example of point mutation is a change of single base pair in the gene for beta globin chain that results in the change of amino acid residue glutamate to valine. It results into a diseased condition called as sickle cell anemia.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the ____ from the point of insertion or deletion.
cards.back: Insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion.
cards.quote: Insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are insertions or deletions of one or two bases called?
cards.back: Insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion. However, such mutations are referred to as frameshift insertion or deletion mutations.
cards.quote: Insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion. However, such mutations are referred to as frameshift insertion or deletion mutations.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens when three or multiples of three bases are inserted or deleted?
cards.back: Insertion or deletion of three or its multiple bases insert or delete in one or multiple codon hence one or multiple amino acids, and reading frame remains unaltered from that point onwards.
cards.quote: Insertion or deletion of three or its multiple bases insert or delete in one or multiple codon hence one or multiple amino acids, and reading frame remains unaltered from that point onwards.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Crick: what did he postulate to read the genetic code?
cards.back: He postulated the presence of an adapter molecule that would on one hand read the code and on other hand would bind to specific amino acids.
cards.quote: He postulated the presence of an adapter molecule that would on one hand read the code and on other hand would bind to specific amino acids.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Structure of tRNA: what are its anticodon loop and amino acid acceptor end?
cards.back: tRNA has an anticodon loop that has bases complementary to the code, and it also has an amino acid acceptor end to which it binds to amino acids.
cards.quote: tRNA has an anticodon loop that has bases complementary to the code, and it also has an amino acid acceptor end to which it binds to amino acids.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which tRNA is used for initiation, and for which codons is there no tRNA?
cards.back: For initiation, there is another specific tRNA that is referred to as initiator tRNA. There are no tRNAs for stop codons.
cards.quote: For initiation, there is another specific tRNA that is referred to as initiator tRNA. There are no tRNAs for stop codons.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What shapes does tRNA show in secondary and actual structure?
cards.back: In figure 5.12, the secondary structure of tRNA has been depicted that looks like a clover-leaf. In actual structure, the tRNA is a compact molecule which looks like inverted L.
cards.quote: In figure 5.12, the secondary structure of tRNA has been depicted that looks like a clover-leaf. In actual structure, the tRNA is a compact molecule which looks like inverted L.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define translation.
cards.back: Translation refers to the process of polymerisation of amino acids to form a polypeptide
cards.quote: Translation refers to the process of polymerisation of amino acids to form a polypeptide

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The amino acids are joined by a bond which is known as a ____.
cards.back: The amino acids are joined by a bond which is known as a peptide bond.
cards.quote: The amino acids are joined by a bond which is known as a peptide bond.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is charging of tRNA?
cards.back: Formation of a peptide bond requires energy. Therefore, in the first phase itself amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA– a process commonly called as charging of tRNA or aminoacylation of tRNA to be more specific.
cards.quote: Formation of a peptide bond requires energy. Therefore, in the first phase itself amino acids are activated in the presence of ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA– a process commonly called as charging of tRNA or aminoacylation of tRNA to be more specific.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the cellular factory for protein synthesis and what does it consist of?
cards.back: The cellular factory responsible for synthesising proteins is the ribosome. The ribosome consists of structural RNAs and about 80 different proteins. In its inactive state, it exists as two subunits; a large subunit and a small subunit.
cards.quote: The cellular factory responsible for synthesising proteins is the ribosome. The ribosome consists of structural RNAs and about 80 different proteins. In its inactive state, it exists as two subunits; a large subunit and a small subunit.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When does the process of translation begin?
cards.back: When the small subunit encounters an mRNA, the process of translation of the mRNA to protein begins.
cards.quote: When the small subunit encounters an mRNA, the process of translation of the mRNA to protein begins.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The ribosome also acts as a catalyst (____ in bacteria is the enzyme-ribozyme) for the formation of peptide bond.
cards.back: The ribosome also acts as a catalyst (23S rRNA in bacteria is the enzyme-ribozyme) for the formation of peptide bond.
cards.quote: The ribosome also acts as a catalyst (23S rRNA in bacteria is the enzyme-ribozyme) for the formation of peptide bond.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a translational unit in mRNA?
cards.back: A translational unit in mRNA is the sequence of RNA that is flanked by the start codon (AUG) and the stop codon and codes for a polypeptide.
cards.quote: A translational unit in mRNA is the sequence of RNA that is flanked by the start codon (AUG) and the stop codon and codes for a polypeptide.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are UTRs in mRNA and where are they present?
cards.back: An mRNA also has some additional sequences that are not translated and are referred as untranslated regions (UTR). The UTRs are present at both 5'-end (before start codon) and at 3'-end (after stop codon). They are required for efficient translation process.
cards.quote: An mRNA also has some additional sequences that are not translated and are referred as untranslated regions (UTR). The UTRs are present at both 5'-end (before start codon) and at 3'-end (after stop codon). They are required for efficient translation process.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: For initiation, the ribosome binds to the mRNA at the start codon (AUG) that is recognised only by the ____.
cards.back: For initiation, the ribosome binds to the mRNA at the start codon (AUG) that is recognised only by the initiator tRNA.
cards.quote: For initiation, the ribosome binds to the mRNA at the start codon (AUG) that is recognised only by the initiator tRNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens during the elongation phase of translation?
cards.back: During this stage, complexes composed of an amino acid linked to tRNA, sequentially bind to the appropriate codon in mRNA by forming complementary base pairs with the tRNA anticodon.
cards.quote: During this stage, complexes composed of an amino acid linked to tRNA, sequentially bind to the appropriate codon in mRNA by forming complementary base pairs with the tRNA anticodon.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: At the end, a ____ binds to the stop codon, terminating translation and releasing the complete polypeptide from the ribosome.
cards.back: At the end, a release factor binds to the stop codon, terminating translation and releasing the complete polypeptide from the ribosome.
cards.quote: At the end, a release factor binds to the stop codon, terminating translation and releasing the complete polypeptide from the ribosome.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the four levels at which gene expression can be regulated in eukaryotes.
cards.back:
transcriptional level (formation of primary transcript)
processing level (regulation of splicing)
transport of mRNA from nucleus to the cytoplasm
translational level
cards.quote: regulation could be exerted at (i) transcriptional level (formation of primary transcript), (ii) processing level (regulation of splicing), (iii) transport of mRNA from nucleus to the cytoplasm, (iv) translational level.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In prokaryotes, control of the rate of ____ is the predominant site for control of gene expression.
cards.back: In prokaryotes, control of the rate of transcriptional initiation is the predominant site for control of gene expression.
cards.quote: In prokaryotes, control of the rate of transcriptional initiation is the predominant site for control of gene expression.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How can regulatory proteins act on RNA polymerase activity in prokaryotes?
cards.back: These regulatory proteins can act both positively (activators) and negatively (repressors).
cards.quote: These regulatory proteins can act both positively (activators) and negatively (repressors).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where is the operator region located, and what binds to it?
cards.back: The operator region is adjacent to the promoter elements in most operons and in most cases the sequences of the operator bind a repressor protein.
cards.quote: The operator region is adjacent to the promoter elements in most operons and in most cases the sequences of the operator bind a repressor protein.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who elucidated the lac operon?
cards.back: The elucidation of the lac operon was also a result of a close association between a geneticist, Francois Jacob and a biochemist, Jacque Monod.
cards.quote: The elucidation of the lac operon was also a result of a close association between a geneticist, Francois Jacob and a biochemist, Jacque Monod.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is an operon?
cards.back: In lac operon (here lac refers to lactose), a polycistronic structural gene is regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes. Such arrangement is very common in bacteria and is referred to as operon.
cards.quote: In lac operon (here lac refers to lactose), a polycistronic structural gene is regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes. Such arrangement is very common in bacteria and is referred to as operon.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three structural genes of the lac operon.
cards.back:
z
y
a
cards.quote: three structural genes (z, y, and a)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The i gene codes for the ____ of the lac operon.
cards.back: The i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon.
cards.quote: The i gene codes for the repressor of the lac operon.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the z gene of the lac operon code for?
cards.back: The z gene codes for beta-galactosidase
cards.quote: The z gene codes for beta-galactosidase

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is beta-galactosidase primarily responsible for?
cards.back: The z gene codes for beta-galactosidase (β-gal), which is primarily responsible for the hydrolysis of the disaccharide, lactose into its monomeric units, galactose and glucose.
cards.quote: The z gene codes for beta-galactosidase (β-gal), which is primarily responsible for the hydrolysis of the disaccharide, lactose into its monomeric units, galactose and glucose.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The y gene codes for ____, which increases permeability of the cell
cards.back: The y gene codes for permease, which increases permeability of the cell
cards.quote: The y gene codes for permease, which increases permeability of the cell

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The a gene encodes a ____.
cards.back: The a gene encodes a transacetylase.
cards.quote: The a gene encodes a transacetylase.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are all three gene products of the lac operon needed?
cards.back: Hence, all the three gene products in lac operon are required for metabolism of lactose.
cards.quote: Hence, all the three gene products in lac operon are required for metabolism of lactose.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which substance is the inducer of the lac operon, and why?
cards.back: Lactose is the substrate for the enzyme beta-galactosidase and it regulates switching on and off of the operon. Hence, it is termed as inducer.
cards.quote: Lactose is the substrate for the enzyme beta-galactosidase and it regulates switching on and off of the operon. Hence, it is termed as inducer.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Lac operon: what does the repressor do when no inducer is present?
cards.back: The repressor of the operon is synthesised (all-the-time – constitutively) from the i gene. The repressor protein binds to the operator region of the operon and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.
cards.quote: The repressor of the operon is synthesised (all-the-time – constitutively) from the i gene. The repressor protein binds to the operator region of the operon and prevents RNA polymerase from transcribing the operon.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Lac operon: what happens to the repressor when an inducer is present?
cards.back: In the presence of an inducer, such as lactose or allolactose, the repressor is inactivated by interaction with the inducer. This allows RNA polymerase access to the promoter and transcription proceeds
cards.quote: In the presence of an inducer, such as lactose or allolactose, the repressor is inactivated by interaction with the inducer. This allows RNA polymerase access to the promoter and transcription proceeds

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Can glucose or galactose act as inducers for the lac operon?
cards.back: Remember, glucose or galactose cannot act as inducers for lac operon.
cards.quote: Remember, glucose or galactose cannot act as inducers for lac operon.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why must a very low level of lac operon expression be present all the time?
cards.back: In the absence of a preferred carbon source such as glucose, if lactose is provided in the growth medium of the bacteria, the lactose is transported into the cells through the action of permease (Remember, a very low level of expression of lac operon has to be present in the cell all the time, otherwise lactose cannot enter the cells).
cards.quote: In the absence of a preferred carbon source such as glucose, if lactose is provided in the growth medium of the bacteria, the lactose is transported into the cells through the action of permease (Remember, a very low level of expression of lac operon has to be present in the cell all the time, otherwise lactose cannot enter the cells).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Regulation of lac operon by repressor is referred to as ____.
cards.back: Regulation of lac operon by repressor is referred to as negative regulation.
cards.quote: Regulation of lac operon by repressor is referred to as negative regulation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How can regulation of the lac operon also be visualised?
cards.back: Essentially, regulation of lac operon can also be visualised as regulation of enzyme synthesis by its substrate.
cards.quote: Essentially, regulation of lac operon can also be visualised as regulation of enzyme synthesis by its substrate.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In which year was the project of sequencing the human genome launched?
cards.back: With the establishment of genetic engineering techniques where it was possible to isolate and clone any piece of DNA and availability of simple and fast techniques for determining DNA sequences, a very ambitious project of sequencing human genome was launched in the year 1990.
cards.quote: With the establishment of genetic engineering techniques where it was possible to isolate and clone any piece of DNA and availability of simple and fast techniques for determining DNA sequences, a very ambitious project of sequencing human genome was launched in the year 1990.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: HGP was closely associated with the rapid development of a new area in biology called ____.
cards.back: HGP was closely associated with the rapid development of a new area in biology called Bioinformatics.
cards.quote: HGP was closely associated with the rapid development of a new area in biology called Bioinformatics.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the goals of the Human Genome Project.
cards.back:
Identify all the approximately 20,000-25,000 genes in human DNA
Determine the sequences of the 3 billion chemical base pairs that make up human DNA
Store this information in databases
Improve tools for data analysis
Transfer related technologies to other sectors, such as industries
Address the ethical, legal, and social issues (ELSI) that may arise from the project
cards.quote: Identify all the approximately 20,000-25,000 genes in human DNA; (ii) Determine the sequences of the 3 billion chemical base pairs that make up human DNA; (iiii) Store this information in databases; (iv) Improve tools for data analysis; (v) Transfer related technologies to other sectors, such as industries; (vi) Address the ethical, legal, and social issues (ELSI) that may arise from the project.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which bodies coordinated the Human Genome Project, and for how long?
cards.back: The Human Genome Project was a 13-year project coordinated by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institute of Health.
cards.quote: The Human Genome Project was a 13-year project coordinated by the U.S. Department of Energy and the National Institute of Health.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In which year was the Human Genome Project completed?
cards.back: The project was completed in 2003.
cards.quote: The project was completed in 2003.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The two major approaches (methodologies) of the Human Genome Project.
cards.back:
Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs)
Sequence Annotation
cards.quote: The methods involved two major approaches. One approach focused on identifying all the genes that are expressed as RNA (referred to as Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs). The other took the blind approach of simply sequencing the whole set of genome that contained all the coding and non-coding sequence, and later assigning different regions in the sequence with functions (a term referred to as Sequence Annotation).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which hosts and vectors were used to clone DNA fragments in the HGP?
cards.back: The commonly used hosts were bacteria and yeast, and the vectors were called as BAC (bacterial artificial chromosomes), and YAC (yeast artificial chromosomes).
cards.quote: The commonly used hosts were bacteria and yeast, and the vectors were called as BAC (bacterial artificial chromosomes), and YAC (yeast artificial chromosomes).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Whose method was the principle of the automated DNA sequencers used in the HGP?
cards.back: The fragments were sequenced using automated DNA sequencers that worked on the principle of a method developed by Frederick Sanger.
cards.quote: The fragments were sequenced using automated DNA sequencers that worked on the principle of a method developed by Frederick Sanger.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why were specialised computer programs developed in the HGP?
cards.back: Alignment of these sequences was humanly not possible. Therefore, specialised computer based programs were developed
cards.quote: Alignment of these sequences was humanly not possible. Therefore, specialised computer based programs were developed

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What information was used to generate the genetic and physical maps of the genome?
cards.back: This was generated using information on polymorphism of restriction endonuclease recognition sites, and some repetitive DNA sequences known as microsatellites
cards.quote: This was generated using information on polymorphism of restriction endonuclease recognition sites, and some repetitive DNA sequences known as microsatellites

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The human genome contains ____ million bp.
cards.back: The human genome contains 3164.7 million bp.
cards.quote: The human genome contains 3164.7 million bp.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The average gene consists of 3000 bases, but sizes vary greatly, with the largest known human gene being ____ at 2.4 million bases.
cards.back: The average gene consists of 3000 bases, but sizes vary greatly, with the largest known human gene being dystrophin at 2.4 million bases.
cards.quote: The average gene consists of 3000 bases, but sizes vary greatly, with the largest known human gene being dystrophin at 2.4 million bases.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Almost all (____) nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all humans.
cards.back: Almost all (99.9 per cent) nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all humans.
cards.quote: Almost all (99.9 per cent) nucleotide bases are exactly the same in all humans.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The functions are unknown for over ____ of the discovered genes.
cards.back: The functions are unknown for over 50 per cent of the discovered genes.
cards.quote: The functions are unknown for over 50 per cent of the discovered genes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Less than ____ of the genome codes for proteins.
cards.back: Less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins.
cards.quote: Less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What makes up a very large portion of the human genome?
cards.back: Repeated sequences make up very large portion of the human genome.
cards.quote: Repeated sequences make up very large portion of the human genome.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are repetitive sequences?
cards.back: Repetitive sequences are stretches of DNA sequences that are repeated many times, sometimes hundred to thousand times. They are thought to have no direct coding functions, but they shed light on chromosome structure, dynamics and evolution.
cards.quote: Repetitive sequences are stretches of DNA sequences that are repeated many times, sometimes hundred to thousand times. They are thought to have no direct coding functions, but they shed light on chromosome structure, dynamics and evolution.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Chromosome 1 has most genes (____), and the Y has the fewest (____).
cards.back: Chromosome 1 has most genes (2968), and the Y has the fewest (231).
cards.quote: Chromosome 1 has most genes (2968), and the Y has the fewest (231).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are SNPs?
cards.back: Scientists have identified about 1.4 million locations where single-base DNA differences (SNPs – single nucleotide polymorphism, pronounced as 'snips') occur in humans.
cards.quote: Scientists have identified about 1.4 million locations where single-base DNA differences (SNPs – single nucleotide polymorphism, pronounced as 'snips') occur in humans.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is DNA fingerprinting?
cards.back: DNA fingerprinting is a very quick way to compare the DNA sequences of any two individuals.
cards.quote: DNA fingerprinting is a very quick way to compare the DNA sequences of any two individuals.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in which DNA regions?
cards.back: DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in some specific regions in DNA sequence called as repetitive DNA, because in these sequences, a small stretch of DNA is repeated many times.
cards.quote: DNA fingerprinting involves identifying differences in some specific regions in DNA sequence called as repetitive DNA, because in these sequences, a small stretch of DNA is repeated many times.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is satellite DNA, and how is it separated from bulk genomic DNA?
cards.back: These repetitive DNA are separated from bulk genomic DNA as different peaks during density gradient centrifugation. The bulk DNA forms a major peak and the other small peaks are referred to as satellite DNA.
cards.quote: These repetitive DNA are separated from bulk genomic DNA as different peaks during density gradient centrifugation. The bulk DNA forms a major peak and the other small peaks are referred to as satellite DNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of satellite DNA.
cards.back:
micro-satellites
mini-satellites
cards.quote: Depending on base composition (A : T rich or G:C rich), length of segment, and number of repetitive units, the satellite DNA is classified into many categories, such as micro-satellites, mini-satellites etc.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What property of repetitive satellite DNA forms the basis of DNA fingerprinting?
cards.back: These sequence show high degree of polymorphism and form the basis of DNA fingerprinting.
cards.quote: These sequence show high degree of polymorphism and form the basis of DNA fingerprinting.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is DNA fingerprinting useful in forensics and paternity testing?
cards.back: Since DNA from every tissue (such as blood, hair-follicle, skin, bone, saliva, sperm etc.), from an individual show the same degree of polymorphism, they become very useful identification tool in forensic applications. Further, as the polymorphisms are inheritable from parents to children, DNA fingerprinting is the basis of paternity testing, in case of disputes.
cards.quote: Since DNA from every tissue (such as blood, hair-follicle, skin, bone, saliva, sperm etc.), from an individual show the same degree of polymorphism, they become very useful identification tool in forensic applications. Further, as the polymorphisms are inheritable from parents to children, DNA fingerprinting is the basis of paternity testing, in case of disputes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Polymorphism (variation at genetic level) arises due to ____.
cards.back: Polymorphism (variation at genetic level) arises due to mutations.
cards.quote: Polymorphism (variation at genetic level) arises due to mutations.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is DNA polymorphism in simple terms?
cards.back: In simple terms, if an inheritable mutation is observed in a population at high frequency, it is referred to as DNA polymorphism.
cards.quote: In simple terms, if an inheritable mutation is observed in a population at high frequency, it is referred to as DNA polymorphism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Allelic variation is a DNA polymorphism if more than one allele at a locus occurs at what frequency?
cards.back: Allelic (again recall the definition of alleles from Chapter 4) sequence variation has traditionally been described as a DNA polymorphism if more than one variant (allele) at a locus occurs in human population with a frequency greater than 0.01.
cards.quote: Allelic (again recall the definition of alleles from Chapter 4) sequence variation has traditionally been described as a DNA polymorphism if more than one variant (allele) at a locus occurs in human population with a frequency greater than 0.01.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is DNA polymorphism more likely in noncoding DNA sequences?
cards.back: The probability of such variation to be observed in noncoding DNA sequence would be higher as mutations in these sequences may not have any immediate effect/impact in an individual's reproductive ability.
cards.quote: The probability of such variation to be observed in noncoding DNA sequence would be higher as mutations in these sequences may not have any immediate effect/impact in an individual's reproductive ability.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who developed DNA fingerprinting, and what probe did he use?
cards.back: The technique of DNA Fingerprinting was initially developed by Alec Jeffreys. He used a satellite DNA as probe that shows very high degree of polymorphism. It was called as Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR).
cards.quote: The technique of DNA Fingerprinting was initially developed by Alec Jeffreys. He used a satellite DNA as probe that shows very high degree of polymorphism. It was called as Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The VNTR belongs to a class of satellite DNA referred to as ____.
cards.back: The VNTR belongs to a class of satellite DNA referred to as mini-satellite.
cards.quote: The VNTR belongs to a class of satellite DNA referred to as mini-satellite.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The technique, as used earlier, involved ____ using radiolabelled VNTR as a probe.
cards.back: The technique, as used earlier, involved Southern blot hybridisation using radiolabelled VNTR as a probe.
cards.quote: The technique, as used earlier, involved Southern blot hybridisation using radiolabelled VNTR as a probe.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Steps of DNA fingerprinting, in order.
cards.back:
isolation of DNA
digestion of DNA by restriction endonucleases
separation of DNA fragments by electrophoresis
transferring (blotting) of separated DNA fragments to synthetic membranes, such as nitrocellulose or nylon
hybridisation using labelled VNTR probe
detection of hybridised DNA fragments by autoradiography
cards.quote: isolation of DNA, (ii) digestion of DNA by restriction endonucleases, (iii) separation of DNA fragments by electrophoresis, (iv) transferring (blotting) of separated DNA fragments to synthetic membranes, such as nitrocellulose or nylon, (v) hybridisation using labelled VNTR probe, and (vi) detection of hybridised DNA fragments by autoradiography.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are VNTRs arranged, and how does their copy number vary?
cards.back: A small DNA sequence is arranged tandemly in many copy numbers. The copy number varies from chromosome to chromosome in an individual. The numbers of repeat show very high degree of polymorphism.
cards.quote: A small DNA sequence is arranged tandemly in many copy numbers. The copy number varies from chromosome to chromosome in an individual. The numbers of repeat show very high degree of polymorphism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In whom is the DNA fingerprint pattern the same?
cards.back: It differs from individual to individual in a population except in the case of monozygotic (identical) twins.
cards.quote: It differs from individual to individual in a population except in the case of monozygotic (identical) twins.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What increased the sensitivity of DNA fingerprinting?
cards.back: The sensitivity of the technique has been increased by use of polymerase chain reaction (PCR– you will study about it in Chapter 9).
cards.quote: The sensitivity of the technique has been increased by use of polymerase chain reaction (PCR– you will study about it in Chapter 9).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which strand of a transcription unit has the same sequence as the RNA (thymine in place of uracil), and what is it called?
cards.back: The other strand which has the polarity (5'→3') and the sequence same as RNA (except thymine at the place of uracil), is displaced during transcription. Strangely, this strand (which does not code for anything) is referred to as coding strand.
cards.quote: The other strand which has the polarity (5'→3') and the sequence same as RNA (except thymine at the place of uracil), is displaced during transcription. Strangely, this strand (which does not code for anything) is referred to as coding strand.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the four levels of biological organisation that Ecology is concerned with.
cards.back: organisms, populations, communities and biomes
cards.quote: Ecology is basically concerned with four levels of biological organisation – organisms, populations, communities and biomes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define population.
cards.back: A population is a group of individuals of a given species sharing or competing for similar resources in a defined geographical area.
cards.quote: A population is a group of individuals of a given species sharing or competing for similar resources in a defined geographical area.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: At which level of biological organisation does natural selection operate?
cards.back: it is at the population level that natural selection operates to evolve the desired traits
cards.quote: it is at the population level that natural selection operates to evolve the desired traits

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is population ecology an important area of ecology?
cards.back: Population ecology is, therefore, an important area because it links ecology to population genetics and evolution.
cards.quote: Population ecology is, therefore, an important area because it links ecology to population genetics and evolution.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the attributes that populations have but individual organisms do not.
cards.back:
birth rates and death rates
sex ratio
age distribution
cards.quote: Populations have attributes that individual organisms do not- birth rates and death rates, sex ratio and age distribution.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In a population, birth rates and death rates refer to what?
cards.back: In a population these rates refer to per capita births and deaths.
cards.quote: In a population these rates refer to per capita births and deaths.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does a population differ from an individual with respect to sex?
cards.back: An individual is either a male or a female but a population has a sex ratio
cards.quote: An individual is either a male or a female but a population has a sex ratio

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is an age pyramid?
cards.back: If the age distribution (per cent individuals of a given age or age group) is plotted for the population, the resulting structure is called an age pyramid
cards.quote: If the age distribution (per cent individuals of a given age or age group) is plotted for the population, the resulting structure is called an age pyramid

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the shape of an age pyramid reflect?
cards.back: The shape of the pyramids reflects the growth status of the population - (a) whether it is growing, (b) stable or (c) declining.
cards.quote: The shape of the pyramids reflects the growth status of the population - (a) whether it is growing, (b) stable or (c) declining.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Population size, technically called ____ (designated as N), need not necessarily be measured in numbers only.
cards.back: Population size, technically called population density (designated as N), need not necessarily be measured in numbers only.
cards.quote: Population size, technically called population density (designated as N), need not necessarily be measured in numbers only.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the ways in which population density may be expressed.
cards.back:
numbers
biomass
per cent cover
cards.quote: which may be expressed in different ways (numbers, biomass, per cent cover, etc.,) depending on the species

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which processes increase and which decrease population density?
cards.back: two of which (natality and immigration) contribute to an increase in population density and two (mortality and emigration) to a decrease.
cards.quote: two of which (natality and immigration) contribute to an increase in population density and two (mortality and emigration) to a decrease.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define natality.
cards.back: Natality refers to the number of births during a given period in the population that are added to the initial density.
cards.quote: Natality refers to the number of births during a given period in the population that are added to the initial density.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define mortality.
cards.back: Mortality is the number of deaths in the population during a given period.
cards.quote: Mortality is the number of deaths in the population during a given period.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define immigration.
cards.back: Immigration is the number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere during the time period under consideration.
cards.quote: Immigration is the number of individuals of the same species that have come into the habitat from elsewhere during the time period under consideration.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define emigration.
cards.back: Emigration is the number of individuals of the population who left the habitat and gone elsewhere during the time period under consideration.
cards.quote: Emigration is the number of individuals of the population who left the habitat and gone elsewhere during the time period under consideration.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: population density at time t+1.
cards.back: if N is the population density at time t, then its density at time t +1 is Nt+1 = Nt + [(B + I) – (D + E)]
cards.quote: if N is the population density at time t, then its density at time t +1 is Nt+1 = Nt + [(B + I) – (D + E)]

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When will population density increase?
cards.back: population density will increase if the number of births plus the number of immigrants (B + I) is more than the number of deaths plus the number of emigrants (D + E)
cards.quote: population density will increase if the number of births plus the number of immigrants (B + I) is more than the number of deaths plus the number of emigrants (D + E)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which factors most influence population density under normal conditions?
cards.back: Under normal conditions, births and deaths are the most important factors influencing population density, the other two factors assuming importance only under special conditions.
cards.quote: Under normal conditions, births and deaths are the most important factors influencing population density, the other two factors assuming importance only under special conditions.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does a population grow when resources are unlimited?
cards.back: Ideally, when resources in the habitat are unlimited, each species has the ability to realise fully its innate potential to grow in number, as Darwin observed while developing his theory of natural selection. Then the population grows in an exponential or geometric fashion.
cards.quote: Ideally, when resources in the habitat are unlimited, each species has the ability to realise fully its innate potential to grow in number, as Darwin observed while developing his theory of natural selection. Then the population grows in an exponential or geometric fashion.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: exponential growth of a population (rate form).
cards.back: If in a population of size N, the birth rates (not total number but per capita births) are represented as b and death rates (again, per capita death rates) as d, then the increase or decrease in N during a unit time period t (dN/dt) will be dN/dt = (b – d) × N Let (b–d) = r, then dN/dt = rN
cards.quote: If in a population of size N, the birth rates (not total number but per capita births) are represented as b and death rates (again, per capita death rates) as d, then the increase or decrease in N during a unit time period t (dN/dt) will be dN/dt = (b – d) × N Let (b–d) = r, then dN/dt = rN

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is r in the exponential growth equation?
cards.back: The r in this equation is called the ‘intrinsic rate of natural increase’ and is a very important parameter chosen for assessing impacts of any biotic or abiotic factor on population growth.
cards.quote: The r in this equation is called the ‘intrinsic rate of natural increase’ and is a very important parameter chosen for assessing impacts of any biotic or abiotic factor on population growth.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The ____ (r) is a measure of the inherent potential of a population to grow.
cards.back: The intrinsic rate of natural increase (r) is a measure of the inherent potential of a population to grow.
cards.quote: The intrinsic rate of natural increase (r) is a measure of the inherent potential of a population to grow.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What curve does exponential growth give when N is plotted against time?
cards.back: The above equation describes the exponential or geometric growth pattern of a population (Figure 11.3) and results in a J-shaped curve when we plot N in relation to time.
cards.quote: The above equation describes the exponential or geometric growth pattern of a population (Figure 11.3) and results in a J-shaped curve when we plot N in relation to time.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: integral form of the exponential growth equation.
cards.back: Nt = N0 e^rt where Nt = Population density after time t N0 = Population density at time zero r = intrinsic rate of natural increase e = the base of natural logarithms (2.71828)
cards.quote: Nt = N0 e^rt where Nt = Population density after time t N0 = Population density at time zero r = intrinsic rate of natural increase e = the base of natural logarithms (2.71828)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is carrying capacity (K)?
cards.back: In nature, a given habitat has enough resources to support a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible. Let us call this limit as nature's carrying capacity (K) for that species in that habitat.
cards.quote: In nature, a given habitat has enough resources to support a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible. Let us call this limit as nature's carrying capacity (K) for that species in that habitat.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Phases of logistic growth, in order.
cards.back:
lag phase
acceleration
deceleration
asymptote
cards.quote: A population growing in a habitat with limited resources show initially a lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration and finally an asymptote, when the population density reaches the carrying capacity.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: A plot of N in relation to time (t) results in a ____ curve. This type of population growth is called Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth
cards.back: A plot of N in relation to time (t) results in a sigmoid curve. This type of population growth is called Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth
cards.quote: A plot of N in relation to time (t) results in a sigmoid curve. This type of population growth is called Verhulst-Pearl Logistic Growth

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth, dN/dt = rN((K – N)/K). What do N, r and K stand for?
cards.back:
N = Population density at time t
r = Intrinsic rate of natural increase
K = Carrying capacity
cards.quote: Where N = Population density at time t r = Intrinsic rate of natural increase K = Carrying capacity
cards.note: Equation as printed on p195: dN/dt = rN((K – N)/K), the Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth model.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is the logistic growth model considered more realistic?
cards.back: Since resources for growth for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, the logistic growth model is considered a more realistic one.
cards.quote: Since resources for growth for most animal populations are finite and become limiting sooner or later, the logistic growth model is considered a more realistic one.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When resources are unlimited, the growth is usually ____ but when resources become progressively limiting, the growth pattern turns ____.
cards.back: When resources are unlimited, the growth is usually exponential but when resources become progressively limiting, the growth pattern turns logistic.
cards.quote: When resources are unlimited, the growth is usually exponential but when resources become progressively limiting, the growth pattern turns logistic.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness, also called ____ (high r value), in the habitat in which they live.
cards.back: Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness, also called Darwinian fitness (high r value), in the habitat in which they live.
cards.quote: Populations evolve to maximise their reproductive fitness, also called Darwinian fitness (high r value), in the habitat in which they live.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name organisms that breed only once in their lifetime and those that breed many times.
cards.back: Some organisms breed only once in their lifetime (Pacific salmon fish, bamboo) while others breed many times during their lifetime (most birds and mammals).
cards.quote: Some organisms breed only once in their lifetime (Pacific salmon fish, bamboo) while others breed many times during their lifetime (most birds and mammals).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which organisms produce many small offspring and which produce few large offspring?
cards.back: Some produce a large number of small-sized offspring (Oysters, pelagic fishes) while others produce a small number of large-sized offspring (birds, mammals).
cards.quote: Some produce a large number of small-sized offspring (Oysters, pelagic fishes) while others produce a small number of large-sized offspring (birds, mammals).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Life history traits of organisms evolve in relation to what?
cards.back: Ecologists suggest that life history traits of organisms have evolved in relation to the constraints imposed by the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat in which they live.
cards.quote: Ecologists suggest that life history traits of organisms have evolved in relation to the constraints imposed by the abiotic and biotic components of the habitat in which they live.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are interspecific interactions?
cards.back: Interspecific interactions arise from the interaction of populations of two different species.
cards.quote: Interspecific interactions arise from the interaction of populations of two different species.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of interspecific interactions.
cards.back:
competition
predation
parasitism
commensalism
amensalism
mutualism
cards.quote: competition (both species suffer), predation and parasitism (one benefits and the other suffers), commensalism (one benefits and the other is unaffected), amensalism (one is harmed, other unaffected) and mutualism (both species benefit)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Population interactions (Table 11.1): the name for each effect on Species A and B (+ benefit, – harm, 0 neutral).
cards.back:
+ + Mutualism
– – Competition
+ – Predation
+ – Parasitism
+ 0 Commensalism
– 0 Amensalism
cards.quote: Species A Species B Name of Interaction + + Mutualism – – Competition + – Predation + – Parasitism + 0 Commensalism – 0 Amensalism

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Both the species benefit in ____ and both lose in ____ in their interactions with each other.
cards.back: Both the species benefit in mutualism and both lose in competition in their interactions with each other.
cards.quote: Both the species benefit in mutualism and both lose in competition in their interactions with each other.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In predation and parasitism, which species benefits and which is harmed?
cards.back: In both parasitism and predation only one species benefits (parasite and predator, respectively) and the interaction is detrimental to the other species (host and prey, respectively).
cards.quote: In both parasitism and predation only one species benefits (parasite and predator, respectively) and the interaction is detrimental to the other species (host and prey, respectively).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define commensalism.
cards.back: The interaction where one species is benefitted and the other is neither benefitted nor harmed is called commensalism.
cards.quote: The interaction where one species is benefitted and the other is neither benefitted nor harmed is called commensalism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define amensalism.
cards.back: In amensalism on the other hand one species is harmed whereas the other is unaffected.
cards.quote: In amensalism on the other hand one species is harmed whereas the other is unaffected.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What common characteristic do predation, parasitism and commensalism share?
cards.back: Predation, parasitism and commensalism share a common characteristic– the interacting species live closely together.
cards.quote: Predation, parasitism and commensalism share a common characteristic– the interacting species live closely together.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: You can think of ____ as nature's way of transferring to higher trophic levels the energy fixed by plants.
cards.back: You can think of predation as nature's way of transferring to higher trophic levels the energy fixed by plants.
cards.quote: You can think of predation as nature's way of transferring to higher trophic levels the energy fixed by plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What roles do predators play besides energy transfer?
cards.back: Besides acting as ‘conduits’ for energy transfer across trophic levels, predators play other important roles. They keep prey populations under control. But for predators, prey species could achieve very high population densities and cause ecosystem instability.
cards.quote: Besides acting as ‘conduits’ for energy transfer across trophic levels, predators play other important roles. They keep prey populations under control. But for predators, prey species could achieve very high population densities and cause ecosystem instability.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How do predators help maintain species diversity in a community?
cards.back: Predators also help in maintaining species diversity in a community, by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species.
cards.quote: Predators also help in maintaining species diversity in a community, by reducing the intensity of competition among competing prey species.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How was the prickly pear cactus controlled in Australia?
cards.back: The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920's caused havoc by spreading rapidly into millions of hectares of rangeland. Finally, the invasive cactus was brought under control only after a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) from its natural habitat was introduced into the country.
cards.quote: The prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1920's caused havoc by spreading rapidly into millions of hectares of rangeland. Finally, the invasive cactus was brought under control only after a cactus-feeding predator (a moth) from its natural habitat was introduced into the country.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why do certain exotic species become invasive?
cards.back: When certain exotic species are introduced into a geographical area, they become invasive and start spreading fast because the invaded land does not have its natural predators.
cards.quote: When certain exotic species are introduced into a geographical area, they become invasive and start spreading fast because the invaded land does not have its natural predators.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which starfish is the important predator of the American Pacific Coast rocky intertidal?
cards.back: In the rocky intertidal communities of the American Pacific Coast the starfish Pisaster is an important predator. In a field experiment, when all the starfish were removed from an enclosed intertidal area, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year, because of interspecific competition.
cards.quote: In the rocky intertidal communities of the American Pacific Coast the starfish Pisaster is an important predator. In a field experiment, when all the starfish were removed from an enclosed intertidal area, more than 10 species of invertebrates became extinct within a year, because of interspecific competition.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are predators in nature ‘prudent’?
cards.back: If a predator is too efficient and overexploits its prey, then the prey might become extinct and following it, the predator will also become extinct for lack of food. This is the reason why predators in nature are ‘prudent’.
