cards.quote: If a predator is too efficient and overexploits its prey, then the prey might become extinct and following it, the predator will also become extinct for lack of food. This is the reason why predators in nature are ‘prudent’.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Some species of insects and frogs are cryptically-coloured (____) to avoid being detected easily by the predator.
cards.back: Some species of insects and frogs are cryptically-coloured (camouflaged) to avoid being detected easily by the predator.
cards.quote: Some species of insects and frogs are cryptically-coloured (camouflaged) to avoid being detected easily by the predator.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is the Monarch butterfly distasteful to birds?
cards.back: The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predator (bird) because of a special chemical present in its body. Interestingly, the butterfly acquires this chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed.
cards.quote: The Monarch butterfly is highly distasteful to its predator (bird) because of a special chemical present in its body. Interestingly, the butterfly acquires this chemical during its caterpillar stage by feeding on a poisonous weed.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the case of plants, who are the predators?
cards.back: For plants, herbivores are the predators.
cards.quote: For plants, herbivores are the predators.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the most common morphological means of defence in plants against herbivores?
cards.back: Thorns (Acacia, Cactus) are the most common morphological means of defence.
cards.quote: Thorns (Acacia, Cactus) are the most common morphological means of defence.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why do cattle and goats not browse on the weed Calotropis?
cards.back: The plant produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides and that is why you never see any cattle or goats browsing on this plant.
cards.quote: The plant produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides and that is why you never see any cattle or goats browsing on this plant.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name plant chemicals extracted commercially that are produced as defences against grazers and browsers.
cards.back:
nicotine
caffeine
quinine
strychnine
opium
cards.quote: nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine, opium

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which unrelated species compete for zooplankton in some shallow South American lakes?
cards.back: in some shallow South American lakes, visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, the zooplankton in the lake.
cards.quote: in some shallow South American lakes, visiting flamingoes and resident fishes compete for their common food, the zooplankton in the lake.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is interference competition?
cards.back: in interference competition, the feeding efficiency of one species might be reduced due to the interfering and inhibitory presence of the other species, even if resources (food and space) are abundant.
cards.quote: in interference competition, the feeding efficiency of one species might be reduced due to the interfering and inhibitory presence of the other species, even if resources (food and space) are abundant.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define competition.
cards.back: competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured in terms of its ‘r’ the intrinsic rate of increase) is significantly lower in the presence of another species.
cards.quote: competition is best defined as a process in which the fitness of one species (measured in terms of its ‘r’ the intrinsic rate of increase) is significantly lower in the presence of another species.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What caused the extinction of the Abingdon tortoise in the Galapagos Islands?
cards.back: The Abingdon tortoise in Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced on the island, apparently due to the greater browsing efficiency of the goats.
cards.quote: The Abingdon tortoise in Galapagos Islands became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced on the island, apparently due to the greater browsing efficiency of the goats.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is competitive release?
cards.back: A species whose distribution is restricted to a small geographical area because of the presence of a competitively superior species, is found to expand its distributional range dramatically when the competing species is experimentally removed.
cards.quote: Another evidence for the occurrence of competition in nature comes from what is called ‘competitive release’. A species whose distribution is restricted to a small geographical area because of the presence of a competitively superior species, is found to expand its distributional range dramatically when the competing species is experimentally removed.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did Connell's experiments show about barnacles on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland?
cards.back: Connell's elegant field experiments showed that on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area, and excludes the smaller barnacle Chathamalus from that zone.
cards.quote: Connell's elegant field experiments showed that on the rocky sea coasts of Scotland, the larger and competitively superior barnacle Balanus dominates the intertidal area, and excludes the smaller barnacle Chathamalus from that zone.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which are more adversely affected by competition, herbivores and plants or carnivores?
cards.back: In general, herbivores and plants appear to be more adversely affected by competition than carnivores.
cards.quote: In general, herbivores and plants appear to be more adversely affected by competition than carnivores.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: State Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle.
cards.back: Gause's ‘Competitive Exclusion Principle’ states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually.
cards.quote: Gause's ‘Competitive Exclusion Principle’ states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot co-exist indefinitely and the competitively inferior one will be eliminated eventually.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is resource partitioning?
cards.back: If two species compete for the same resource, they could avoid competition by choosing, for instance, different times for feeding or different foraging patterns.
cards.quote: One such mechanism is ‘resource partitioning’. If two species compete for the same resource, they could avoid competition by choosing, for instance, different times for feeding or different foraging patterns.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did MacArthur show about five closely related species of warblers on the same tree?
cards.back: MacArthur showed that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree were able to avoid competition and co-exist due to behavioural differences in their foraging activities.
cards.quote: MacArthur showed that five closely related species of warblers living on the same tree were able to avoid competition and co-exist due to behavioural differences in their foraging activities.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is meant by a host-specific parasite?
cards.back: Many parasites have evolved to be host-specific (they can parasitise only a single species of host)
cards.quote: Many parasites have evolved to be host-specific (they can parasitise only a single species of host)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the special adaptations evolved by parasites.
cards.back:
loss of unnecessary sense organs
presence of adhesive organs or suckers to cling on to the host
loss of digestive system
high reproductive capacity
cards.quote: In accordance with their life styles, parasites evolved special adaptations such as the loss of unnecessary sense organs, presence of adhesive organs or suckers to cling on to the host, loss of digestive system and high reproductive capacity.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do the human liver fluke and the malarial parasite depend on to complete their life cycle?
cards.back: The human liver fluke (a trematode parasite) depends on two intermediate hosts (a snail and a fish) to complete its life cycle. The malarial parasite needs a vector (mosquito) to spread to other hosts.
cards.quote: The human liver fluke (a trematode parasite) depends on two intermediate hosts (a snail and a fish) to complete its life cycle. The malarial parasite needs a vector (mosquito) to spread to other hosts.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How do most parasites harm the host?
cards.back: Majority of the parasites harm the host; they may reduce the survival, growth and reproduction of the host and reduce its population density.
cards.quote: Majority of the parasites harm the host; they may reduce the survival, growth and reproduction of the host and reduce its population density.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are ectoparasites?
cards.back: Parasites that feed on the external surface of the host organism are called ectoparasites. The most familiar examples of this group are the lice on humans and ticks on dogs.
cards.quote: Parasites that feed on the external surface of the host organism are called ectoparasites. The most familiar examples of this group are the lice on humans and ticks on dogs.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What has the parasitic plant Cuscuta lost in the course of evolution?
cards.back: Cuscuta, a parasitic plant that is commonly found growing on hedge plants, has lost its chlorophyll and leaves in the course of evolution.
cards.quote: Cuscuta, a parasitic plant that is commonly found growing on hedge plants, has lost its chlorophyll and leaves in the course of evolution.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are endoparasites?
cards.back: In contrast, endoparasites are those that live inside the host body at different sites (liver, kidney, lungs, red blood cells, etc.).
cards.quote: In contrast, endoparasites are those that live inside the host body at different sites (liver, kidney, lungs, red blood cells, etc.).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is brood parasitism in birds?
cards.back: Brood parasitism in birds is a fascinating example of parasitism in which the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of its host and lets the host incubate them.
cards.quote: Brood parasitism in birds is a fascinating example of parasitism in which the parasitic bird lays its eggs in the nest of its host and lets the host incubate them.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Give examples of commensalism involving an orchid and barnacles.
cards.back: An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch, and barnacles growing on the back of a whale benefit while neither the mango tree nor the whale derives any apparent benefit.
cards.quote: An orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch, and barnacles growing on the back of a whale benefit while neither the mango tree nor the whale derives any apparent benefit.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which association of a bird and grazing animals is a classic example of commensalism?
cards.back: The cattle egret and grazing cattle in close association, a sight you are most likely to catch if you live in farmed rural areas, is a classic example of commensalism.
cards.quote: The cattle egret and grazing cattle in close association, a sight you are most likely to catch if you live in farmed rural areas, is a classic example of commensalism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which sea anemone association is an example of commensalism, and who benefits?
cards.back: Another example of commensalism is the interaction between sea anemone that has stinging tentacles and the clown fish that lives among them. The fish gets protection from predators which stay away from the stinging tentacles.
cards.quote: Another example of commensalism is the interaction between sea anemone that has stinging tentacles and the clown fish that lives among them. The fish gets protection from predators which stay away from the stinging tentacles.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define mutualism.
cards.back: Mutualism: This interaction confers benefits on both the interacting species.
cards.quote: Mutualism: This interaction confers benefits on both the interacting species.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do lichens represent?
cards.back: Lichens represent an intimate mutualistic relationship between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria.
cards.quote: Lichens represent an intimate mutualistic relationship between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are mycorrhizae?
cards.back: the mycorrhizae are associations between fungi and the roots of higher plants. The fungi help the plant in the absorption of essential nutrients from the soil while the plant in turn provides the fungi with energy-yielding carbohydrates.
cards.quote: Similarly, the mycorrhizae are associations between fungi and the roots of higher plants. The fungi help the plant in the absorption of essential nutrients from the soil while the plant in turn provides the fungi with energy-yielding carbohydrates.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What rewards do plants offer to pollinators and to seed dispersers?
cards.back: Plants offer rewards or fees in the form of pollen and nectar for pollinators and juicy and nutritious fruits for seed dispersers.
cards.quote: Plants offer rewards or fees in the form of pollen and nectar for pollinators and juicy and nutritious fruits for seed dispersers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is co-evolution of mutualists in plant-animal interactions?
cards.back: plant-animal interactions often involve co-evolution of the mutualists, that is, the evolutions of the flower and its pollinator species are tightly linked with one another.
cards.quote: plant-animal interactions often involve co-evolution of the mutualists, that is, the evolutions of the flower and its pollinator species are tightly linked with one another.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Describe the mutualism between the fig tree and the wasp.
cards.back: In many species of fig trees, there is a tight one-to-one relationship with the pollinator species of wasp (Figure 11.4). It means that a given fig species can be pollinated only by its ‘partner’ wasp species and no other species.
cards.quote: In many species of fig trees, there is a tight one-to-one relationship with the pollinator species of wasp (Figure 11.4). It means that a given fig species can be pollinated only by its ‘partner’ wasp species and no other species.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the fig offer the wasp in return for pollination?
cards.back: In return for the favour of pollination the fig offers the wasp some of its developing seeds, as food for the developing wasp larvae.
cards.quote: In return for the favour of pollination the fig offers the wasp some of its developing seeds, as food for the developing wasp larvae.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employ to get pollination done by a species of bee?
cards.back: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs ‘sexual deceit’ to get pollination done by a species of bee.
cards.quote: The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs ‘sexual deceit’ to get pollination done by a species of bee.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define Ecology.
cards.back: As a branch of biology, Ecology is the study of the relationships of living organisms with the abiotic (physico-chemical factors) and biotic components (other species) of their environment.
cards.quote: As a branch of biology, Ecology is the study of the relationships of living organisms with the abiotic (physico-chemical factors) and biotic components (other species) of their environment.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: For how many years, and when, did Gregor Mendel hybridise garden peas?
cards.back: Gregor Mendel, conducted hybridisation experiments on garden peas for seven years (1856-1863) and proposed the laws of inheritance in living organisms.
cards.quote: Gregor Mendel, conducted hybridisation experiments on garden peas for seven years (1856-1863) and proposed the laws of inheritance in living organisms.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What were applied for the first time to problems in biology in Mendel's investigations into inheritance patterns?
cards.back: During Mendel's investigations into inheritance patterns it was for the first time that statistical analysis and mathematical logic were applied to problems in biology.
cards.quote: During Mendel's investigations into inheritance patterns it was for the first time that statistical analysis and mathematical logic were applied to problems in biology.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a true-breeding line?
cards.back: A true-breeding line is one that, having undergone continuous self-pollination, shows the stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations.
cards.quote: A true-breeding line is one that, having undergone continuous self-pollination, shows the stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many true-breeding pea plant varieties did Mendel select, and how were they paired?
cards.back: Mendel selected 14 true-breeding pea plant varieties, as pairs which were similar except for one character with contrasting traits.
cards.quote: Mendel selected 14 true-breeding pea plant varieties, as pairs which were similar except for one character with contrasting traits.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the seven characters Mendel studied in pea and their contrasting traits (Table 4.1).
cards.back:
Stem height: Tall/dwarf
Flower colour: Violet/white
Flower position: Axial/terminal
Pod shape: Inflated/constricted
Pod colour: Green/yellow
Seed shape: Round/wrinkled
Seed colour: Yellow/green
cards.quote: 1. Stem height Tall/dwarf 2. Flower colour Violet/white 3. Flower position Axial/terminal 4. Pod shape Inflated/constricted 5. Pod colour Green/yellow 6. Seed shape Round/wrinkled 7. Seed colour Yellow/green

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the first hybrid generation also called?
cards.back: He collected the seeds produced as a result of this cross and grew them to generate plants of the first hybrid generation. This generation is also called the Filial1 progeny or the F1.
cards.quote: He collected the seeds produced as a result of this cross and grew them to generate plants of the first hybrid generation. This generation is also called the Filial1 progeny or the F1.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In Mendel's tall x dwarf cross, what were the F1 progeny plants like?
cards.back: Mendel observed that all the F1 progeny plants were tall, like one of its parents; none were dwarf (Figure 4.3).
cards.quote: Mendel observed that all the F1 progeny plants were tall, like one of its parents; none were dwarf (Figure 4.3).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In what proportion were both parental traits expressed at the F2 stage in Mendel's crosses?
cards.back: Similar results were obtained with the other traits that he studied: only one of the parental traits was expressed in the F1 generation while at the F2 stage both the traits were expressed in the proportion 3:1.
cards.quote: Similar results were obtained with the other traits that he studied: only one of the parental traits was expressed in the F1 generation while at the F2 stage both the traits were expressed in the proportion 3:1.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The contrasting traits did not show any ____ at either F1 or F2 stage.
cards.back: The contrasting traits did not show any blending at either F1 or F2 stage.
cards.quote: The contrasting traits did not show any blending at either F1 or F2 stage.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are genes (Mendel's 'factors')?
cards.back: Genes, therefore, are the units of inheritance. They contain the information that is required to express a particular trait in an organism.
cards.quote: Genes, therefore, are the units of inheritance. They contain the information that is required to express a particular trait in an organism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are alleles?
cards.back: Genes which code for a pair of contrasting traits are known as alleles, i.e., they are slightly different forms of the same gene.
cards.quote: Genes which code for a pair of contrasting traits are known as alleles, i.e., they are slightly different forms of the same gene.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are letters used as symbols for the two alleles of a gene?
cards.back: the capital letter is used for the trait expressed at the F1 stage and the small alphabet for the other trait.
cards.quote: If we use alphabetical symbols for each gene, then the capital letter is used for the trait expressed at the F1 stage and the small alphabet for the other trait.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is meant by homozygous (as in TT and tt)?
cards.back: the allelic pair of genes for height are identical or homozygous, TT and tt, respectively.
cards.quote: Mendel also proposed that in a true breeding, tall or dwarf pea variety the allelic pair of genes for height are identical or homozygous, TT and tt, respectively.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: TT and tt are called the ____ of the plant while the descriptive terms tall and dwarf are the ____.
cards.back: TT and tt are called the genotype of the plant while the descriptive terms tall and dwarf are the phenotype.
cards.quote: TT and tt are called the genotype of the plant while the descriptive terms tall and dwarf are the phenotype.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the dominant factor and the recessive factor?
cards.back: in a pair of dissimilar factors, one dominates the other (as in the F1) and hence is called the dominant factor while the other factor is recessive.
cards.quote: in a pair of dissimilar factors, one dominates the other (as in the F1) and hence is called the dominant factor while the other factor is recessive.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Since these hybrids contain alleles which express contrasting traits, the plants are ____.
cards.back: Since these hybrids contain alleles which express contrasting traits, the plants are heterozygous.
cards.quote: Since these hybrids contain alleles which express contrasting traits, the plants are heterozygous.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a Punnett square, and who developed it?
cards.back: It was developed by a British geneticist, Reginald C. Punnett. It is a graphical representation to calculate the probability of all possible genotypes of offspring in a genetic cross.
cards.quote: It was developed by a British geneticist, Reginald C. Punnett. It is a graphical representation to calculate the probability of all possible genotypes of offspring in a genetic cross.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In a monohybrid F2, what fractions of random fertilisations give TT, Tt and tt?
cards.back: From the Punnett square it is easily seen that 1/4th of the random fertilisations lead to TT, 1/2 lead to Tt and 1/4th to tt.
cards.quote: From the Punnett square it is easily seen that 1/4th of the random fertilisations lead to TT, 1/2 lead to Tt and 1/4th to tt.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the phenotypic and genotypic ratios of a monohybrid F2?
cards.back: This leads to a phenotypic ratio of 3/4th tall : (1/4 TT + 1/2 Tt) and 1/4th tt, i.e., a 3:1 ratio, but a genotypic ratio of 1:2:1.
cards.quote: This leads to a phenotypic ratio of 3/4th tall : (1/4 TT + 1/2 Tt) and 1/4th tt, i.e., a 3:1 ratio, but a genotypic ratio of 1:2:1.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: the binomial expansion of the 1/4 : 1/2 : 1/4 ratio of TT : Tt : tt.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a test cross?
cards.back: In a typical test cross an organism (pea plants here) showing a dominant phenotype (and whose genotype is to be determined) is crossed with the recessive parent instead of self-crossing.
cards.quote: In a typical test cross an organism (pea plants here) showing a dominant phenotype (and whose genotype is to be determined) is crossed with the recessive parent instead of self-crossing.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are Mendel's First Law and Second Law of Inheritance called?
cards.back: Today these rules are called the Principles or Laws of Inheritance: the First Law or Law of Dominance and the Second Law or Law of Segregation.
cards.quote: Today these rules are called the Principles or Laws of Inheritance: the First Law or Law of Dominance and the Second Law or Law of Segregation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: State the three points of Mendel's Law of Dominance.
cards.back:
(i) Characters are controlled by discrete units called factors.
(ii) Factors occur in pairs.
(iii) In a dissimilar pair of factors one member of the pair dominates (dominant) the other (recessive).
cards.quote: (i) Characters are controlled by discrete units called factors. (ii) Factors occur in pairs. (iii) In a dissimilar pair of factors one member of the pair dominates (dominant) the other (recessive).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the Law of Dominance explain?
cards.back: The law of dominance is used to explain the expression of only one of the parental characters in a monohybrid cross in the F1 and the expression of both in the F2. It also explains the proportion of 3:1 obtained at the F2.
cards.quote: The law of dominance is used to explain the expression of only one of the parental characters in a monohybrid cross in the F1 and the expression of both in the F2. It also explains the proportion of 3:1 obtained at the F2.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: State Mendel's Law of Segregation.
cards.back: Though the parents contain two alleles during gamete formation, the factors or alleles of a pair segregate from each other such that a gamete receives only one of the two factors.
cards.quote: Though the parents contain two alleles during gamete formation, the factors or alleles of a pair segregate from each other such that a gamete receives only one of the two factors.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What kinds of gametes do a homozygous parent and a heterozygous parent produce?
cards.back: Of course, a homozygous parent produces all gametes that are similar while a heterozygous one produces two kinds of gametes each having one allele with equal proportion.
cards.quote: Of course, a homozygous parent produces all gametes that are similar while a heterozygous one produces two kinds of gametes each having one allele with equal proportion.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is incomplete dominance?
cards.back: sometimes the F1 had a phenotype that did not resemble either of the two parents and was in between the two.
cards.quote: sometimes the F1 had a phenotype that did not resemble either of the two parents and was in between the two.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In snapdragon, what is the F1 colour of a cross between true-breeding red (RR) and white (rr)?
cards.back: In a cross between true-breeding red-flowered (RR) and true-breeding white-flowered plants (rr), the F1 (Rr) was pink (Figure 4.6).
cards.quote: In a cross between true-breeding red-flowered (RR) and true-breeding white-flowered plants (rr), the F1 (Rr) was pink (Figure 4.6).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In snapdragon, what is the F2 phenotypic ratio when the pink F1 (Rr) is self-pollinated?
cards.back: When the F1 was self-pollinated the F2 resulted in the following ratio 1 (RR) Red : 2 (Rr) Pink : 1 (rr) White.
cards.quote: When the F1 was self-pollinated the F2 resulted in the following ratio 1 (RR) Red : 2 (Rr) Pink : 1 (rr) White.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Enzyme explanation of dominance: is the unmodified (functioning) allele or the modified allele the dominant one?
cards.back: The unmodified (functioning) allele, which represents the original phenotype is the dominant allele and the modified allele is generally the recessive allele.
cards.quote: The unmodified (functioning) allele, which represents the original phenotype is the dominant allele and the modified allele is generally the recessive allele.

source.section: Explanation of the concept of dominance

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is co-dominance? Give the human example.
cards.back: in the case of co-dominance the F1 generation resembles both parents. A good example is different types of red blood cells that determine ABO blood grouping in human beings.
cards.quote: in the case of co-dominance the F1 generation resembles both parents. A good example is different types of red blood cells that determine ABO blood grouping in human beings.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The gene (I) has three alleles ____.
cards.back: The gene (I) has three alleles IA, IB and i.
cards.quote: The gene (I) has three alleles IA, IB and i.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do the alleles IA, IB and i produce on the red blood cell surface?
cards.back: The alleles IA and IB produce a slightly different form of the sugar while allele i does not produce any sugar.
cards.quote: The alleles IA and IB produce a slightly different form of the sugar while allele i does not produce any sugar.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When IA and IB are present together, what happens, and why?
cards.back: But when IA and IB are present together they both express their own types of sugars: this is because of co-dominance.
cards.quote: But when IA and IB are present together they both express their own types of sugars: this is because of co-dominance.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many genotypes of human ABO blood types are possible with three alleles?
cards.back: Since there are three different alleles, there are six different combinations of these three alleles that are possible, and therefore, a total of six different genotypes of the human ABO blood types (Table 4.2).
cards.quote: Since there are three different alleles, there are six different combinations of these three alleles that are possible, and therefore, a total of six different genotypes of the human ABO blood types (Table 4.2).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Table 4.2 (parent 1 allele, parent 2 allele, offspring genotype, blood type): rows IA+IA, IA+IB and IA+i.
cards.back:
IA IA IAIA A
IA IB IAIB AB
IA i IAi A
cards.quote: IA IA IAIA A IA IB IAIB AB IA i IAi A

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Table 4.2 (parent 1 allele, parent 2 allele, offspring genotype, blood type): rows IB+IA, IB+IB, IB+i and i+i.
cards.back:
IB IA IAIB AB
IB IB IBIB B
IB i IBi B
i i ii O
cards.quote: IB IA IAIB AB IB IB IBIB B IB i IBi B i i ii O

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is ABO blood grouping an example of multiple alleles, and when can multiple alleles be found?
cards.back: Here you can see that there are more than two, i.e., three alleles, governing the same character. Since in an individual only two alleles can be present, multiple alleles can be found only when population studies are made.
cards.quote: Here you can see that there are more than two, i.e., three alleles, governing the same character. Since in an individual only two alleles can be present, multiple alleles can be found only when population studies are made.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In Mendel's yellow-round x green-wrinkled seed cross, which traits were dominant?
cards.back: Thus, yellow colour was dominant over green and round shape dominant over wrinkled.
cards.quote: Thus, yellow colour was dominant over green and round shape dominant over wrinkled.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the parental gametes and F1 hybrid genotype of the RRYY x rryy cross?
cards.back: The gametes RY and ry unite on fertilisation to produce the F1 hybrid RrYy.
cards.quote: The gametes RY and ry unite on fertilisation to produce the F1 hybrid RrYy.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a dihybrid cross?
cards.back: crosses between plants differing in two traits
cards.quote: crosses between plants differing in two traits

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In Mendel's dihybrid cross, in what ratio did the four F2 phenotypes appear?
cards.back: In the dihybrid cross (Figure 4.7), the phenotypes round, yellow; wrinkled, yellow; round, green and wrinkled, green appeared in the ratio 9:3:3:1.
cards.quote: In the dihybrid cross (Figure 4.7), the phenotypes round, yellow; wrinkled, yellow; round, green and wrinkled, green appeared in the ratio 9:3:3:1.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Formula: how is the 9:3:3:1 ratio derived as a combination series?
cards.back: (3 Round : 1 Wrinkled) (3 Yellow : 1 Green) = 9 Round, Yellow : 3 Wrinkled, Yellow: 3 Round, Green : 1 Wrinkled, Green
cards.quote: (3 Round : 1 Wrinkled) (3 Yellow : 1 Green) = 9 Round, Yellow : 3 Wrinkled, Yellow: 3 Round, Green : 1 Wrinkled, Green

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: State Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment.
cards.back: when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters
cards.quote: when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What gamete types does the F1 RrYy plant produce, and in what frequency?
cards.back: Thus there are four genotypes of gametes (four types of pollen and four types of eggs). The four types are RY, Ry, rY and ry each with a frequency of 25 per cent or 1/4th of the total gametes produced.
cards.quote: Thus there are four genotypes of gametes (four types of pollen and four types of eggs). The four types are RY, Ry, rY and ry each with a frequency of 25 per cent or 1/4th of the total gametes produced.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When did Mendel publish his work, and until when did it remain unrecognised?
cards.back: Mendel published his work on inheritance of characters in 1865 but for several reasons, it remained unrecognised till 1900.
cards.quote: Mendel published his work on inheritance of characters in 1865 but for several reasons, it remained unrecognised till 1900.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which three scientists independently rediscovered Mendel's results in 1900?
cards.back: In 1900, three Scientists (de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak) independently rediscovered Mendel's results on the inheritance of characters.
cards.quote: In 1900, three Scientists (de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak) independently rediscovered Mendel's results on the inheritance of characters.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who noted that chromosome behaviour parallels gene behaviour and used it to explain Mendel's laws?
cards.back: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted that the behaviour of chromosomes was parallel to the behaviour of genes and used chromosome movement (Figure 4.8) to explain Mendel's laws (Table 4.3).
cards.quote: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted that the behaviour of chromosomes was parallel to the behaviour of genes and used chromosome movement (Figure 4.8) to explain Mendel's laws (Table 4.3).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The two alleles of a gene pair are located on ____ on homologous chromosomes.
cards.back: The two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites on homologous chromosomes.
cards.quote: The two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites on homologous chromosomes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the chromosomal theory of inheritance, and who called it so?
cards.back: Sutton and Boveri argued that the pairing and separation of a pair of chromosomes would lead to the segregation of a pair of factors they carried. Sutton united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance.
cards.quote: Sutton and Boveri argued that the pairing and separation of a pair of chromosomes would lead to the segregation of a pair of factors they carried. Sutton united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which organism did Thomas Hunt Morgan use to verify the chromosomal theory?
cards.back: Morgan worked with the tiny fruit flies, Drosophila melanogaster (Figure 4.10), which were found very suitable for such studies.
cards.quote: Morgan worked with the tiny fruit flies, Drosophila melanogaster (Figure 4.10), which were found very suitable for such studies.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did Morgan observe about the F2 ratio for two sex-linked genes in his dihybrid cross?
cards.back: He observed that the two genes did not segregate independently of each other and the F2 ratio deviated very significantly from the 9:3:3:1 ratio (expected when the two genes are independent).
cards.quote: He observed that the two genes did not segregate independently of each other and the F2 ratio deviated very significantly from the 9:3:3:1 ratio (expected when the two genes are independent).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define linkage (term coined by Morgan).
cards.back: Morgan attributed this due to the physical association or linkage of the two genes and coined the term linkage to describe this physical association of genes on a chromosome
cards.quote: Morgan attributed this due to the physical association or linkage of the two genes and coined the term linkage to describe this physical association of genes on a chromosome

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define recombination (term coined by Morgan).
cards.back: Morgan attributed this due to the physical association or linkage of the two genes and coined the term linkage to describe this physical association of genes on a chromosome and the term recombination to describe the generation of non-parental gene combinations
cards.quote: Morgan attributed this due to the physical association or linkage of the two genes and coined the term linkage to describe this physical association of genes on a chromosome and the term recombination to describe the generation of non-parental gene combinations

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When two genes of a dihybrid cross lie on the same chromosome, which gene combinations are more frequent?
cards.back: when the two genes in a dihybrid cross were situated on the same chromosome, the proportion of parental gene combinations were much higher than the non-parental type.
cards.quote: when the two genes in a dihybrid cross were situated on the same chromosome, the proportion of parental gene combinations were much higher than the non-parental type.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What did Morgan's group find about genes on the same chromosome and recombination?
cards.back: some genes were very tightly linked (showed very low recombination) (Figure 4.11, Cross A) while others were loosely linked (showed higher recombination) (Figure 4.11, Cross B).
cards.quote: some genes were very tightly linked (showed very low recombination) (Figure 4.11, Cross A) while others were loosely linked (showed higher recombination) (Figure 4.11, Cross B).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What recombination frequencies did white-yellow and white-miniature wing genes show?
cards.back: he found that the genes white and yellow were very tightly linked and showed only 1.3 per cent recombination while white and miniature wing showed 37.2 per cent recombination.
cards.quote: he found that the genes white and yellow were very tightly linked and showed only 1.3 per cent recombination while white and miniature wing showed 37.2 per cent recombination.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Who used recombination frequency as a measure of the distance between genes to map them?
cards.back: His student Alfred Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes and `mapped' their position on the chromosome.
cards.quote: His student Alfred Sturtevant used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes and `mapped' their position on the chromosome.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are polygenic traits?
cards.back: Such traits are generally controlled by three or more genes and are thus called as polygenic traits.
cards.quote: Such traits are generally controlled by three or more genes and are thus called as polygenic traits.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Besides the involvement of multiple genes polygenic inheritance also takes into account the influence of ____.
cards.back: Besides the involvement of multiple genes polygenic inheritance also takes into account the influence of environment.
cards.quote: Besides the involvement of multiple genes polygenic inheritance also takes into account the influence of environment.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In a polygenic trait the phenotype reflects the contribution of each allele, i.e., the effect of each allele is ____.
cards.back: In a polygenic trait the phenotype reflects the contribution of each allele, i.e., the effect of each allele is additive.
cards.quote: In a polygenic trait the phenotype reflects the contribution of each allele, i.e., the effect of each allele is additive.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the three-gene model of human skin colour, which genotypes give the darkest and the lightest skin?
cards.back: The genotype with all the dominant alleles (AABBCC) will have the darkest skin colour and that with all the recessive alleles (aabbcc) will have the lightest skin colour.
cards.quote: The genotype with all the dominant alleles (AABBCC) will have the darkest skin colour and that with all the recessive alleles (aabbcc) will have the lightest skin colour.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a pleiotropic gene?
cards.back: There are however instances where a single gene can exhibit multiple phenotypic expression. Such a gene is called a pleiotropic gene.
cards.quote: There are however instances where a single gene can exhibit multiple phenotypic expression. Such a gene is called a pleiotropic gene.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the mechanism of pleiotropy, and which human disease is an example?
cards.back: The underlying mechanism of pleiotropy in most cases is the effect of a gene on metabolic pathways which contribute towards different phenotypes. An example of this is the disease phenylketonuria, which occurs in humans.
cards.quote: The underlying mechanism of pleiotropy in most cases is the effect of a gene on metabolic pathways which contribute towards different phenotypes. An example of this is the disease phenylketonuria, which occurs in humans.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Describe XO type sex determination in insects: which eggs and sperms carry X?
cards.back: in a large number of insects the mechanism of sex determination is of the XO type, i.e., all eggs bear an additional X-chromosome besides the other chromosomes (autosomes). On the other hand, some of the sperms bear the X-chromosome whereas some do not.
cards.quote: in a large number of insects the mechanism of sex determination is of the XO type, i.e., all eggs bear an additional X-chromosome besides the other chromosomes (autosomes). On the other hand, some of the sperms bear the X-chromosome whereas some do not.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which insect is an example of XO type sex determination, and what are its male and female compositions?
cards.back: Grasshopper is an example of XO type of sex determination in which the males have only one X-chromosome besides the autosomes, whereas females have a pair of X-chromosomes.
cards.quote: Grasshopper is an example of XO type of sex determination in which the males have only one X-chromosome besides the autosomes, whereas females have a pair of X-chromosomes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What sex chromosomes do males and females have in humans and Drosophila?
cards.back: In human beings and in Drosophila the males have one X and one Y chromosome, whereas females have a pair of X-chromosomes besides autosomes (Figure 4.12 a, b).
cards.quote: In human beings and in Drosophila the males have one X and one Y chromosome, whereas females have a pair of X-chromosomes besides autosomes (Figure 4.12 a, b).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is male heterogamety?
cards.back: males produce two different types of gametes, (a) either with or without X-chromosome or (b) some gametes with X-chromosome and some with Y-chromosome. Such types of sex determination mechanism is designated to be the example of male heterogamety.
cards.quote: males produce two different types of gametes, (a) either with or without X-chromosome or (b) some gametes with X-chromosome and some with Y-chromosome. Such types of sex determination mechanism is designated to be the example of male heterogamety.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In birds, which sex chromosomes do females and males have?
cards.back: In order to have a distinction with the mechanism of sex determination described earlier, the two different sex chromosomes of a female bird has been designated to be the Z and W chromosomes. In these organisms the females have one Z and one W chromosome, whereas males have a pair of Z-chromosomes besides the autosomes.
cards.quote: In order to have a distinction with the mechanism of sex determination described earlier, the two different sex chromosomes of a female bird has been designated to be the Z and W chromosomes. In these organisms the females have one Z and one W chromosome, whereas males have a pair of Z-chromosomes besides the autosomes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Of the 23 pairs of human chromosomes, how many pairs are autosomes?
cards.back: Out of 23 pairs of chromosomes present, 22 pairs are exactly same in both males and females; these are the autosomes.
cards.quote: Out of 23 pairs of chromosomes present, 22 pairs are exactly same in both males and females; these are the autosomes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What proportion of human sperm carry X and Y, and what type of ovum do females produce?
cards.back: 50 per cent of the total sperm produced carry the X-chromosome and the rest 50 per cent has Y-chromosome besides the autosomes. Females, however, produce only one type of ovum with an X-chromosome.
cards.quote: 50 per cent of the total sperm produced carry the X-chromosome and the rest 50 per cent has Y-chromosome besides the autosomes. Females, however, produce only one type of ovum with an X-chromosome.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In humans, whose genetic makeup determines the sex of the child?
cards.back: In case the ovum fertilises with a sperm carrying X-chromosome the zygote develops into a female (XX) and the fertilisation of ovum with Y-chromosome carrying sperm results into a male offspring. Thus, it is evident that it is the genetic makeup of the sperm that determines the sex of the child.
cards.quote: In case the ovum fertilises with a sperm carrying X-chromosome the zygote develops into a female (XX) and the fertilisation of ovum with Y-chromosome carrying sperm results into a male offspring. Thus, it is evident that it is the genetic makeup of the sperm that determines the sex of the child.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does an offspring develop as female or male in the honey bee?
cards.back: An offspring formed from the union of a sperm and an egg develops as a female (queen or worker), and an unfertilised egg develops as a male (drone) by means of parthenogenesis.
cards.quote: An offspring formed from the union of a sperm and an egg develops as a female (queen or worker), and an unfertilised egg develops as a male (drone) by means of parthenogenesis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the haplodiploid sex-determination system of the honey bee?
cards.back: The females are diploid having 32 chromosomes and males are haploid, i.e., having 16 chromosomes. This is called as haplodiploid sex-determination system
cards.quote: The females are diploid having 32 chromosomes and males are haploid, i.e., having 16 chromosomes. This is called as haplodiploid sex-determination system

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Define mutation.
cards.back: Mutation is a phenomenon which results in alteration of DNA sequences and consequently results in changes in the genotype and the phenotype of an organism.
cards.quote: Mutation is a phenomenon which results in alteration of DNA sequences and consequently results in changes in the genotype and the phenotype of an organism.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In addition to recombination, ____ is another phenomenon that leads to variation in DNA.
cards.back: In addition to recombination, mutation is another phenomenon that leads to variation in DNA.
cards.quote: In addition to recombination, mutation is another phenomenon that leads to variation in DNA.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What DNA changes result in alteration in chromosomes?
cards.back: Therefore loss (deletions) or gain (insertion/duplication) of a segment of DNA, result in alteration in chromosomes.
cards.quote: Therefore loss (deletions) or gain (insertion/duplication) of a segment of DNA, result in alteration in chromosomes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Chromosomal aberrations are commonly observed in ____.
cards.back: Chromosomal aberrations are commonly observed in cancer cells.
cards.quote: Chromosomal aberrations are commonly observed in cancer cells.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a point mutation? Give the classical example.
cards.back: mutation also arise due to change in a single base pair of DNA. This is known as point mutation. A classical example of such a mutation is sickle cell anemia.
cards.quote: mutation also arise due to change in a single base pair of DNA. This is known as point mutation. A classical example of such a mutation is sickle cell anemia.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are mutagens?
cards.back: there are many chemical and physical factors that induce mutations. These are referred to as mutagens.
cards.quote: there are many chemical and physical factors that induce mutations. These are referred to as mutagens.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is pedigree analysis?
cards.back: Such an analysis of traits in a several of generations of a family is called the pedigree analysis.
cards.quote: Such an analysis of traits in a several of generations of a family is called the pedigree analysis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Into which two categories may genetic disorders broadly be grouped?
cards.back:
Mendelian disorders
Chromosomal disorders
cards.quote: Broadly, genetic disorders may be grouped into two categories – Mendelian disorders and Chromosomal disorders.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in the ____.
cards.back: Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in the single gene.
cards.quote: Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in the single gene.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the common and prevalent Mendelian disorders listed by NCERT.
cards.back:
Haemophilia
Cystic fibrosis
Sickle-cell anaemia
Colour blindness
Phenylketonuria
Thalassemia
cards.quote: Most common and prevalent Mendelian disorders are Haemophilia, Cystic fibrosis, Sickle-cell anaemia, Colour blindness, Phenylketonuria, Thalassemia, etc.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is colour blindness and what is its cause?
cards.back: Colour Blindness : It is a sex-linked recessive disorder due to defect in either red or green cone of eye resulting in failure to discriminate between red and green colour. This defect is due to mutation in certain genes present in the X chromosome.
cards.quote: Colour Blindness : It is a sex-linked recessive disorder due to defect in either red or green cone of eye resulting in failure to discriminate between red and green colour. This defect is due to mutation in certain genes present in the X chromosome.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is haemophilia and how is it transmitted?
cards.back: This sex linked recessive disease, which shows its transmission from unaffected carrier female to some of the male progeny has been widely studied.
cards.quote: This sex linked recessive disease, which shows its transmission from unaffected carrier female to some of the male progeny has been widely studied.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is affected in haemophilia, and what happens after a simple cut?
cards.back: In this disease, a single protein that is a part of the cascade of proteins involved in the clotting of blood is affected. Due to this, in an affected individual a simple cut will result in non-stop bleeding.
cards.quote: In this disease, a single protein that is a part of the cascade of proteins involved in the clotting of blood is affected. Due to this, in an affected individual a simple cut will result in non-stop bleeding.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Whose family pedigree shows a number of haemophilic descendants?
cards.back: The family pedigree of Queen Victoria shows a number of haemophilic descendents as she was a carrier of the disease.
cards.quote: The family pedigree of Queen Victoria shows a number of haemophilic descendents as she was a carrier of the disease.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is sickle-cell anaemia and when is it transmitted to offspring?
cards.back: This is an autosome linked recessive trait that can be transmitted from parents to the offspring when both the partners are carrier for the gene (or heterozygous).
cards.quote: This is an autosome linked recessive trait that can be transmitted from parents to the offspring when both the partners are carrier for the gene (or heterozygous).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In sickle-cell anaemia, which genotype shows the diseased phenotype?
cards.back: The disease is controlled by a single pair of allele, HbA and HbS. Out of the three possible genotypes only homozygous individuals for HbS (HbSHbS) show the diseased phenotype.
cards.quote: The disease is controlled by a single pair of allele, HbA and HbS. Out of the three possible genotypes only homozygous individuals for HbS (HbSHbS) show the diseased phenotype.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the status of heterozygous (HbAHbS) individuals in sickle-cell anaemia?
cards.back: Heterozygous (HbAHbS) individuals appear apparently unaffected but they are carrier of the disease as there is 50 per cent probability of transmission of the mutant gene to the progeny, thus exhibiting sickle-cell trait (Figure 4.15).
cards.quote: Heterozygous (HbAHbS) individuals appear apparently unaffected but they are carrier of the disease as there is 50 per cent probability of transmission of the mutant gene to the progeny, thus exhibiting sickle-cell trait (Figure 4.15).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In sickle-cell anaemia, which amino acid replaces glutamic acid (Glu) at the sixth position of the beta globin chain?
cards.back:
Valine (Val), replacing glutamic acid (Glu)
Valine (Val) at the sixth position of the beta globin chain of the haemoglobin molecule.
cards.quote: Valine (Val) at the sixth position of the beta globin chain of the haemoglobin molecule.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What single base substitution at the sixth codon causes the amino acid change in sickle-cell anaemia?
cards.back: The substitution of amino acid in the globin protein results due to the single base substitution at the sixth codon of the beta globin gene from GAG to GUG.
cards.quote: The substitution of amino acid in the globin protein results due to the single base substitution at the sixth codon of the beta globin gene from GAG to GUG.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens to mutant haemoglobin under low oxygen tension?
cards.back: The mutant haemoglobin molecule undergoes polymerisation under low oxygen tension causing the change in the shape of the RBC from biconcave disc to elongated sickle like structure (Figure 4.15).
cards.quote: The mutant haemoglobin molecule undergoes polymerisation under low oxygen tension causing the change in the shape of the RBC from biconcave disc to elongated sickle like structure (Figure 4.15).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is phenylketonuria and which enzyme is lacking?
cards.back: This inborn error of metabolism is also inherited as the autosomal recessive trait. The affected individual lacks an enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine.
cards.quote: This inborn error of metabolism is also inherited as the autosomal recessive trait. The affected individual lacks an enzyme that converts the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In phenylketonuria, what accumulates and what is the effect on the brain?
cards.back: As a result of this phenylalanine is accumulated and converted into phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives. Accumulation of these in brain results in mental retardation.
cards.quote: As a result of this phenylalanine is accumulated and converted into phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives. Accumulation of these in brain results in mental retardation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is thalassemia and when is it transmitted to offspring?
cards.back: This is also an autosome-linked recessive blood disease transmitted from parents to the offspring when both the partners are unaffected carrier for the gene (or heterozygous).
cards.quote: This is also an autosome-linked recessive blood disease transmitted from parents to the offspring when both the partners are unaffected carrier for the gene (or heterozygous).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How is thalassemia classified (alpha and beta types)?
cards.back: Thalassemia can be classified according to which chain of the haemoglobin molecule is affected. In α Thalassemia, production of α globin chain is affected while in β Thalassemia, production of β globin chain is affected.
cards.quote: Thalassemia can be classified according to which chain of the haemoglobin molecule is affected. In α Thalassemia, production of α globin chain is affected while in β Thalassemia, production of β globin chain is affected.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which genes and chromosome control alpha thalassemia?
cards.back: α Thalassemia is controlled by two closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 of each parent and it is observed due to mutation or deletion of one or more of the four genes.
cards.quote: α Thalassemia is controlled by two closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 of each parent and it is observed due to mutation or deletion of one or more of the four genes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which gene and chromosome control beta thalassemia?
cards.back: β Thalassemia is controlled by a single gene HBB on chromosome 11 of each parent and occurs due to mutation of one or both the genes.
cards.quote: β Thalassemia is controlled by a single gene HBB on chromosome 11 of each parent and occurs due to mutation of one or both the genes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Thalassemia vs sickle-cell anaemia: the difference in the type of problem.
cards.back: Thalassemia differs from sickle-cell anaemia in that the former is a quantitative problem of synthesising too few globin molecules while the latter is a qualitative problem of synthesising an incorrectly functioning globin.
cards.quote: Thalassemia differs from sickle-cell anaemia in that the former is a quantitative problem of synthesising too few globin molecules while the latter is a qualitative problem of synthesising an incorrectly functioning globin.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are chromosomal disorders?
cards.back: The chromosomal disorders on the other hand are caused due to absence or excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes.
cards.quote: The chromosomal disorders on the other hand are caused due to absence or excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is aneuploidy?
cards.back: Failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division cycle results in the gain or loss of a chromosome(s), called aneuploidy.
cards.quote: Failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division cycle results in the gain or loss of a chromosome(s), called aneuploidy.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What chromosomal change causes Down's syndrome and Turner's syndrome?
cards.back: Down's syndrome results in the gain of extra copy of chromosome 21. Similarly, Turner's syndrome results due to loss of an X chromosome in human females.
cards.quote: Down's syndrome results in the gain of extra copy of chromosome 21. Similarly, Turner's syndrome results due to loss of an X chromosome in human females.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Failure of cytokinesis after telophase gives a whole extra set of chromosomes: name this phenomenon and where it is seen.
cards.back: this phenomenon is known as polyploidy. This condition is often seen in plants.
cards.quote: this phenomenon is known as polyploidy. This condition is often seen in plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the total number of chromosomes in a normal human cell?
cards.back: The total number of chromosomes in a normal human cell is 46 (23 pairs).
cards.quote: The total number of chromosomes in a normal human cell is 46 (23 pairs).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What causes Down's syndrome, and who first described it?
cards.back: The cause of this genetic disorder is the presence of an additional copy of the chromosome number 21 (trisomy of 21). This disorder was first described by Langdon Down (1866).
cards.quote: The cause of this genetic disorder is the presence of an additional copy of the chromosome number 21 (trisomy of 21). This disorder was first described by Langdon Down (1866).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the physical features of an individual with Down's syndrome.
cards.back: The affected individual is short statured with small round head, furrowed tongue and partially open mouth (Figure 4.16). Palm is broad with characteristic palm crease. Physical, psychomotor and mental development is retarded.
cards.quote: The affected individual is short statured with small round head, furrowed tongue and partially open mouth (Figure 4.16). Palm is broad with characteristic palm crease. Physical, psychomotor and mental development is retarded.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What causes Klinefelter's syndrome and what is the karyotype?
cards.back: This genetic disorder is also caused due to the presence of an additional copy of X-chromosome resulting into a karyotype of 47, XXY.
cards.quote: This genetic disorder is also caused due to the presence of an additional copy of X-chromosome resulting into a karyotype of 47, XXY.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the features of an individual with Klinefelter's syndrome?
cards.back: Such an individual has overall masculine development, however, the feminine development (development of breast, i.e., Gynaecomastia) is also expressed (Figure 4.17 a). Such individuals are sterile.
cards.quote: Such an individual has overall masculine development, however, the feminine development (development of breast, i.e., Gynaecomastia) is also expressed (Figure 4.17 a). Such individuals are sterile.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are females with Turner's syndrome sterile?
cards.back: Such females are sterile as ovaries are rudimentary besides other features including lack of other secondary sexual characters (Figure 4.17 b).
cards.quote: Such females are sterile as ovaries are rudimentary besides other features including lack of other secondary sexual characters (Figure 4.17 b).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which genes do not obey the law of independent assortment, and what are they called?
cards.back: Later, it was found that Mendel's law of independent assortment does not hold true for the genes that were located on the same chromosomes. These genes were called as `linked genes'.
cards.quote: Later, it was found that Mendel's law of independent assortment does not hold true for the genes that were located on the same chromosomes. These genes were called as `linked genes'.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many chromosomes does a person with Down's syndrome have?
cards.back: consequently the total number of chromosome becomes 47.
cards.quote: Down's syndrome is due to trisomy of chromosome 21, where there is an extra copy of chromosome 21 and consequently the total number of chromosome becomes 47.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the sex chromosome conditions in Turner's and Klinefelter's syndromes?
cards.back: In Turner's syndrome, one X chromosome is missing and the sex chromosome is as XO, and in Klinefelter's syndrome, the condition is XXY.
cards.quote: In Turner's syndrome, one X chromosome is missing and the sex chromosome is as XO, and in Klinefelter's syndrome, the condition is XXY.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does reproductive health mean, according to the WHO?
cards.back: According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), reproductive health means a total well-being in all aspects of reproduction, i.e., physical, emotional, behavioural and social.
cards.quote: According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), reproductive health means a total well-being in all aspects of reproduction, i.e., physical, emotional, behavioural and social.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In which year were India's 'family planning' programmes initiated?
cards.back: These programmes called ‘family planning’ were initiated in 1951
cards.quote: These programmes called ‘family planning’ were initiated in 1951

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Under what popular name are the improved family planning programmes now run in India?
cards.back: reproduction-related areas are currently in operation under the popular name ‘Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes’.
cards.quote: reproduction-related areas are currently in operation under the popular name ‘Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes’.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the major tasks under the RCH programmes?
cards.back: Creating awareness among people about various reproduction related aspects and providing facilities and support for building up a reproductively healthy society are the major tasks under these programmes.
cards.quote: Creating awareness among people about various reproduction related aspects and providing facilities and support for building up a reproductively healthy society are the major tasks under these programmes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why should sex education be introduced in schools, according to NCERT?
cards.back: Introduction of sex education in schools should also be encouraged to provide right information to the young so as to discourage children from believing in myths and having misconceptions about sex-related aspects.
cards.quote: Introduction of sex education in schools should also be encouraged to provide right information to the young so as to discourage children from believing in myths and having misconceptions about sex-related aspects.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which procedure has a statutory ban for sex-determination, to check female foeticides?
cards.back: Statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex-determination to legally check increasing menace of female foeticides
cards.quote: Statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex-determination to legally check increasing menace of female foeticides

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is amniocentesis?
cards.back:
Amniocentesis
some of the amniotic fluid of the developing foetus is taken to analyse the fetal cells and dissolved substances.
cards.quote: some of the amniotic fluid of the developing foetus is taken to analyse the fetal cells and dissolved substances.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where was the oral contraceptive 'Saheli' developed?
cards.back: by scientists at Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI) in Lucknow, India
cards.quote: by scientists at Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI) in Lucknow, India

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the indicators of improved reproductive health of a society.
cards.back:
Better awareness about sex related matters
increased number of medically assisted deliveries and better post-natal care leading to decreased maternal and infant mortality rates
increased number of couples with small families
better detection and cure of STDs
overall increased medical facilities for all sex-related problems
cards.quote: Better awareness about sex related matters, increased number of medically assisted deliveries and better post-natal care leading to decreased maternal and infant mortality rates, increased number of couples with small families, better detection and cure of STDs and overall increased medical facilities for all sex-related problems, etc. all indicate improved reproductive health of the society.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the probable reasons for the explosive growth of population?
cards.back: A rapid decline in death rate, maternal mortality rate (MMR) and infant mortality rate (IMR) as well as an increase in number of people in reproducible age are probable reasons for this.
cards.quote: A rapid decline in death rate, maternal mortality rate (MMR) and infant mortality rate (IMR) as well as an increase in number of people in reproducible age are probable reasons for this.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which slogan shows a happy couple with two children in family planning advertisements?
cards.back: showing a happy couple with two children with a slogan Hum Do Hamare Do (we two, our two)
cards.quote: showing a happy couple with two children with a slogan Hum Do Hamare Do (we two, our two)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Statutory raising of marriageable age of the female to ____ years and that of males to ____ years
cards.back: Statutory raising of marriageable age of the female to 18 years and that of males to 21 years
cards.quote: Statutory raising of marriageable age of the female to 18 years and that of males to 21 years

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What qualities should an ideal contraceptive have?
cards.back: An ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible with no or least side-effects.
cards.quote: An ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible with no or least side-effects.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What should an ideal contraceptive not interfere with, besides being effective and reversible?
cards.back: effective and reversible with no or least side-effects. It also should in no way interfere with the sexual drive, desire and/or the sexual act of the user.
cards.quote: effective and reversible with no or least side-effects. It also should in no way interfere with the sexual drive, desire and/or the sexual act of the user.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of contraceptive methods (broad categories).
cards.back:
Natural/Traditional
Barrier
IUDs
Oral contraceptives
Injectables
Implants
Surgical methods
cards.quote: Natural/Traditional, Barrier, IUDs, Oral contraceptives, Injectables, Implants and Surgical methods

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: On what principle do natural methods of contraception work?
cards.back: Natural methods work on the principle of avoiding chances of ovum and sperms meeting.
cards.quote: Natural methods work on the principle of avoiding chances of ovum and sperms meeting.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which days of the menstrual cycle form the fertile period avoided in periodic abstinence?
cards.back: abstain from coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle when ovulation could be expected. As chances of fertilisation are very high during this period, it is called the fertile period.
cards.quote: abstain from coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle when ovulation could be expected. As chances of fertilisation are very high during this period, it is called the fertile period.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is withdrawal or coitus interruptus?
cards.back: Withdrawal or coitus interruptus is another method in which the male partner withdraws his penis from the vagina just before ejaculation
cards.quote: Withdrawal or coitus interruptus is another method in which the male partner withdraws his penis from the vagina just before ejaculation

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the lactational amenorrhea method?
cards.back: Lactational amenorrhea (absence of menstruation) method is based on the fact that ovulation and therefore the cycle do not occur during the period of intense lactation following parturition.
cards.quote: Lactational amenorrhea (absence of menstruation) method is based on the fact that ovulation and therefore the cycle do not occur during the period of intense lactation following parturition.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: For how long is the lactational amenorrhea method effective?
cards.back: this method has been reported to be effective only upto a maximum period of six months following parturition.
cards.quote: this method has been reported to be effective only upto a maximum period of six months following parturition.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are barrier methods of contraception?
cards.back: In barrier methods, ovum and sperms are prevented from physically meeting with the help of barriers.
cards.quote: In barrier methods, ovum and sperms are prevented from physically meeting with the help of barriers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are condoms?
cards.back: Condoms (Figure 3.1 a, b) are barriers made of thin rubber/latex sheath that are used to cover the penis in the male or vagina and cervix in the female, just before coitus so that the ejaculated semen would not enter into the female reproductive tract.
cards.quote: Condoms (Figure 3.1 a, b) are barriers made of thin rubber/latex sheath that are used to cover the penis in the male or vagina and cervix in the female, just before coitus so that the ejaculated semen would not enter into the female reproductive tract.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why has the use of condoms increased in recent years?
cards.back: Use of condoms has increased in recent years due to its additional benefit of protecting the user from contracting STIs and AIDS.
cards.quote: Use of condoms has increased in recent years due to its additional benefit of protecting the user from contracting STIs and AIDS.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults?
cards.back: Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults are also barriers made of rubber that are inserted into the female reproductive tract to cover the cervix during coitus.
cards.quote: Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults are also barriers made of rubber that are inserted into the female reproductive tract to cover the cervix during coitus.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are spermicidal creams, jellies and foams used along with barriers?
cards.back: foams are usually used alongwith these barriers to increase their contraceptive efficiency
cards.quote: foams are usually used alongwith these barriers to increase their contraceptive efficiency

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: By whom and where are Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs) inserted?
cards.back: Another effective and popular method is the use of Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs). These devices are inserted by doctors or expert nurses in the uterus through vagina.
cards.quote: Another effective and popular method is the use of Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs). These devices are inserted by doctors or expert nurses in the uterus through vagina.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs), with examples.
cards.back:
non-medicated IUDs (e.g., Lippes loop)
copper releasing IUDs (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375)
hormone releasing IUDs (Progestasert, LNG-20)
cards.quote: These Intra Uterine Devices are presently available as the non-medicated IUDs (e.g., Lippes loop), copper releasing IUDs (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and the hormone releasing IUDs (Progestasert, LNG-20)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How do IUDs, and the Cu ions they release, prevent conception?
cards.back: IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus and the Cu ions released suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms.
cards.quote: IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus and the Cu ions released suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What additional effect do hormone releasing IUDs have?
cards.back: make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to the sperms
cards.quote: make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to the sperms

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: For whom are IUDs ideal contraceptives?
cards.back: IUDs are ideal contraceptives for the females who want to delay pregnancy and/or space children.
cards.quote: IUDs are ideal contraceptives for the females who want to delay pregnancy and/or space children.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are contraceptive pills?
cards.back: Oral administration of small doses of either progestogens or progestogen–estrogen combinations is another contraceptive method used by the females.
cards.quote: Oral administration of small doses of either progestogens or progestogen–estrogen combinations is another contraceptive method used by the females.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Pills have to be taken daily for a period of ____ days
cards.back: Pills have to be taken daily for a period of 21 days
cards.quote: Pills have to be taken daily for a period of 21 days

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: After the 21-day course of pills, what is the gap before the course is repeated?
cards.back: After a gap of 7 days (during which menstruation occurs) it has to be repeated in the same pattern till the female desires to prevent conception.
cards.quote: After a gap of 7 days (during which menstruation occurs) it has to be repeated in the same pattern till the female desires to prevent conception.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How do contraceptive pills prevent conception?
cards.back: They inhibit ovulation and implantation as well as alter the quality of cervical mucus to prevent/retard entry of sperms.
cards.quote: They inhibit ovulation and implantation as well as alter the quality of cervical mucus to prevent/retard entry of sperms.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is Saheli and what is special about it?
cards.back: Saheli—the new oral contraceptive for the females contains a non-steroidal preparation. It is a ‘once a week’ pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value.
cards.quote: Saheli—the new oral contraceptive for the females contains a non-steroidal preparation. It is a ‘once a week’ pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value.

cards.subject: biology
