cards.front: What do injectables and implants contain, and how do they compare with pills?
cards.back: Progestogens alone or in combination with estrogen can also be used by females as injections or implants under the skin (Figure 3.3). Their mode of action is similar to that of pills and their effective periods are much longer.
cards.quote: Progestogens alone or in combination with estrogen can also be used by females as injections or implants under the skin (Figure 3.3). Their mode of action is similar to that of pills and their effective periods are much longer.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Within what time after coitus can progestogens or IUDs act as emergency contraceptives?
cards.back: Administration of progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus have been found to be very effective as emergency contraceptives as they could be used to avoid possible pregnancy due to rape or casual unprotected intercourse.
cards.quote: Administration of progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus have been found to be very effective as emergency contraceptives as they could be used to avoid possible pregnancy due to rape or casual unprotected intercourse.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are surgical methods of contraception also called, and for whom are they advised?
cards.back: Surgical methods, also called sterilisation, are generally advised for the male/female partner as a terminal method
cards.quote: Surgical methods, also called sterilisation, are generally advised for the male/female partner as a terminal method

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Surgical intervention blocks ____ and thereby prevent conception.
cards.back: Surgical intervention blocks gamete transport and thereby prevent conception.
cards.quote: Surgical intervention blocks gamete transport and thereby prevent conception.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Sterilisation procedure in the male is called ‘____’ and that in the female, ‘____’.
cards.back: Sterilisation procedure in the male is called ‘vasectomy’ and that in the female, ‘tubectomy’.
cards.quote: Sterilisation procedure in the male is called ‘vasectomy’ and that in the female, ‘tubectomy’.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is vasectomy?
cards.back: In vasectomy, a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum
cards.quote: In vasectomy, a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is tubectomy?
cards.back: in tubectomy, a small part of the fallopian tube is removed (Figure 3.4b) or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through vagina.
cards.quote: in tubectomy, a small part of the fallopian tube is removed (Figure 3.4b) or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through vagina.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How effective, and how reversible, are surgical methods of sterilisation?
cards.back: These techniques are highly effective but their reversibility is very poor.
cards.quote: These techniques are highly effective but their reversibility is very poor.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which possible ill-effects of contraceptives does NCERT mention?
cards.back: their possible ill-effects like nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular menstrual bleeding or even breast cancer, though not very significant, should not be totally ignored.
cards.quote: their possible ill-effects like nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular menstrual bleeding or even breast cancer, though not very significant, should not be totally ignored.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)?
cards.back: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is called medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) or induced abortion.
cards.quote: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is called medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) or induced abortion.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Government of India legalised MTP in ____ with some strict conditions to avoid its misuse.
cards.back: Government of India legalised MTP in 1971 with some strict conditions to avoid its misuse.
cards.quote: Government of India legalised MTP in 1971 with some strict conditions to avoid its misuse.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why was the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017 enacted?
cards.back: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2017 was enacted by the government of India with the intension of reducing the incidence of illegal abortion and consequent maternal mortality and morbidity.
cards.quote: The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2017 was enacted by the government of India with the intension of reducing the incidence of illegal abortion and consequent maternal mortality and morbidity.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Under the MTP Act, whose opinion is needed to terminate a pregnancy within the first 12 weeks?
cards.back: According to this Act, a pregnancy may be terminated on certain considered grounds within the first 12 weeks of pregnancy on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner.
cards.quote: According to this Act, a pregnancy may be terminated on certain considered grounds within the first 12 weeks of pregnancy on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Under the MTP Act, whose opinion is needed if the pregnancy has lasted 12 to 24 weeks?
cards.back: If the pregnancy has lasted more than 12 weeks, but fewer than 24 weeks, two registered medical practitioners must be of the opinion, formed in good faith, that the required ground exist.
cards.quote: If the pregnancy has lasted more than 12 weeks, but fewer than 24 weeks, two registered medical practitioners must be of the opinion, formed in good faith, that the required ground exist.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the grounds for termination of pregnancy under the MTP Act.
cards.back:
The continuation of the pregnancy would involve a risk to the life of the pregnant woman or of grave injury physical or mental health
There is a substantial risk that of the child were born, it would suffer from such physical or mental abnormalities as to be seriously handicapped
cards.quote: The grounds for such termination of pregnancies are: (i) The continuation of the pregnancy would involve a risk to the life of the pregnant woman or of grave injury physical or mental health; or (ii) There is a substantial risk that of the child were born, it would suffer from such physical or mental abnormalities as to be seriously handicapped.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is MTP needed?
cards.back: to get rid of unwanted pregnancies either due to casual unprotected intercourse or failure of the contraceptive used during coitus or rapes.
cards.quote: to get rid of unwanted pregnancies either due to casual unprotected intercourse or failure of the contraceptive used during coitus or rapes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In which cases is MTP essential even apart from unwanted pregnancy?
cards.back: MTPs are also essential in certain cases where continuation of the pregnancy could be harmful or even fatal either to the mother or to the foetus or both.
cards.quote: MTPs are also essential in certain cases where continuation of the pregnancy could be harmful or even fatal either to the mother or to the foetus or both.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: During which period is MTP considered relatively safe?
cards.back: MTPs are considered relatively safe during the first trimester, i.e., upto 12 weeks of pregnancy. Second trimester abortions are much more riskier.
cards.quote: MTPs are considered relatively safe during the first trimester, i.e., upto 12 weeks of pregnancy. Second trimester abortions are much more riskier.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What dangerous trend involving amniocentesis does NCERT point out?
cards.back: Another dangerous trend is the misuse of amniocentesis to determine the sex of the unborn child.
cards.quote: Another dangerous trend is the misuse of amniocentesis to determine the sex of the unborn child.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are sexually transmitted infections (STIs)?
cards.back: Infections or diseases which are transmitted through sexual intercourse are collectively called sexually transmitted infections (STI) or venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI).
cards.quote: Infections or diseases which are transmitted through sexual intercourse are collectively called sexually transmitted infections (STI) or venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the common STIs listed by NCERT.
cards.back:
Gonorrhoea
syphilis
genital herpes
chlamydiasis
genital warts
trichomoniasis
hepatitis-B
HIV leading to AIDS
cards.quote: Gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and of course, the most discussed infection in the recent years, HIV leading to AIDS are some of the common STIs.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How can hepatitis-B and HIV be transmitted other than by sexual contact?
cards.back: Some of these infections like hepatitis-B and HIV can also be transmitted by sharing of injection needles, surgical instruments, etc., with infected persons, transfusion of blood, or from an infected mother to the foetus too.
cards.quote: Some of these infections like hepatitis-B and HIV can also be transmitted by sharing of injection needles, surgical instruments, etc., with infected persons, transfusion of blood, or from an infected mother to the foetus too.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which STIs are not completely curable?
cards.back: Except for hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV infections, other diseases are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.
cards.quote: Except for hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV infections, other diseases are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are the early symptoms of most STIs?
cards.back: Early symptoms of most of these are minor and include itching, fluid discharge, slight pain, swellings, etc., in the genital region.
cards.quote: Early symptoms of most of these are minor and include itching, fluid discharge, slight pain, swellings, etc., in the genital region.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why may STIs in infected females remain undetected for long?
cards.back: Infected females may often be asymptomatic and hence, may remain undetected for long.
cards.quote: Infected females may often be asymptomatic and hence, may remain undetected for long.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the complications that STIs can lead to later.
cards.back:
pelvic inflammatory diseases (PID)
abortions
still births
ectopic pregnancies
infertility
cancer of the reproductive tract
cards.quote: This could lead to complications later, which include pelvic inflammatory diseases (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility or even cancer of the reproductive tract.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In which age group are STI incidences reported to be very high?
cards.back: their incidences are reported to be very high among persons in the age group of 15-24 years
cards.quote: their incidences are reported to be very high among persons in the age group of 15-24 years

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the simple principles for preventing STIs.
cards.back:
Avoid sex with unknown partners/multiple partners
Always try to use condoms during coitus
In case of doubt, one should go to a qualified doctor for early detection and get complete treatment if diagnosed with infection
cards.quote: (i) Avoid sex with unknown partners/multiple partners. (ii) Always try to use condoms during coitus. (iii) In case of doubt, one should go to a qualified doctor for early detection and get complete treatment if diagnosed with infection.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is infertility?
cards.back: Inability to conceive or produce children even after 2 years of unprotected sexual cohabitation is called infertility.
cards.quote: Inability to conceive or produce children even after 2 years of unprotected sexual cohabitation is called infertility.
cards.note: Infertility: no conception even after 2 years of unprotected sexual cohabitation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In India, who is usually blamed for a childless couple, and where does the problem often lie?
cards.back: In India, often the female is blamed for the couple being childless, but more often than not, the problem lies in the male partner.
cards.quote: In India, often the female is blamed for the couple being childless, but more often than not, the problem lies in the male partner.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What reasons can cause infertility?
cards.back: The reasons for this could be many—physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological.
cards.quote: The reasons for this could be many—physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are assisted reproductive technologies (ART)?
cards.back: However, where such corrections are not possible, the couples could be assisted to have children through certain special techniques commonly known as assisted reproductive technologies (ART).
cards.quote: However, where such corrections are not possible, the couples could be assisted to have children through certain special techniques commonly known as assisted reproductive technologies (ART).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is in vitro fertilisation (IVF) followed by embryo transfer (ET)?
cards.back: In vitro fertilisation (IVF—fertilisation outside the body in almost similar conditions as that in the body) followed by embryo transfer (ET) is one of such methods.
cards.quote: In vitro fertilisation (IVF—fertilisation outside the body in almost similar conditions as that in the body) followed by embryo transfer (ET) is one of such methods.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is done in the test tube baby programme?
cards.back: In this method, popularly known as test tube baby programme, ova from the wife/donor (female) and sperms from the husband/donor (male) are collected and are induced to form zygote under simulated conditions in the laboratory.
cards.quote: In this method, popularly known as test tube baby programme, ova from the wife/donor (female) and sperms from the husband/donor (male) are collected and are induced to form zygote under simulated conditions in the laboratory.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is ZIFT, and which stage is transferred in it?
cards.back: The zygote or early embryos (with upto 8 blastomeres) could then be transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT—zygote intra fallopian transfer)
cards.quote: The zygote or early embryos (with upto 8 blastomeres) could then be transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT—zygote intra fallopian transfer)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is IUT, and which embryos does it transfer?
cards.back: embryos with more than 8 blastomeres, into the uterus (IUT — intra uterine transfer), to complete its further development.
cards.quote: embryos with more than 8 blastomeres, into the uterus (IUT — intra uterine transfer), to complete its further development.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which embryos can be used for transfer to assist females who cannot conceive?
cards.back: Embryos formed by in-vivo fertilisation (fusion of gametes within the female) also could be used for such transfer to assist those females who cannot conceive.
cards.quote: Embryos formed by in-vivo fertilisation (fusion of gametes within the female) also could be used for such transfer to assist those females who cannot conceive.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is GIFT (gamete intra fallopian transfer)?
cards.back: Transfer of an ovum collected from a donor into the fallopian tube (GIFT — gamete intra fallopian transfer) of another female who cannot produce one, but can provide suitable environment for fertilisation and further development is another method attempted.
cards.quote: Transfer of an ovum collected from a donor into the fallopian tube (GIFT — gamete intra fallopian transfer) of another female who cannot produce one, but can provide suitable environment for fertilisation and further development is another method attempted.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is intra cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)?
cards.back: Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is another specialised procedure to form an embryo in the laboratory in which a sperm is directly injected into the ovum.
cards.quote: Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) is another specialised procedure to form an embryo in the laboratory in which a sperm is directly injected into the ovum.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which technique corrects infertility due to inability of the male to inseminate or very low sperm counts?
cards.back: Infertility cases either due to inability of the male partner to inseminate the female or due to very low sperm counts in the ejaculates, could be corrected by artificial insemination (AI) technique.
cards.quote: Infertility cases either due to inability of the male partner to inseminate the female or due to very low sperm counts in the ejaculates, could be corrected by artificial insemination (AI) technique.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is intra-uterine insemination (IUI)?
cards.back: In this technique, the semen collected either from the husband or a healthy donor is artificially introduced either into the vagina or into the uterus (IUI — intra-uterine insemination) of the female.
cards.quote: In this technique, the semen collected either from the husband or a healthy donor is artificially introduced either into the vagina or into the uterus (IUI — intra-uterine insemination) of the female.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: You would recollect that the ____ consists of a whorl of stamens representing the male reproductive organ
cards.back: You would recollect that the androecium consists of a whorl of stamens representing the male reproductive organ
cards.quote: You would recollect that the androecium consists of a whorl of stamens representing the male reproductive organ

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the two parts of a typical stamen.
cards.back:
filament
anther
cards.quote: the long and slender stalk called the filament, and the terminal generally bilobed structure called the anther

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed with each lobe having two theca, i.e., they are ____
cards.back: A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed with each lobe having two theca, i.e., they are dithecous
cards.quote: A typical angiosperm anther is bilobed with each lobe having two theca, i.e., they are dithecous

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many microsporangia does a typical anther have?
cards.back: four microsporangia
cards.quote: The anther is a four-sided (tetragonal) structure consisting of four microsporangia

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the four wall layers surrounding a microsporangium.
cards.back:
epidermis
endothecium
middle layers
tapetum
cards.quote: the epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and the tapetum

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the function of the outer three wall layers of a microsporangium?
cards.back: The outer three wall layers perform the function of protection and help in dehiscence of anther to release the pollen.
cards.quote: The outer three wall layers perform the function of protection and help in dehiscence of anther to release the pollen.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The innermost wall layer is the ____. It nourishes the developing pollen grains.
cards.back: The innermost wall layer is the tapetum. It nourishes the developing pollen grains.
cards.quote: The innermost wall layer is the tapetum. It nourishes the developing pollen grains.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is notable about the nuclei of tapetal cells?
cards.back: Cells of the tapetum possess dense cytoplasm and generally have more than one nucleus.
cards.quote: Cells of the tapetum possess dense cytoplasm and generally have more than one nucleus.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which tissue occupies the centre of each young microsporangium?
cards.back: the sporogenous tissue
cards.quote: cells called the sporogenous tissue occupies the centre of each microsporangium.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Microsporogenesis : As the anther develops, the cells of the sporogenous tissue undergo meiotic divisions to form ____.
cards.back: Microsporogenesis : As the anther develops, the cells of the sporogenous tissue undergo meiotic divisions to form microspore tetrads.
cards.quote: Microsporogenesis : As the anther develops, the cells of the sporogenous tissue undergo meiotic divisions to form microspore tetrads.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is microsporogenesis?
cards.back: The process of formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell (PMC) through meiosis is called microsporogenesis.
cards.quote: The process of formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell (PMC) through meiosis is called microsporogenesis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens to the microspores as the anthers mature and dehydrate?
cards.back: the microspores dissociate from each other and develop into pollen grains
cards.quote: As the anthers mature and dehydrate, the microspores dissociate from each other and develop into pollen grains

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The pollen grains represent the ____.
cards.back: The pollen grains represent the male gametophytes.
cards.quote: The pollen grains represent the male gametophytes.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the usual shape and size of pollen grains?
cards.back: Pollen grains are generally spherical measuring about 25-50 micrometers in diameter.
cards.quote: Pollen grains are generally spherical measuring about 25-50 micrometers in diameter.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The hard outer layer called the exine is made up of ____ which is one of the most resistant organic material known.
cards.back: The hard outer layer called the exine is made up of sporopollenin which is one of the most resistant organic material known.
cards.quote: The hard outer layer called the exine is made up of sporopollenin which is one of the most resistant organic material known.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Pollen grains are well-preserved as fossils because of the presence of ____.
cards.back: Pollen grains are well-preserved as fossils because of the presence of sporopollenin.
cards.quote: Pollen grains are well-preserved as fossils because of the presence of sporopollenin.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are germ pores of a pollen grain?
cards.back: Pollen grain exine has prominent apertures called germ pores where sporopollenin is absent.
cards.quote: Pollen grain exine has prominent apertures called germ pores where sporopollenin is absent.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the intine of a pollen grain?
cards.back: The inner wall of the pollen grain is called the intine. It is a thin and continuous layer made up of cellulose and pectin.
cards.quote: The inner wall of the pollen grain is called the intine. It is a thin and continuous layer made up of cellulose and pectin.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the two cells present in a mature pollen grain.
cards.back:
vegetative cell
generative cell
cards.quote: it contains two cells, the vegetative cell and generative cell

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Vegetative cell vs generative cell of a pollen grain: size, reserves and nucleus.
cards.back: The vegetative cell is bigger, has abundant food reserve and a large irregularly shaped nucleus. The generative cell is small and floats in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell. It is spindle shaped with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus.
cards.quote: The vegetative cell is bigger, has abundant food reserve and a large irregularly shaped nucleus. The generative cell is small and floats in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell. It is spindle shaped with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: At what stage are pollen grains shed in over 60 per cent of angiosperms?
cards.back: 2-celled stage
cards.quote: In over 60 per cent of angiosperms, pollen grains are shed at this 2-celled stage.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are the two male gametes formed in plants whose pollen is shed at the 3-celled stage?
cards.back: generative cell divides mitotically to give rise to the two male gametes
cards.quote: generative cell divides mitotically to give rise to the two male gametes before pollen grains are shed (3-celled stage)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which weed, a contaminant of imported wheat, causes pollen allergy in India?
cards.back: Parthenium or carrot grass
cards.quote: Parthenium or carrot grass that came into India as a contaminant with imported wheat, has become ubiquitous in occurrence and causes pollen allergy.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Within how many minutes do pollen grains of rice and wheat lose viability?
cards.back: 30 minutes
cards.quote: In some cereals such as rice and wheat, pollen grains lose viability within 30 minutes of their release

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In what can pollen grains be stored for years, to make pollen banks for crop breeding?
cards.back: liquid nitrogen
cards.quote: It is possible to store pollen grains of a large number of species for years in liquid nitrogen

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The ____ represents the female reproductive part of the flower.
cards.back: The gynoecium represents the female reproductive part of the flower.
cards.quote: The gynoecium represents the female reproductive part of the flower.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Types of multicarpellary gynoecium.
cards.back:
fused together (syncarpous)
free (apocarpous)
cards.quote: the pistils may be fused together (syncarpous) (Figure 1.7b) or may be free (apocarpous)

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the three parts of a pistil.
cards.back:
stigma
style
ovary
cards.quote: Each pistil has three parts (Figure 1.7a), the stigma, style and ovary.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The ____ serves as a landing platform for pollen grains.
cards.back: The stigma serves as a landing platform for pollen grains.
cards.quote: The stigma serves as a landing platform for pollen grains.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The ____ is the elongated slender part beneath the stigma.
cards.back: The style is the elongated slender part beneath the stigma.
cards.quote: The style is the elongated slender part beneath the stigma.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Arising from the placenta are the megasporangia, commonly called ____.
cards.back: Arising from the placenta are the megasporangia, commonly called ovules.
cards.quote: Arising from the placenta are the megasporangia, commonly called ovules.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The ovule is a small structure attached to the placenta by means of a stalk called ____.
cards.back: The ovule is a small structure attached to the placenta by means of a stalk called funicle.
cards.quote: The ovule is a small structure attached to the placenta by means of a stalk called funicle.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The body of the ovule fuses with funicle in the region called ____.
cards.back: The body of the ovule fuses with funicle in the region called hilum.
cards.quote: The body of the ovule fuses with funicle in the region called hilum.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Each ovule has one or two protective envelopes called ____.
cards.back: Each ovule has one or two protective envelopes called integuments.
cards.quote: Each ovule has one or two protective envelopes called integuments.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Integuments encircle the nucellus except at the tip where a small opening called the ____ is organised.
cards.back: Integuments encircle the nucellus except at the tip where a small opening called the micropyle is organised.
cards.quote: Integuments encircle the nucellus except at the tip where a small opening called the micropyle is organised.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Opposite the micropylar end, is the ____, representing the basal part of the ovule.
cards.back: Opposite the micropylar end, is the chalaza, representing the basal part of the ovule.
cards.quote: Opposite the micropylar end, is the chalaza, representing the basal part of the ovule.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Enclosed within the integuments is a mass of cells called the ____.
cards.back: Enclosed within the integuments is a mass of cells called the nucellus.
cards.quote: Enclosed within the integuments is a mass of cells called the nucellus.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In which tissue of the ovule is the embryo sac (female gametophyte) located?
cards.back: nucellus
cards.quote: nucellus is the embryo sac or female gametophyte.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is megasporogenesis?
cards.back: The process of formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell is called megasporogenesis.
cards.quote: The process of formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell is called megasporogenesis.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many megaspores are produced when the megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis?
cards.back: four megaspores
cards.quote: production of four megaspores

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is monosporic development of the embryo sac?
cards.back: This method of embryo sac formation from a single megaspore is termed monosporic development.
cards.quote: This method of embryo sac formation from a single megaspore is termed monosporic development.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Only the ____ develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac).
cards.back: Only the functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac).
cards.quote: Only the functional megaspore develops into the female gametophyte (embryo sac).

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Stages of embryo sac formation, in order.
cards.back:
2-nucleate
4-nucleate
8-nucleate
cards.quote: forming the 2-nucleate embryo sac. Two more sequential mitotic nuclear divisions result in the formation of the 4-nucleate and later the 8-nucleate stages of the embryo sac.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are the mitotic divisions that form the 8-nucleate embryo sac described?
cards.back: strictly free nuclear
cards.quote: these mitotic divisions are strictly free nuclear, that is, nuclear divisions are not followed immediately by cell wall formation.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: After the ____ stage, cell walls are laid down leading to the organisation of the typical female gametophyte or embryo sac.
cards.back: After the 8-nucleate stage, cell walls are laid down leading to the organisation of the typical female gametophyte or embryo sac.
cards.quote: After the 8-nucleate stage, cell walls are laid down leading to the organisation of the typical female gametophyte or embryo sac.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which two nuclei lie in the large central cell of the embryo sac?
cards.back: polar nuclei
cards.quote: the remaining two nuclei, called polar nuclei are situated below the egg apparatus in the large central cell

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Three cells are grouped together at the micropylar end and constitute the ____.
cards.back: Three cells are grouped together at the micropylar end and constitute the egg apparatus.
cards.quote: Three cells are grouped together at the micropylar end and constitute the egg apparatus.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the cells that make up the egg apparatus.
cards.back:
two synergids
one egg cell
cards.quote: The egg apparatus, in turn, consists of two synergids and one egg cell.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip called ____
cards.back: The synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip called filiform apparatus
cards.quote: The synergids have special cellular thickenings at the micropylar tip called filiform apparatus

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the role of the filiform apparatus?
cards.back: guiding the pollen tubes into the synergid
cards.quote: which play an important role in guiding the pollen tubes into the synergid

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Three cells are at the chalazal end and are called the ____.
cards.back: Three cells are at the chalazal end and are called the antipodals.
cards.quote: Three cells are at the chalazal end and are called the antipodals.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many cells does a mature angiosperm embryo sac have, though it is 8-nucleate?
cards.back: Thus, a typical angiosperm embryo sac, at maturity, though 8-nucleate is 7-celled.
cards.quote: Thus, a typical angiosperm embryo sac, at maturity, though 8-nucleate is 7-celled.

source.section: 1.2.2 The Pistil, Megasporangium (ovule) and Embryo sac

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is pollination?
cards.back: Transfer of pollen grains (shed from the anther) to the stigma of a pistil is termed pollination.
cards.quote: Transfer of pollen grains (shed from the anther) to the stigma of a pistil is termed pollination.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is autogamy?
cards.back: Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower
cards.quote: In this type, pollination is achieved within the same flower. Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of the same flower

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are chasmogamous flowers?
cards.back: flowers which are similar to flowers of other species with exposed anthers and stigma
cards.quote: chasmogamous flowers which are similar to flowers of other species with exposed anthers and stigma

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are cleistogamous flowers?
cards.back: flowers which do not open at all
cards.quote: cleistogamous flowers which do not open at all

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are cleistogamous flowers invariably autogamous?
cards.back: cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous as there is no chance of cross-pollen landing on the stigma.
cards.quote: Thus, cleistogamous flowers are invariably autogamous as there is no chance of cross-pollen landing on the stigma.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What advantage do cleistogamous flowers have when pollinators are absent?
cards.back: Cleistogamous flowers produce assured seed-set even in the absence of pollinators.
cards.quote: Cleistogamous flowers produce assured seed-set even in the absence of pollinators.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is geitonogamy?
cards.back: Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of another flower of the same plant.
cards.quote: Transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of another flower of the same plant.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How is geitonogamy classified functionally and genetically?
cards.back: Although geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination involving a pollinating agent, genetically it is similar to autogamy since the pollen grains come from the same plant.
cards.quote: Although geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination involving a pollinating agent, genetically it is similar to autogamy since the pollen grains come from the same plant.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is xenogamy?
cards.back: Transfer of pollen grains from anther to the stigma of a different plant
cards.quote: Transfer of pollen grains from anther to the stigma of a different plant

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which is the only type of pollination that brings genetically different pollen grains to the stigma?
cards.back: Xenogamy
cards.quote: Xenogamy — Transfer of pollen grains from anther to the stigma of a different plant (Figure 1.9b). This is the only type of pollination which during pollination brings genetically different types of pollen grains to the stigma.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the agents of pollination (abiotic and biotic).
cards.back:
abiotic (wind and water)
biotic (animals)
cards.quote: Plants use two abiotic (wind and water) and one biotic (animals) agents to achieve pollination.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which agents of pollination do the majority of plants use?
cards.back: biotic agents
cards.quote: Majority of plants use biotic agents for pollination.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why do flowers pollinated by wind and water produce enormous amounts of pollen?
cards.back: To compensate for this uncertainties and associated loss of pollen grains, the flowers produce enormous amount of pollen when compared to the number of ovules available for pollination.
cards.quote: To compensate for this uncertainties and associated loss of pollen grains, the flowers produce enormous amount of pollen when compared to the number of ovules available for pollination.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which abiotic agent is more common in pollination?
cards.back: wind
cards.quote: Pollination by wind is more common amongst abiotic pollinations.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What kind of pollen grains do wind-pollinated flowers have?
cards.back: light and non-sticky
cards.quote: Wind pollination also requires that the pollen grains are light and non-sticky so that they can be transported in wind currents.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What kind of stigma do wind-pollinated flowers have?
cards.back: large often-feathery stigma
cards.quote: large often-feathery stigma to easily trap air-borne pollen grains

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How many ovules do wind-pollinated flowers often have in each ovary?
cards.back: a single ovule
cards.quote: Wind-pollinated flowers often have a single ovule in each ovary and numerous flowers packed into an inflorescence

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Pollination by water is quite rare in flowering plants and is limited to about ____ genera, mostly monocotyledons.
cards.back: Pollination by water is quite rare in flowering plants and is limited to about 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons.
cards.quote: Pollination by water is quite rare in flowering plants and is limited to about 30 genera, mostly monocotyledons.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name water-pollinated plants (two freshwater, one marine).
cards.back: Vallisneria and Hydrilla which grow in fresh water and several marine sea-grasses such as Zostera
cards.quote: Some examples of water pollinated plants are Vallisneria and Hydrilla which grow in fresh water and several marine sea-grasses such as Zostera.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In most of the water-pollinated species, pollen grains are protected from wetting by a ____.
cards.back: In most of the water-pollinated species, pollen grains are protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering.
cards.quote: In most of the water-pollinated species, pollen grains are protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Among the animals, insects, particularly ____ are the dominant biotic pollinating agents.
cards.back: Among the animals, insects, particularly bees are the dominant biotic pollinating agents.
cards.quote: Among the animals, insects, particularly bees are the dominant biotic pollinating agents.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the common animal pollinating agents.
cards.back:
Bees
butterflies
flies
beetles
wasps
ants
moths
birds (sunbirds and humming birds)
bats
cards.quote: Bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, ants, moths, birds (sunbirds and humming birds) and bats

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are majority of insect-pollinated flowers like?
cards.back: large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar
cards.quote: Majority of insect-pollinated flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The flowers pollinated by flies and beetles secrete ____ to attract these animals.
cards.back: The flowers pollinated by flies and beetles secrete foul odours to attract these animals.
cards.quote: The flowers pollinated by flies and beetles secrete foul odours to attract these animals.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: ____ are the usual floral rewards.
cards.back: Nectar and pollen grains are the usual floral rewards.
cards.quote: Nectar and pollen grains are the usual floral rewards.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the Yucca moth do in the flower, and how does the flower benefit?
cards.back: The moth deposits its eggs in the locule of the ovary and the flower, in turn, gets pollinated by the moth.
cards.quote: The moth deposits its eggs in the locule of the ovary and the flower, in turn, gets pollinated by the moth.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are pollen/nectar robbers?
cards.back: Many insects may consume pollen or the nectar without bringing about pollination. Such floral visitors are referred to as pollen/nectar robbers.
cards.quote: Many insects may consume pollen or the nectar without bringing about pollination. Such floral visitors are referred to as pollen/nectar robbers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Continued self-pollination result in ____.
cards.back: Continued self-pollination result in inbreeding depression.
cards.quote: Continued self-pollination result in inbreeding depression.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does non-synchrony of pollen release and stigma receptivity prevent autogamy?
cards.back: Either the pollen is released before the stigma becomes receptive or stigma becomes receptive much before the release of pollen.
cards.quote: Either the pollen is released before the stigma becomes receptive or stigma becomes receptive much before the release of pollen.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does placing the anther and stigma at different positions prevent autogamy?
cards.back: In some other species, the anther and stigma are placed at different positions so that the pollen cannot come in contact with the stigma of the same flower.
cards.quote: In some other species, the anther and stigma are placed at different positions so that the pollen cannot come in contact with the stigma of the same flower.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is self-incompatibility, the third device to prevent inbreeding?
cards.back: The third device to prevent inbreeding is self-incompatibility. This is a genetic mechanism and prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.
cards.quote: The third device to prevent inbreeding is self-incompatibility. This is a genetic mechanism and prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the monoecious condition and what does it prevent?
cards.back: If both male and female flowers are present on the same plant such as castor and maize (monoecious), it prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy.
cards.quote: If both male and female flowers are present on the same plant such as castor and maize (monoecious), it prevents autogamy but not geitonogamy.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is dioecy and what does it prevent?
cards.back: In several species such as papaya, male and female flowers are present on different plants, that is each plant is either male or female (dioecy). This condition prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.
cards.quote: In several species such as papaya, male and female flowers are present on different plants, that is each plant is either male or female (dioecy). This condition prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the devices that discourage self-pollination and encourage cross-pollination.
cards.back:
pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised
the anther and stigma are placed at different positions
self-incompatibility
the production of unisexual flowers
cards.quote: pollen release and stigma receptivity are not synchronised. Either the pollen is released before the stigma becomes receptive or stigma becomes receptive much before the release of pollen. In some other species, the anther and stigma are placed at different positions so that the pollen cannot come in contact with the stigma of the same flower. Both these devices prevent autogamy. The third device to prevent inbreeding is self-incompatibility. This is a genetic mechanism and prevents self-pollen (from the same flower or other flowers of the same plant) from fertilising the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in the pistil. Another device to prevent self-pollination is the production of unisexual flowers.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What ability of the pistil decides whether pollen is accepted or rejected?
cards.back: to recognise the pollen, whether it is of the right type (compatible) or of the wrong type (incompatible)
cards.quote: The pistil has the ability to recognise the pollen, whether it is of the right type (compatible) or of the wrong type (incompatible).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does the pistil reject pollen of the wrong type?
cards.back: by preventing pollen germination on the stigma or the pollen tube growth in the style
cards.quote: If the pollen is of the wrong type, the pistil rejects the pollen by preventing pollen germination on the stigma or the pollen tube growth in the style

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What decides the acceptance or rejection of pollen by the pistil?
cards.back: a continuous dialogue between pollen grain and the pistil
cards.quote: The ability of the pistil to recognise the pollen followed by its acceptance or rejection is the result of a continuous dialogue between pollen grain and the pistil.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Through what does the pollen grain produce a pollen tube on the stigma?
cards.back: one of the germ pores
cards.quote: following compatible pollination, the pollen grain germinates on the stigma to produce a pollen tube through one of the germ pores

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Through which tissues does the pollen tube grow to reach the ovary?
cards.back: the tissues of the stigma and style
cards.quote: Pollen tube grows through the tissues of the stigma and style and reaches the ovary

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: When are the two male gametes formed in plants that shed 2-celled pollen?
cards.back: In such plants, the generative cell divides and forms the two male gametes during the growth of pollen tube in the stigma.
cards.quote: In such plants, the generative cell divides and forms the two male gametes during the growth of pollen tube in the stigma.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Path of the pollen tube into the embryo sac, in order.
cards.back:
the ovary
the micropyle
one of the synergids through the filiform apparatus
cards.quote: Pollen tube, after reaching the ovary, enters the ovule through the micropyle and then enters one of the synergids through the filiform apparatus

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is pollen-pistil interaction?
cards.back: All these events—from pollen deposition on the stigma until pollen tubes enter the ovule—are together referred to as pollen-pistil interaction.
cards.quote: All these events—from pollen deposition on the stigma until pollen tubes enter the ovule—are together referred to as pollen-pistil interaction.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What kind of process is pollen-pistil interaction?
cards.back: a dynamic process involving pollen recognition followed by promotion or inhibition of the pollen
cards.quote: pollen-pistil interaction is a dynamic process involving pollen recognition followed by promotion or inhibition of the pollen

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which two techniques protect the stigma from unwanted pollen in artificial hybridisation?
cards.back: emasculation and bagging
cards.quote: This is achieved by emasculation and bagging techniques.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is emasculation?
cards.back: If the female parent bears bisexual flowers, removal of anthers from the flower bud before the anther dehisces using a pair of forceps is necessary. This step is referred to as emasculation.
cards.quote: If the female parent bears bisexual flowers, removal of anthers from the flower bud before the anther dehisces using a pair of forceps is necessary. This step is referred to as emasculation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is bagging?
cards.back: Emasculated flowers have to be covered with a bag of suitable size, generally made up of butter paper, to prevent contamination of its stigma with unwanted pollen. This process is called bagging.
cards.quote: Emasculated flowers have to be covered with a bag of suitable size, generally made up of butter paper, to prevent contamination of its stigma with unwanted pollen. This process is called bagging.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is emasculation not needed if the female parent bears unisexual flowers?
cards.back: If the female parent produces unisexual flowers, there is no need for emasculation. The female flower buds are bagged before the flowers open.
cards.quote: If the female parent produces unisexual flowers, there is no need for emasculation. The female flower buds are bagged before the flowers open.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is syngamy, and what does it form?
cards.back: One of the male gametes moves towards the egg cell and fuses with its nucleus thus completing the syngamy. This results in the formation of a diploid cell, the zygote.
cards.quote: One of the male gametes moves towards the egg cell and fuses with its nucleus thus completing the syngamy. This results in the formation of a diploid cell, the zygote.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the second male gamete form on fusing with the two polar nuclei?
cards.back: a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)
cards.quote: The other male gamete moves towards the two polar nuclei located in the central cell and fuses with them to produce a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN)

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is triple fusion?
cards.back: The other male gamete moves towards the two polar nuclei located in the central cell and fuses with them to produce a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) (Figure 1.13a). As this involves the fusion of three haploid nuclei it is termed triple fusion.
cards.quote: The other male gamete moves towards the two polar nuclei located in the central cell and fuses with them to produce a triploid primary endosperm nucleus (PEN) (Figure 1.13a). As this involves the fusion of three haploid nuclei it is termed triple fusion.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is double fertilisation?
cards.back: Since two types of fusions, syngamy and triple fusion take place in an embryo sac the phenomenon is termed double fertilisation, an event unique to flowering plants.
cards.quote: Since two types of fusions, syngamy and triple fusion take place in an embryo sac the phenomenon is termed double fertilisation, an event unique to flowering plants.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do the primary endosperm cell and the zygote develop into?
cards.back: The central cell after triple fusion becomes the primary endosperm cell (PEC) and develops into the endosperm while the zygote develops into an embryo.
cards.quote: The central cell after triple fusion becomes the primary endosperm cell (PEC) and develops into the endosperm while the zygote develops into an embryo.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which develops first, endosperm or embryo?
cards.back: Endosperm development precedes embryo development.
cards.quote: Endosperm development precedes embryo development.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the endosperm tissue used for?
cards.back: The cells of this tissue are filled with reserve food materials and are used for the nutrition of the developing embryo.
cards.quote: The cells of this tissue are filled with reserve food materials and are used for the nutrition of the developing embryo.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is free-nuclear endosperm?
cards.back: In the most common type of endosperm development, the PEN undergoes successive nuclear divisions to give rise to free nuclei. This stage of endosperm development is called free-nuclear endosperm.
cards.quote: In the most common type of endosperm development, the PEN undergoes successive nuclear divisions to give rise to free nuclei. This stage of endosperm development is called free-nuclear endosperm.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are tender coconut water and the white kernel of coconut?
cards.back: The coconut water from tender coconut that you are familiar with, is nothing but free-nuclear endosperm (made up of thousands of nuclei) and the surrounding white kernel is the cellular endosperm.
cards.quote: The coconut water from tender coconut that you are familiar with, is nothing but free-nuclear endosperm (made up of thousands of nuclei) and the surrounding white kernel is the cellular endosperm.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which seeds does NCERT give as examples of endosperm consumed versus persisting in the mature seed?
cards.back: Endosperm may either be completely consumed by the developing embryo (e.g., pea, groundnut, beans) before seed maturation or it may persist in the mature seed (e.g. castor and coconut) and be used up during seed germination.
cards.quote: Endosperm may either be completely consumed by the developing embryo (e.g., pea, groundnut, beans) before seed maturation or it may persist in the mature seed (e.g. castor and coconut) and be used up during seed germination.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Where does the embryo develop in the embryo sac?
cards.back: Embryo develops at the micropylar end of the embryo sac where the zygote is situated.
cards.quote: Embryo develops at the micropylar end of the embryo sac where the zygote is situated.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why do most zygotes divide only after some endosperm is formed?
cards.back: Most zygotes divide only after certain amount of endosperm is formed. This is an adaptation to provide assured nutrition to the developing embryo.
cards.quote: Most zygotes divide only after certain amount of endosperm is formed. This is an adaptation to provide assured nutrition to the developing embryo.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Though the seeds differ greatly, the early stages of embryo development (____) are similar in both monocotyledons and dicotyledons.
cards.back: Though the seeds differ greatly, the early stages of embryo development (embryogeny) are similar in both monocotyledons and dicotyledons.
cards.quote: Though the seeds differ greatly, the early stages of embryo development (embryogeny) are similar in both monocotyledons and dicotyledons.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Stages of embryogeny in a dicot, in order.
cards.back:
proembryo
globular
heart-shaped
mature embryo
cards.quote: The zygote gives rise to the proembryo and subsequently to the globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the parts of a typical dicotyledonous embryo.
cards.back:
an embryonal axis
two cotyledons
cards.quote: A typical dicotyledonous embryo (Figure 1.14a), consists of an embryonal axis and two cotyledons.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Epicotyl vs hypocotyl of a dicot embryo: position and what each ends in.
cards.back: The portion of embryonal axis above the level of cotyledons is the epicotyl, which terminates with the plumule or stem tip. The cylindrical portion below the level of cotyledons is hypocotyl that terminates at its lower end in the radicle or root tip.
cards.quote: The portion of embryonal axis above the level of cotyledons is the epicotyl, which terminates with the plumule or stem tip. The cylindrical portion below the level of cotyledons is hypocotyl that terminates at its lower end in the radicle or root tip.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Embryos of monocotyledons (Figure 1.14 b) possess only ____.
cards.back: Embryos of monocotyledons (Figure 1.14 b) possess only one cotyledon.
cards.quote: Embryos of monocotyledons (Figure 1.14 b) possess only one cotyledon.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In the grass family the cotyledon is called ____ that is situated towards one side (lateral) of the embryonal axis.
cards.back: In the grass family the cotyledon is called scutellum that is situated towards one side (lateral) of the embryonal axis.
cards.quote: In the grass family the cotyledon is called scutellum that is situated towards one side (lateral) of the embryonal axis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the undifferentiated sheath enclosing the radicle and root cap of a monocot embryo called?
cards.back: coleorrhiza
cards.quote: an undifferentiated sheath called coleorrhiza

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Epicotyl has a shoot apex and a few leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure, the ____.
cards.back: Epicotyl has a shoot apex and a few leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure, the coleoptile.
cards.quote: Epicotyl has a shoot apex and a few leaf primordia enclosed in a hollow foliar structure, the coleoptile.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In angiosperms, the ____ is the final product of sexual reproduction.
cards.back: In angiosperms, the seed is the final product of sexual reproduction.
cards.quote: In angiosperms, the seed is the final product of sexual reproduction.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is a seed often described as?
cards.back: a fertilised ovule
cards.quote: It is often described as a fertilised ovule.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Name the parts a seed typically consists of.
cards.back:
seed coat(s)
cotyledon(s)
an embryo axis
cards.quote: A seed typically consists of seed coat(s), cotyledon(s) and an embryo axis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Non-albuminous vs albuminous seeds: residual endosperm and examples.
cards.back: Non-albuminous seeds have no residual endosperm as it is completely consumed during embryo development (e.g., pea, groundnut). Albuminous seeds retain a part of endosperm as it is not completely used up during embryo development (e.g., wheat, maize, barley, castor).
cards.quote: Non-albuminous seeds have no residual endosperm as it is completely consumed during embryo development (e.g., pea, groundnut). Albuminous seeds retain a part of endosperm as it is not completely used up during embryo development (e.g., wheat, maize, barley, castor).

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is perisperm?
cards.back: Occasionally, in some seeds such as black pepper and beet, remnants of nucellus are also persistent. This residual, persistent nucellus is the perisperm.
cards.quote: Occasionally, in some seeds such as black pepper and beet, remnants of nucellus are also persistent. This residual, persistent nucellus is the perisperm.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do the integuments of ovules become in the seed?
cards.back: tough protective seed coats
cards.quote: Integuments of ovules harden as tough protective seed coats

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is the function of the micropyle that remains in the seed coat?
cards.back: The micropyle remains as a small pore in the seed coat. This facilitates entry of oxygen and water into the seed during germination.
cards.quote: The micropyle remains as a small pore in the seed coat. This facilitates entry of oxygen and water into the seed during germination.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The embryo may enter a state of inactivity called ____
cards.back: The embryo may enter a state of inactivity called dormancy
cards.quote: The embryo may enter a state of inactivity called dormancy

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: The wall of the ovary develops into the wall of fruit called ____.
cards.back: The wall of the ovary develops into the wall of fruit called pericarp.
cards.quote: The wall of the ovary develops into the wall of fruit called pericarp.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are false fruits?
cards.back: In most plants, by the time the fruit develops from the ovary, other floral parts degenerate and fall off. However, in a few species such as apple, strawberry, cashew, etc., the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation. Such fruits are called false fruits
cards.quote: In most plants, by the time the fruit develops from the ovary, other floral parts degenerate and fall off. However, in a few species such as apple, strawberry, cashew, etc., the thalamus also contributes to fruit formation. Such fruits are called false fruits

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are true fruits?
cards.back: Most fruits however develop only from the ovary and are called true fruits.
cards.quote: Most fruits however develop only from the ovary and are called true fruits.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What are parthenocarpic fruits? Give an example.
cards.back: Although in most of the species, fruits are the results of fertilisation, there are a few species in which fruits develop without fertilisation. Such fruits are called parthenocarpic fruits. Banana is one such example.
cards.quote: Although in most of the species, fruits are the results of fertilisation, there are a few species in which fruits develop without fertilisation. Such fruits are called parthenocarpic fruits. Banana is one such example.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How can parthenocarpy be induced?
cards.back: through the application of growth hormones
cards.quote: be induced through the application of growth hormones and such fruits are seedless

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is seed formation more dependable in angiosperms?
cards.back: reproductive processes such as pollination and fertilisation are independent of water
cards.quote: since reproductive processes such as pollination and fertilisation are independent of water, seed formation is more dependable

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What adaptive advantage do seeds have for spreading the species?
cards.back: better adaptive strategies for dispersal to new habitats
cards.quote: Also seeds have better adaptive strategies for dispersal to new habitats and help the species

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How are young seedlings nourished until they can photosynthesise?
cards.back: As they have sufficient food reserves, young seedlings are nourished until they are capable of photosynthesis on their own.
cards.quote: As they have sufficient food reserves, young seedlings are nourished until they are capable of photosynthesis on their own.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What does the hard seed coat provide to the young embryo?
cards.back: protection
cards.quote: The hard seed coat provides protection to the young embryo.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why do seeds lead to variations?
cards.back: Being products of sexual reproduction, they generate new genetic combinations leading to variations.
cards.quote: Being products of sexual reproduction, they generate new genetic combinations leading to variations.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why are dehydration and dormancy of mature seeds crucial for agriculture?
cards.back: Dehydration and dormancy of mature seeds are crucial for storage of seeds which can be used as food throughout the year and also to raise crop in the next season.
cards.quote: Dehydration and dormancy of mature seeds are crucial for storage of seeds which can be used as food throughout the year and also to raise crop in the next season.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Which seed germinated and flowered after an estimated 10,000 years of dormancy?
cards.back: a lupine, Lupinus arcticus
cards.quote: The oldest is that of a lupine, Lupinus arcticus excavated from Arctic Tundra. The seed germinated and flowered after an estimated record of 10,000 years of dormancy.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is apomixis?
cards.back: Thus, apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.
cards.quote: Thus, apomixis is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In which flowering plants has apomixis evolved as a mechanism to produce seeds without fertilisation?
cards.back: some species of Asteraceae and grasses
cards.quote: plants such as some species of Asteraceae and grasses, have evolved a special mechanism, to produce seeds without fertilisation, called apomixis.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: How does the embryo form in apomixis when a diploid egg cell is involved?
cards.back: In some species, the diploid egg cell is formed without reduction division and develops into the embryo without fertilisation.
cards.quote: In some species, the diploid egg cell is formed without reduction division and develops into the embryo without fertilisation.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: In Citrus and Mango apomixis, which cells develop into the embryos?
cards.back: the nucellar cells
cards.quote: varieties some of the nucellar cells surrounding the embryo sac start dividing, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into the embryos.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What is polyembryony?
cards.back: Occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed is referred to as polyembryony.
cards.quote: Occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed is referred to as polyembryony.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: Why is apomixis important in the hybrid seed industry?
cards.back: If these hybrids are made into apomicts, there is no segregation of characters in the hybrid progeny. Then the farmers can keep on using the hybrid seeds to raise new crop year after year and he does not have to buy hybrid seeds every year.
cards.quote: If these hybrids are made into apomicts, there is no segregation of characters in the hybrid progeny. Then the farmers can keep on using the hybrid seeds to raise new crop year after year and he does not have to buy hybrid seeds every year.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: A typical anther is bilobed, dithecous and ____.
cards.back: A typical anther is bilobed, dithecous and tetrasporangiate.
cards.quote: A typical anther is bilobed, dithecous and tetrasporangiate.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: A cell of the ____, the megaspore mother cell divides meiotically
cards.back: A cell of the archesporium, the megaspore mother cell divides meiotically
cards.quote: A cell of the archesporium, the megaspore mother cell divides meiotically

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What do the ovary and the ovules develop into after fertilisation?
cards.back: After fertilisation, ovary develops into fruit and ovules develop into seeds.
cards.quote: After fertilisation, ovary develops into fruit and ovules develop into seeds.

cards.subject: biology
cards.front: What happens to the free-nuclear endosperm after the nuclear divisions?
cards.back: Subsequently cell wall formation occurs and the endosperm becomes cellular.
cards.quote: Subsequently cell wall formation occurs and the endosperm becomes cellular.
